<p>Trump announced his candidacy in June 2015.<sup id="cite_ref-165" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-165">&#91;164&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-166" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-166">&#91;165&#93;</a></sup> <a href="/wiki/Donald_Trump_2016_presidential_campaign" title="Donald Trump 2016 presidential campaign">His campaign</a> was initially not taken seriously by political analysts, but he quickly rose to the top of opinion polls.<sup id="cite_ref-167" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-167">&#91;166&#93;</a></sup> He became the front-runner in March 2016<sup id="cite_ref-168" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-168">&#91;167&#93;</a></sup> and was declared the presumptive Republican nominee in May.<sup id="cite_ref-169" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-169">&#91;168&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p><a href="/wiki/Hillary_Clinton" title="Hillary Clinton">Hillary Clinton</a> led Trump in <a href="/wiki/Nationwide_opinion_polling_for_the_United_States_presidential_election,_2016" class="mw-redirect" title="Nationwide opinion polling for the United States presidential election, 2016">national polling averages</a> throughout the campaign, but, in early July, her lead narrowed.<sup id="cite_ref-170" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-170">&#91;169&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-171" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-171">&#91;170&#93;</a></sup> In mid-July Trump selected Indiana governor <a href="/wiki/Mike_Pence" title="Mike Pence">Mike Pence</a> as his vice presidential running mate,<sup id="cite_ref-172" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-172">&#91;171&#93;</a></sup> and the two were officially nominated at the <a href="/wiki/2016_Republican_National_Convention" title="2016 Republican National Convention">2016 Republican National Convention</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-173" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-173">&#91;172&#93;</a></sup>
Trump and Clinton faced off in <a href="/wiki/2016_United_States_presidential_debates" title="2016 United States presidential debates">three presidential debates</a> in September and October 2016. Trump twice refused to say whether he would accept the result of the election.<sup id="cite_ref-174" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-174">&#91;173&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h5><span class="mw-headline" id="Campaign_rhetoric_and_political_positions">Campaign rhetoric and political positions</span></h5>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1033289096"><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Main article: <a href="/wiki/Political_positions_of_Donald_Trump" title="Political positions of Donald Trump">Political positions of Donald Trump</a></div>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1033289096"><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Further information: <a href="/wiki/2016_United_States_presidential_debates" title="2016 United States presidential debates">2016 United States presidential debates</a></div>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1033289096"><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">See also: <a href="/wiki/Foreign_policy_of_Donald_Trump_during_the_2016_presidential_election" title="Foreign policy of Donald Trump during the 2016 presidential election">Foreign policy of Donald Trump during the 2016 presidential election</a> and <a href="/wiki/Trumpism" title="Trumpism">Trumpism</a></div>
<p>Trump's political positions and rhetoric were <a href="/wiki/Right-wing_populism" title="Right-wing populism">right-wing populist</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-175" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-175">&#91;174&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-176" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-176">&#91;175&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-177" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-177">&#91;176&#93;</a></sup> <i><a href="/wiki/Politico" title="Politico">Politico</a></i> described them as "eclectic, improvisational and often contradictory", quoting a health-care policy expert at the <a href="/wiki/American_Enterprise_Institute" title="American Enterprise Institute">American Enterprise Institute</a> as saying that his political positions were "a total random assortment of whatever plays publicly".<sup id="cite_ref-178" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-178">&#91;177&#93;</a></sup> <a href="/wiki/NBC_News" title="NBC News">NBC News</a> counted "141 distinct shifts on 23 major issues" during his campaign.<sup id="cite_ref-179" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-179">&#91;178&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>Trump questioned the need for <a href="/wiki/NATO" title="NATO">NATO</a> and espoused views that were described as isolationist, <a href="/wiki/Non-interventionism" title="Non-interventionism">non-interventionist</a>, and protectionist.<sup id="cite_ref-180" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-180">&#91;179&#93;</a></sup> His campaign platform emphasized renegotiating <a href="/wiki/China%E2%80%93United_States_relations" title="China–United States relations">U.S.–China relations</a> and free trade agreements such as <a href="/wiki/NAFTA" class="mw-redirect" title="NAFTA">NAFTA</a> and the <a href="/wiki/Trans-Pacific_Partnership" title="Trans-Pacific Partnership">Trans-Pacific Partnership</a>, strongly enforcing immigration laws, and building <a href="/wiki/Trump_wall" title="Trump wall">a new wall</a> along the <a href="/wiki/U.S.%E2%80%93Mexico_border" class="mw-redirect" title="U.S.–Mexico border">U.S.–Mexico border</a>. Other campaign positions included pursuing <a href="/wiki/Energy_independence" title="Energy independence">energy independence</a> while opposing climate change regulations such as the <a href="/wiki/Clean_Power_Plan" title="Clean Power Plan">Clean Power Plan</a> and the <a href="/wiki/Paris_Agreement" title="Paris Agreement">Paris Agreement</a>, modernizing and expediting <a href="/wiki/United_States_Department_of_Veterans_Affairs#Veterans_Benefits_Administration" title="United States Department of Veterans Affairs">services for veterans</a>, repealing and replacing the <a href="/wiki/Affordable_Care_Act" title="Affordable Care Act">Affordable Care Act</a>, abolishing <a href="/wiki/Common_Core" title="Common Core">Common Core</a> education standards, <a href="/wiki/Infrastructure-based_development" title="Infrastructure-based development">investing in infrastructure</a>, simplifying the <a href="/wiki/Internal_Revenue_Code" title="Internal Revenue Code">tax code</a> while reducing taxes for all economic classes, and imposing <a href="/wiki/Tariff" title="Tariff">tariffs</a> on imports by companies that offshore jobs. He advocated a largely <a href="/wiki/United_States_non-interventionism" title="United States non-interventionism">non-interventionist</a> approach to foreign policy while increasing military spending, extreme vetting or banning immigrants from Muslim-majority countries<sup id="cite_ref-181" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-181">&#91;180&#93;</a></sup> to pre-empt domestic <a href="/wiki/Islamic_terrorism" title="Islamic terrorism">Islamic terrorism</a>, and aggressive military action against the <a href="/wiki/Islamic_State_of_Iraq_and_the_Levant" class="mw-redirect" title="Islamic State of Iraq and the Levant">Islamic State of Iraq and the Levant</a>. He described NATO as "obsolete".<sup id="cite_ref-182" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-182">&#91;181&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-183" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-183">&#91;182&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>Trump helped bring <a href="/wiki/Far-right_politics" title="Far-right politics">far-right</a> fringe ideas, beliefs, and organizations into the mainstream.<sup id="cite_ref-184" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-184">&#91;183&#93;</a></sup> Trump was slow to disavow an endorsement from <a href="/wiki/David_Duke" title="David Duke">David Duke</a> after he was questioned about it during a <i>CNN</i> interview on February 28, 2016.<sup id="cite_ref-185" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-185">&#91;184&#93;</a></sup> Duke enthusiastically supported Trump and said he and like-minded people voted for Trump because of his promises to "take our country back".<sup id="cite_ref-186" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-186">&#91;185&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-187" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-187">&#91;186&#93;</a></sup> In August 2016, Trump hired <a href="/wiki/Steve_Bannon" title="Steve Bannon">Steve Bannon</a>, the executive chairman of <i><a href="/wiki/Breitbart_News" title="Breitbart News">Breitbart News</a></i>—described by Bannon as "the platform for the alt-right"—as his campaign CEO.<sup id="cite_ref-188" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-188">&#91;187&#93;</a></sup> The <a href="/wiki/Alt-right" title="Alt-right">alt-right</a> movement coalesced around and supported Trump's candidacy, due in part to its <a href="/wiki/Opposition_to_multiculturalism" class="mw-redirect" title="Opposition to multiculturalism">opposition to multiculturalism</a> and <a href="/wiki/Opposition_to_immigration" title="Opposition to immigration">immigration</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-189" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-189">&#91;188&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-190" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-190">&#91;189&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-191" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-191">&#91;190&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h5><span class="mw-headline" id="Financial_disclosures">Financial disclosures</span></h5>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1033289096"><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Further information: <a href="/wiki/Tax_returns_of_Donald_Trump" title="Tax returns of Donald Trump">Tax returns of Donald Trump</a></div>
<p>Trump's FEC-required reports listed assets above $1.4&#160;billion and outstanding debts of at least $315&#160;million.<sup id="cite_ref-disclosure_35-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-disclosure-35">&#91;34&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-192" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-192">&#91;191&#93;</a></sup>
Trump did not release <a href="/wiki/Donald_Trump%27s_tax_returns" class="mw-redirect" title="Donald Trump&#39;s tax returns">his tax returns</a>, contrary to the practice of every major candidate since 1976 and his promises in 2014 and 2015 to do so if he ran for office.<sup id="cite_ref-193" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-193">&#91;192&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-194" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-194">&#91;193&#93;</a></sup> He said his tax returns were being <a href="/wiki/Income_tax_audit" title="Income tax audit">audited</a>, and that his lawyers had advised him against releasing them.<sup id="cite_ref-195" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-195">&#91;194&#93;</a></sup> After a lengthy court battle to block release of his tax returns and other records to the <a href="/wiki/New_York_County_District_Attorney" title="New York County District Attorney">Manhattan district attorney</a> for a criminal investigation, including two appeals by Trump to the <a href="/wiki/United_States_Supreme_Court" class="mw-redirect" title="United States Supreme Court">United States Supreme Court</a>, in February 2021 the high court allowed the records to be released to the prosecutor for review by a grand jury.<sup id="cite_ref-196" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-196">&#91;195&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-197" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-197">&#91;196&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>In October 2016, portions of Trump's state filings for 1995 were leaked to a reporter from <i>The New York Times</i>. They show that Trump had declared a loss of $916&#160;million that year, which could have let him avoid taxes for up to 18 years.<sup id="cite_ref-198" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-198">&#91;197&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h5><span class="mw-headline" id="Election_to_the_presidency">Election to the presidency</span></h5>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1033289096"><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Main article: <a href="/wiki/2016_United_States_presidential_election" title="2016 United States presidential election">2016 United States presidential election</a></div>
<figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:ElectoralCollege2016.svg" class="mw-file-description"><img alt="Electoral college map, depicting Trump winning many states in the South and Midwest and Biden winning many states in the Northeast and Pacific West" src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/ec/ElectoralCollege2016.svg/290px-ElectoralCollege2016.svg.png" decoding="async" width="290" height="169" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/ec/ElectoralCollege2016.svg/435px-ElectoralCollege2016.svg.png 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/ec/ElectoralCollege2016.svg/580px-ElectoralCollege2016.svg.png 2x" data-file-width="1020" data-file-height="593" /></a><figcaption>2016 electoral vote results. Trump won 304–227.</figcaption></figure>
<p>On November 8, 2016, Trump received 306 pledged <a href="/wiki/Electoral_College_(United_States)" class="mw-redirect" title="Electoral College (United States)">electoral votes</a> versus 232 for Clinton, though, after elector <a href="/wiki/Faithless_electors_in_the_United_States_presidential_election,_2016" class="mw-redirect" title="Faithless electors in the United States presidential election, 2016">defections on both sides</a>, the official count was ultimately 304 to 227.<sup id="cite_ref-199" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-199">&#91;198&#93;</a></sup> Trump received nearly 2.9&#160;million fewer popular votes than Clinton, which made him the fifth person to be elected president <a href="/wiki/United_States_presidential_elections_in_which_the_winner_lost_the_popular_vote" class="mw-redirect" title="United States presidential elections in which the winner lost the popular vote">while losing the popular vote</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-200" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-200">&#91;199&#93;</a></sup> Trump also became the only president who <a href="/wiki/List_of_presidents_of_the_United_States_by_previous_experience" title="List of presidents of the United States by previous experience">neither served in the military nor held any government office</a> prior to becoming president.<sup id="cite_ref-201" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-201">&#91;200&#93;</a></sup> 
Trump's victory was a <a href="/wiki/Political_upset" class="mw-redirect" title="Political upset">political upset</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-202" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-202">&#91;201&#93;</a></sup> Polls had consistently shown Clinton with a <a href="/wiki/Nationwide_opinion_polling_for_the_2016_United_States_presidential_election" title="Nationwide opinion polling for the 2016 United States presidential election">nationwide</a>—though diminishing—lead, as well as an advantage in most of the <a href="/wiki/Statewide_opinion_polling_for_the_2016_United_States_presidential_election" title="Statewide opinion polling for the 2016 United States presidential election">competitive states</a>. Trump's support had been modestly underestimated, while Clinton's had been overestimated.<sup id="cite_ref-203" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-203">&#91;202&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>Trump won 30 states, including <a href="/wiki/Michigan" title="Michigan">Michigan</a>, <a href="/wiki/Pennsylvania" title="Pennsylvania">Pennsylvania</a>, and <a href="/wiki/Wisconsin" title="Wisconsin">Wisconsin</a>, states which had been considered a <a href="/wiki/Blue_wall_(U.S._politics)" title="Blue wall (U.S. politics)">blue wall</a> of Democratic strongholds since the 1990s. Clinton won 20 states and the <a href="/wiki/District_of_Columbia" class="mw-redirect" title="District of Columbia">District of Columbia</a>. Trump's victory marked the return of an <a href="/wiki/Divided_government_in_the_United_States" title="Divided government in the United States">undivided</a> Republican government—a Republican White House combined with Republican control of both chambers of <a href="/wiki/United_States_Congress" title="United States Congress">Congress</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-204" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-204">&#91;203&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:Women%27s_March_on_Washington_(32593123745).jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img alt="Pennsylvania Ave., completely packed with protesters, mostly women, many wearing pink and holding signs with progressive feminist slogans" src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/c9/Women%27s_March_on_Washington_%2832593123745%29.jpg/220px-Women%27s_March_on_Washington_%2832593123745%29.jpg" decoding="async" width="220" height="147" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/c9/Women%27s_March_on_Washington_%2832593123745%29.jpg/330px-Women%27s_March_on_Washington_%2832593123745%29.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/c9/Women%27s_March_on_Washington_%2832593123745%29.jpg/440px-Women%27s_March_on_Washington_%2832593123745%29.jpg 2x" data-file-width="5325" data-file-height="3550" /></a><figcaption><a href="/wiki/2017_Women%27s_March" title="2017 Women&#39;s March">Women's March</a> in Washington on January 21, 2017</figcaption></figure>
<p>Trump's election victory sparked <a href="/wiki/Protests_against_Donald_Trump#After_the_election" title="Protests against Donald Trump">protests</a> in major U.S. cities in the days following the election.<sup id="cite_ref-205" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-205">&#91;204&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-206" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-206">&#91;205&#93;</a></sup> On the day after Trump's inauguration, an estimated 2.6&#160;million people worldwide, including an estimated half million in Washington, D.C., protested against Trump in the <a href="/wiki/2017_Women%27s_March" title="2017 Women&#39;s March">Women's Marches</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-207" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-207">&#91;206&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h2><span id="Presidency_.282017.E2.80.932021.29"></span><span class="mw-headline" id="Presidency_(2017–2021)">Presidency (2017–2021)</span></h2>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1033289096"><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Main article: <a href="/wiki/Presidency_of_Donald_Trump" title="Presidency of Donald Trump">Presidency of Donald Trump</a></div>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1033289096"><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">See also: <a href="/wiki/Timeline_of_the_Donald_Trump_presidency" title="Timeline of the Donald Trump presidency">Timeline of the Donald Trump presidency</a></div>
<h3><span class="mw-headline" id="Early_actions">Early actions</span></h3>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1033289096"><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">See also: <a href="/wiki/Presidential_transition_of_Donald_Trump" title="Presidential transition of Donald Trump">Presidential transition of Donald Trump</a> and <a href="/wiki/First_100_days_of_Donald_Trump%27s_presidency" title="First 100 days of Donald Trump&#39;s presidency">First 100 days of Donald Trump's presidency</a></div>
<figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:Donald_Trump_swearing_in_ceremony.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img alt="Trump, with his family watching, raises his right hand and places his left hand on the Bible as he takes the oath of office. Roberts stands opposite him administering the oath." src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/6c/Donald_Trump_swearing_in_ceremony.jpg/220px-Donald_Trump_swearing_in_ceremony.jpg" decoding="async" width="220" height="147" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/6c/Donald_Trump_swearing_in_ceremony.jpg/330px-Donald_Trump_swearing_in_ceremony.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/6c/Donald_Trump_swearing_in_ceremony.jpg/440px-Donald_Trump_swearing_in_ceremony.jpg 2x" data-file-width="1600" data-file-height="1066" /></a><figcaption>Trump is <a href="/wiki/Inauguration_of_Donald_Trump" title="Inauguration of Donald Trump">sworn in</a> as president by Chief Justice <a href="/wiki/John_Roberts" title="John Roberts">John Roberts</a>.</figcaption></figure>
<p><a href="/wiki/Inauguration_of_Donald_Trump" title="Inauguration of Donald Trump">Trump was inaugurated</a> on January 20, 2017. During his first week in office, he signed <a href="/wiki/List_of_executive_actions_by_Donald_Trump#Executive_orders" title="List of executive actions by Donald Trump">six executive orders</a>, which authorized: interim procedures in anticipation of repealing the Affordable Care Act ("Obamacare"), withdrawal from the Trans-Pacific Partnership negotiations, reinstatement of the <a href="/wiki/Mexico_City_policy" title="Mexico City policy">Mexico City policy</a>, advancement of the <a href="/wiki/Keystone_Pipeline" title="Keystone Pipeline">Keystone XL</a> and <a href="/wiki/Dakota_Access_Pipeline" title="Dakota Access Pipeline">Dakota Access Pipeline</a> construction projects, reinforcement of border security, and a planning and design process to construct a wall along the U.S. border with Mexico.<sup id="cite_ref-208" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-208">&#91;207&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>Trump's daughter Ivanka and son-in-law <a href="/wiki/Jared_Kushner" title="Jared Kushner">Jared Kushner</a> became his <a href="/wiki/Assistant_to_the_President" class="mw-redirect" title="Assistant to the President">assistant</a> and <a href="/wiki/Senior_Advisor_to_the_President_of_the_United_States" title="Senior Advisor to the President of the United States">senior advisor</a>, respectively.<sup id="cite_ref-209" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-209">&#91;208&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-210" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-210">&#91;209&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h3><span class="mw-headline" id="Conflicts_of_interest">Conflicts of interest</span></h3>
<p>Before being inaugurated, Trump moved his businesses into a <a href="/wiki/Revocable_trust" class="mw-redirect" title="Revocable trust">revocable trust</a> run by his sons, Eric and Donald Jr., and a business associate.<sup id="cite_ref-211" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-211">&#91;210&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-BBC041817_212-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-BBC041817-212">&#91;211&#93;</a></sup> Though he said he would eschew "new foreign deals", the Trump Organization pursued expansions of its operations in Dubai, Scotland, and the Dominican Republic. Trump continued to profit from his businesses and to know how his administration's policies affected his businesses.<sup id="cite_ref-BBC041817_212-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-BBC041817-212">&#91;211&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-Venook_213-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Venook-213">&#91;212&#93;</a></sup> 
</p><p>He was sued for violating the <a href="/wiki/Domestic_Emoluments_Clause" class="mw-redirect" title="Domestic Emoluments Clause">Domestic</a> and <a href="/wiki/Foreign_Emoluments_Clause" title="Foreign Emoluments Clause">Foreign Emoluments Clauses</a> of the <a href="/wiki/U.S._Constitution" class="mw-redirect" title="U.S. Constitution">U.S. Constitution</a>, marking the first time that the clauses had been substantively litigated.<sup id="cite_ref-CRSRpt_214-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-CRSRpt-214">&#91;213&#93;</a></sup> One case was dismissed in lower court.<sup id="cite_ref-215" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-215">&#91;214&#93;</a></sup> Two were dismissed by the U.S. Supreme Court as moot after the end of Trump's term.<sup id="cite_ref-216" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-216">&#91;215&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h3><span class="mw-headline" id="Domestic_policy">Domestic policy</span></h3>
<h4><span class="mw-headline" id="Economy">Economy</span></h4>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1033289096"><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Main article: <a href="/wiki/Economic_policy_of_the_Donald_Trump_administration" title="Economic policy of the Donald Trump administration">Economic policy of the Donald Trump administration</a></div>
<figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:Donald_Trump_in_Ypsilanti_(33998674940)_(cropped2).jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img alt="Trump speaks at a lectern, with a crowd in front of and behind him. A banner behind him reads &quot;Buy American – Hire American&quot;" src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/ec/Donald_Trump_in_Ypsilanti_%2833998674940%29_%28cropped2%29.jpg/220px-Donald_Trump_in_Ypsilanti_%2833998674940%29_%28cropped2%29.jpg" decoding="async" width="220" height="163" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/ec/Donald_Trump_in_Ypsilanti_%2833998674940%29_%28cropped2%29.jpg/330px-Donald_Trump_in_Ypsilanti_%2833998674940%29_%28cropped2%29.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/ec/Donald_Trump_in_Ypsilanti_%2833998674940%29_%28cropped2%29.jpg/440px-Donald_Trump_in_Ypsilanti_%2833998674940%29_%28cropped2%29.jpg 2x" data-file-width="1780" data-file-height="1315" /></a><figcaption>Trump speaks to automobile workers in Michigan, March 2017.</figcaption></figure>
<p>Trump took office at the height of the longest <a href="/wiki/Economic_expansion" title="Economic expansion">economic expansion</a> in American history,<sup id="cite_ref-VanDam_217-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-VanDam-217">&#91;216&#93;</a></sup> which began in June 2009 and continued until February 2020, when the <a href="/wiki/COVID-19_recession" title="COVID-19 recession">COVID-19 recession</a> began.<sup id="cite_ref-218" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-218">&#91;217&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>In December 2017, Trump signed the <a href="/wiki/Tax_Cuts_and_Jobs_Act_of_2017" class="mw-redirect" title="Tax Cuts and Jobs Act of 2017">Tax Cuts and Jobs Act of 2017</a>. The bill had been passed by both Republican-controlled chambers of Congress without any Democratic votes. It reduced tax rates for businesses and individuals, with business tax cuts to be permanent and individual tax cuts set to expire after 2025, and eliminated the penalty associated with <a href="/wiki/Affordable_Care_Act" title="Affordable Care Act">Affordable Care Act</a>'s individual mandate.<sup id="cite_ref-219" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-219">&#91;218&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-220" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-220">&#91;219&#93;</a></sup> The Trump administration claimed that the act would either increase tax revenues or pay for itself by prompting economic growth. Instead, revenues in 2018 were 7.6 percent lower than projected.<sup id="cite_ref-221" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-221">&#91;220&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>Despite a campaign promise to eliminate the national debt in eight years, Trump approved large increases in government spending and the 2017 tax cut. As a result, the federal budget deficit increased by almost 50 percent, to nearly $1&#160;trillion in 2019.<sup id="cite_ref-222" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-222">&#91;221&#93;</a></sup> Under Trump, the <a href="/wiki/U.S._national_debt" class="mw-redirect" title="U.S. national debt">U.S. national debt</a> increased by 39 percent, reaching $27.75<span class="nowrap">&#160;</span>trillion by the end of his term, and the U.S. <a href="/wiki/Debt-to-GDP_ratio" title="Debt-to-GDP ratio">debt-to-GDP ratio</a> hit a post-World War II high.<sup id="cite_ref-223" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-223">&#91;222&#93;</a></sup> Trump also failed to deliver the $1&#160;trillion infrastructure spending plan on which he had campaigned.<sup id="cite_ref-224" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-224">&#91;223&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>Trump is the only modern U.S. president to leave office with a smaller workforce than when he took office, by 3&#160;million people.<sup id="cite_ref-VanDam_217-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-VanDam-217">&#91;216&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h4><span id="Climate_change.2C_environment.2C_and_energy"></span><span class="mw-headline" id="Climate_change,_environment,_and_energy">Climate change, environment, and energy</span></h4>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1033289096"><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Main article: <a href="/wiki/Environmental_policy_of_the_Donald_Trump_administration" title="Environmental policy of the Donald Trump administration">Environmental policy of the Donald Trump administration</a></div>
<p>Trump rejects the <a href="/wiki/Scientific_consensus_on_climate_change" title="Scientific consensus on climate change">scientific consensus on climate change</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-225" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-225">&#91;224&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-226" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-226">&#91;225&#93;</a></sup> He reduced the budget for renewable energy research by 40 percent and reversed Obama-era policies directed at curbing climate change.<sup id="cite_ref-227" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-227">&#91;226&#93;</a></sup> In June 2017, Trump announced the <a href="/wiki/Withdrawal_of_the_United_States_from_the_Paris_Agreement" class="mw-redirect" title="Withdrawal of the United States from the Paris Agreement">withdrawal of the United States from the Paris Agreement</a>, making the U.S. the only nation in the world to not ratify the agreement.<sup id="cite_ref-228" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-228">&#91;227&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>Trump aimed to boost the production and exports of <a href="/wiki/Fossil_fuel" title="Fossil fuel">fossil fuels</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-229" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-229">&#91;228&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-230" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-230">&#91;229&#93;</a></sup> Natural gas expanded under Trump, but coal continued to decline.<sup id="cite_ref-231" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-231">&#91;230&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-Subramaniam_232-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Subramaniam-232">&#91;231&#93;</a></sup> Trump rolled back more than 100 federal environmental regulations, including those that curbed <a href="/wiki/Greenhouse_gas_emissions" title="Greenhouse gas emissions">greenhouse gas emissions</a>, air and water pollution, and the use of toxic substances. He weakened protections for animals and environmental standards for federal infrastructure projects, and expanded permitted areas for drilling and resource extraction, such as allowing <a href="/wiki/Arctic_Refuge_drilling_controversy" title="Arctic Refuge drilling controversy">drilling in the Arctic Refuge</a>. Trump's actions while president have been called "a very aggressive attempt to rewrite our laws and reinterpret the meaning of environmental protections".<sup id="cite_ref-233" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-233">&#91;232&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h4><span class="mw-headline" id="Deregulation">Deregulation</span></h4>
<p>In January 2017, Trump signed <a href="/wiki/Executive_Order_13771" title="Executive Order 13771">Executive Order 13771</a>, which directed that, for every new regulation, federal agencies "identify" two existing regulations for elimination, though it did not require elimination.<sup id="cite_ref-234" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-234">&#91;233&#93;</a></sup> He dismantled many federal regulations on health,<sup id="cite_ref-235" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-235">&#91;234&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-midnight_236-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-midnight-236">&#91;235&#93;</a></sup> labor,<sup id="cite_ref-237" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-237">&#91;236&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-midnight_236-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-midnight-236">&#91;235&#93;</a></sup> and the environment,<sup id="cite_ref-238" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-238">&#91;237&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-midnight_236-2" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-midnight-236">&#91;235&#93;</a></sup> among other topics. Trump signed 14 <a href="/wiki/Congressional_Review_Act" title="Congressional Review Act">Congressional Review Act</a> resolutions repealing federal regulations, including a bill that made it easier for severely mentally ill persons to buy guns.<sup id="cite_ref-239" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-239">&#91;238&#93;</a></sup> During his first six weeks in office, he delayed, suspended, or reversed ninety federal regulations,<sup id="cite_ref-240" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-240">&#91;239&#93;</a></sup> often "after requests by the regulated industries".<sup id="cite_ref-241" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-241">&#91;240&#93;</a></sup> The <a href="/wiki/Institute_for_Policy_Integrity" title="Institute for Policy Integrity">Institute for Policy Integrity</a> found that 78 percent of Trump's proposals were blocked by courts or did not prevail over litigation.<sup id="cite_ref-242" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-242">&#91;241&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h4><span class="mw-headline" id="Health_care">Health care</span></h4>
<p>During his campaign, Trump vowed to repeal and replace the <a href="/wiki/Affordable_Care_Act" title="Affordable Care Act">Affordable Care Act</a> (ACA).<sup id="cite_ref-243" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-243">&#91;242&#93;</a></sup> In office, he scaled back the Act's implementation through executive orders <a href="/wiki/Executive_Order_13765" title="Executive Order 13765">13765</a><sup id="cite_ref-244" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-244">&#91;243&#93;</a></sup> and <a href="/wiki/Executive_Order_13813" title="Executive Order 13813">13813</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-245" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-245">&#91;244&#93;</a></sup> Trump expressed a desire to "let Obamacare fail"; his administration cut the ACA <a href="/wiki/Annual_enrollment" title="Annual enrollment">enrollment period</a> in half and drastically reduced funding for advertising and other ways to encourage enrollment.<sup id="cite_ref-246" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-246">&#91;245&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-247" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-247">&#91;246&#93;</a></sup> Trump falsely claimed he saved the coverage of pre-existing conditions provided by the ACA.<sup id="cite_ref-248" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-248">&#91;247&#93;</a></sup> In June 2018, the Trump administration <a href="/wiki/California_v._Texas" title="California v. Texas">joined 18 Republican-led states in arguing before the Supreme Court</a> that the elimination of the financial penalties associated with the individual mandate had rendered the ACA unconstitutional.<sup id="cite_ref-StolbergACA_249-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-StolbergACA-249">&#91;248&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-250" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-250">&#91;249&#93;</a></sup> If they had succeeded, it would have eliminated <a href="/wiki/Health_insurance_coverage_in_the_United_States" title="Health insurance coverage in the United States">health insurance coverage</a> for up to 23&#160;million Americans.<sup id="cite_ref-StolbergACA_249-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-StolbergACA-249">&#91;248&#93;</a></sup> During the 2016 campaign, Trump promised to protect funding for Medicare and other social safety-net programs, but in January 2020, he suggested he was willing to consider cuts to such programs.<sup id="cite_ref-251" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-251">&#91;250&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>In response to the opioid epidemic, Trump signed legislation in 2018 to increase funding for drug treatments, but was widely criticized for failing to make a concrete strategy. U.S. opioid overdose deaths declined slightly in 2018, but surged to a record 50,052 deaths in 2019.<sup id="cite_ref-252" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-252">&#91;251&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h4><span class="mw-headline" id="Social_issues">Social issues</span></h4>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1033289096"><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Main article: <a href="/wiki/Social_policy_of_Donald_Trump" title="Social policy of Donald Trump">Social policy of Donald Trump</a></div>
<p>Trump barred organizations that provide abortions or abortion referrals from receiving federal funds.<sup id="cite_ref-253" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-253">&#91;252&#93;</a></sup> He said he supported "traditional marriage" but considered the <a href="/wiki/Same-sex_marriage_in_the_United_States" title="Same-sex marriage in the United States">nationwide legality</a> of <a href="/wiki/Same-sex_marriage" title="Same-sex marriage">same-sex marriage</a> a "settled" issue.<sup id="cite_ref-254" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-254">&#91;253&#93;</a></sup> In March 2017, his administration rolled back key components of the Obama administration's workplace protections against <a href="/wiki/Discrimination_against_LGBT_people" title="Discrimination against LGBT people">discrimination of LGBT people</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-255" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-255">&#91;254&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>Trump has said he is <a href="/wiki/Gun_politics_in_the_United_States" title="Gun politics in the United States">opposed</a> to <a href="/wiki/Gun_control" title="Gun control">gun control</a> in general, although his views have shifted over time.<sup id="cite_ref-256" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-256">&#91;255&#93;</a></sup> After several <a href="/wiki/Mass_shootings_in_the_United_States" title="Mass shootings in the United States">mass shootings</a> during his term, he said he would propose legislation to curtail gun violence, but he abandoned that effort in November 2019.<sup id="cite_ref-257" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-257">&#91;256&#93;</a></sup> His administration took an <a href="/wiki/Cannabis_policy_of_the_Donald_Trump_administration" title="Cannabis policy of the Donald Trump administration">anti-marijuana position</a>, revoking <a href="/wiki/Cole_Memorandum" title="Cole Memorandum">Obama-era policies</a> that provided protections for states that legalized marijuana.<sup id="cite_ref-258" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-258">&#91;257&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>Trump is a long-time advocate of <a href="/wiki/Capital_punishment" title="Capital punishment">capital punishment</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-259" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-259">&#91;258&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-260" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-260">&#91;259&#93;</a></sup> Under his administration, the <a href="/wiki/Capital_punishment_by_the_United_States_federal_government" title="Capital punishment by the United States federal government">federal government executed</a> 13 prisoners, more than in the previous 56 years combined and after a 17-year moratorium.<sup id="cite_ref-261" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-261">&#91;260&#93;</a></sup> In 2016, Trump said he supported the use of interrogation torture methods such as <a href="/wiki/Waterboarding" title="Waterboarding">waterboarding</a><sup id="cite_ref-262" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-262">&#91;261&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-263" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-263">&#91;262&#93;</a></sup> but later appeared to recant this due to the opposition of Defense Secretary <a href="/wiki/James_Mattis" class="mw-redirect" title="James Mattis">James Mattis</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-264" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-264">&#91;263&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h3><span class="mw-headline" id="Pardons_and_commutations">Pardons and commutations</span></h3>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1033289096"><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Further information: <a href="/wiki/List_of_people_granted_executive_clemency_by_Donald_Trump" title="List of people granted executive clemency by Donald Trump">List of people granted executive clemency by Donald Trump</a></div>
<p>Trump granted 237 requests for clemency, fewer than all presidents since 1900 with the exception of <a href="/wiki/George_H._W._Bush" title="George H. W. Bush">George H. W. Bush</a> and <a href="/wiki/George_W._Bush" title="George W. Bush">George W. Bush</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-265" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-265">&#91;264&#93;</a></sup>
Only 25 of them had been vetted by the Justice Department's <a href="/wiki/Office_of_the_Pardon_Attorney" title="Office of the Pardon Attorney">Office of the Pardon Attorney</a>; the others were granted to people with personal or political connections to him, his family, and his allies, or recommended by celebrities.<sup id="cite_ref-266" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-266">&#91;265&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-OloDaw_267-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-OloDaw-267">&#91;266&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>From 2017 to 2019, he pardoned, amongst others, former Navy sailor <a href="/wiki/Kristian_Saucier" title="Kristian Saucier">Kristian Saucier</a>, who was convicted of taking classified photographs of classified areas inside a submarine;<sup id="cite_ref-268" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-268">&#91;267&#93;</a></sup> and <a href="/wiki/Right-wing" class="mw-redirect" title="Right-wing">right-wing</a> commentator <a href="/wiki/Dinesh_D%27Souza" title="Dinesh D&#39;Souza">Dinesh D'Souza</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-269" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-269">&#91;268&#93;</a></sup> Following a request by celebrity <a href="/wiki/Kim_Kardashian" title="Kim Kardashian">Kim Kardashian</a>, Trump commuted the life sentence of <a href="/wiki/Alice_Marie_Johnson" title="Alice Marie Johnson">Alice Marie Johnson</a>, who had been convicted of drug trafficking.<sup id="cite_ref-270" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-270">&#91;269&#93;</a></sup> Trump also pardoned or reversed the sentences of three American servicemen convicted or accused of committing war crimes in Afghanistan or Iraq.<sup id="cite_ref-271" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-271">&#91;270&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>In November and December 2020, Trump pardoned four <a href="/wiki/Academi" class="mw-redirect" title="Academi">Blackwater</a> <a href="/wiki/Private_military_company" title="Private military company">private security contractors</a> convicted of killing Iraqi civilians in the 2007 <a href="/wiki/Nisour_Square_massacre" title="Nisour Square massacre">Nisour Square massacre</a>;<sup id="cite_ref-Blackwater_272-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Blackwater-272">&#91;271&#93;</a></sup> white-collar criminals <a href="/wiki/Michael_Milken" title="Michael Milken">Michael Milken</a> and <a href="/wiki/Bernard_Kerik" title="Bernard Kerik">Bernard Kerik</a>;<sup id="cite_ref-273" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-273">&#91;272&#93;</a></sup> daughter Ivanka's father-in-law <a href="/wiki/Charles_Kushner" title="Charles Kushner">Charles Kushner</a>;<sup id="cite_ref-OloDaw_267-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-OloDaw-267">&#91;266&#93;</a></sup> and five people convicted as a result of investigations into Russian interference in the 2016 presidential elections. Among them were Michael Flynn; Roger Stone, whose 40-month sentence for lying to Congress, witness tampering, and obstruction he had already commuted in July; and <a href="/wiki/Paul_Manafort" title="Paul Manafort">Paul Manafort</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-274" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-274">&#91;273&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>In his last full day in office, Trump granted 73 pardons, including to Steve Bannon and Trump fundraiser <a href="/wiki/Elliott_Broidy" title="Elliott Broidy">Elliott Broidy</a>, and commuted 70 sentences.<sup id="cite_ref-275" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-275">&#91;274&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h3><span class="mw-headline" id="Lafayette_Square_protester_removal_and_photo_op">Lafayette Square protester removal and photo op</span></h3>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1033289096"><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Main article: <a href="/wiki/Donald_Trump_photo_op_at_St._John%27s_Church" title="Donald Trump photo op at St. John&#39;s Church">Donald Trump photo op at St. John's Church</a></div>
<figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:President_Trump_Visits_St._John%27s_Episcopal_Church_(49964153176).jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/93/President_Trump_Visits_St._John%27s_Episcopal_Church_%2849964153176%29.jpg/220px-President_Trump_Visits_St._John%27s_Episcopal_Church_%2849964153176%29.jpg" decoding="async" width="220" height="147" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/93/President_Trump_Visits_St._John%27s_Episcopal_Church_%2849964153176%29.jpg/330px-President_Trump_Visits_St._John%27s_Episcopal_Church_%2849964153176%29.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/93/President_Trump_Visits_St._John%27s_Episcopal_Church_%2849964153176%29.jpg/440px-President_Trump_Visits_St._John%27s_Episcopal_Church_%2849964153176%29.jpg 2x" data-file-width="2800" data-file-height="1867" /></a><figcaption>Trump and group of officials and advisors on the way from White House complex to St. John's Church</figcaption></figure>
<p>On June 1, 2020, federal law-enforcement officials used batons, rubber bullets, <a href="/wiki/Pepper_spray" title="Pepper spray">pepper spray</a> projectiles, <a href="/wiki/Stun_grenade" title="Stun grenade">stun grenades</a>, and smoke to remove a largely peaceful crowd of protesters from <a href="/wiki/Lafayette_Square,_Washington,_D.C." title="Lafayette Square, Washington, D.C.">Lafayette Square</a>, outside the <a href="/wiki/White_House" title="White House">White House</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-wb_276-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-wb-276">&#91;275&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-bumpline_277-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-bumpline-277">&#91;276&#93;</a></sup> Trump then walked to <a href="/wiki/St._John%27s_Episcopal_Church,_Lafayette_Square" title="St. John&#39;s Episcopal Church, Lafayette Square">St. John's Episcopal Church</a>, where protesters had set a small fire the night before; he posed for photographs holding a Bible, with senior administration officials later joining him in photos.<sup id="cite_ref-wb_276-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-wb-276">&#91;275&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-278" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-278">&#91;277&#93;</a></sup> Trump said on June 3 that the protesters were cleared because "they tried to burn down the church [on May 31] and almost succeeded", describing the church as "badly hurt".<sup id="cite_ref-Shear_279-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Shear-279">&#91;278&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>Religious leaders condemned the treatment of protesters and the photo opportunity itself.<sup id="cite_ref-280" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-280">&#91;279&#93;</a></sup> Many retired military leaders and defense officials condemned Trump's proposal to use the U.S. military against anti-police-brutality protesters.<sup id="cite_ref-281" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-281">&#91;280&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h3><span class="mw-headline" id="Immigration">Immigration</span></h3>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1033289096"><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Main article: <a href="/wiki/Immigration_policy_of_Donald_Trump" title="Immigration policy of Donald Trump">Immigration policy of Donald Trump</a></div>
<p>Trump's proposed immigration policies were a topic of bitter and contentious debate during the campaign. He promised to build <a href="/wiki/Trump_wall" title="Trump wall">a wall</a> on the <a href="/wiki/Mexico%E2%80%93United_States_border" title="Mexico–United States border">Mexico–United States border</a> to restrict illegal movement and vowed Mexico would pay for it.<sup id="cite_ref-282" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-282">&#91;281&#93;</a></sup> He pledged to deport millions of <a href="/wiki/Illegal_immigrant_population_of_the_United_States" class="mw-redirect" title="Illegal immigrant population of the United States">illegal immigrants residing in the United States</a>,<sup id="cite_ref-283" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-283">&#91;282&#93;</a></sup> and criticized <a href="/wiki/Birthright_citizenship_in_the_United_States" title="Birthright citizenship in the United States">birthright citizenship</a> for incentivizing "<a href="/wiki/Anchor_babies" class="mw-redirect" title="Anchor babies">anchor babies</a>".<sup id="cite_ref-284" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-284">&#91;283&#93;</a></sup> As president, he frequently described illegal immigration as an "invasion" and conflated immigrants with the criminal gang <a href="/wiki/MS-13" title="MS-13">MS-13</a>,<sup id="cite_ref-285" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-285">&#91;284&#93;</a></sup> though available research shows <a href="/wiki/Undocumented_immigrant_population_of_the_United_States" title="Undocumented immigrant population of the United States">undocumented immigrants</a> have a lower crime rate than native-born Americans.<sup id="cite_ref-286" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-286">&#91;285&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-287" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-287">&#91;286&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>Trump attempted to drastically escalate immigration enforcement, including implementing harsher immigration enforcement policies against asylum seekers from Central America than any modern U.S. president.<sup id="cite_ref-288" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-288">&#91;287&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-289" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-289">&#91;288&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>From 2018 onward, Trump <a href="/wiki/Operation_Faithful_Patriot" title="Operation Faithful Patriot">deployed nearly 6,000 troops to the U.S.–Mexico border</a><sup id="cite_ref-290" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-290">&#91;289&#93;</a></sup> to stop most Central American migrants from seeking U.S. asylum. In 2020, his administration widened the <a href="/wiki/Public_charge_rule" title="Public charge rule">public charge rule</a> to further restrict immigrants who might use government benefits from getting permanent residency via <a href="/wiki/Green_card" title="Green card">green cards</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-291" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-291">&#91;290&#93;</a></sup> Trump reduced the number of <a href="/wiki/United_States_Refugee_Admissions_Program" title="United States Refugee Admissions Program">refugees admitted</a> into the U.S. to record lows. When Trump took office, the annual limit was 110,000; Trump set a limit of 18,000 in the 2020 fiscal year and 15,000 in the 2021 fiscal year.<sup id="cite_ref-292" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-292">&#91;291&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-293" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-293">&#91;292&#93;</a></sup> Additional restrictions implemented by the Trump administration caused significant bottlenecks in processing refugee applications, resulting in fewer refugees accepted compared to the allowed limits.<sup id="cite_ref-294" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-294">&#91;293&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h4><span class="mw-headline" id="Travel_ban">Travel ban</span></h4>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1033289096"><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Main article: <a href="/wiki/Trump_travel_ban" title="Trump travel ban">Trump travel ban</a></div>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1033289096"><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Further information: <a href="/wiki/Executive_Order_13769" title="Executive Order 13769">Executive Order 13769</a> and <a href="/wiki/Executive_Order_13780" title="Executive Order 13780">Executive Order 13780</a></div>
<p>Following the <a href="/wiki/2015_San_Bernardino_attack" title="2015 San Bernardino attack">2015 San Bernardino attack</a>, Trump proposed to ban <a href="/wiki/Muslims" title="Muslims">Muslim</a> foreigners from entering the United States until stronger vetting systems could be implemented.<sup id="cite_ref-295" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-295">&#91;294&#93;</a></sup> He later reframed the proposed ban to apply to countries with a "proven history of terrorism".<sup id="cite_ref-296" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-296">&#91;295&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>On January 27, 2017, Trump signed <a href="/wiki/Executive_Order_13769" title="Executive Order 13769">Executive Order 13769</a>, which suspended admission of refugees for 120 days and denied entry to citizens of Iraq, Iran, Libya, Somalia, Sudan, Syria, and Yemen for 90 days, citing security concerns. The order took effect immediately and without warning, causing confusion and chaos at airports.<sup id="cite_ref-frontline_297-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-frontline-297">&#91;296&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-airport_298-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-airport-298">&#91;297&#93;</a></sup> <a href="/wiki/Protests_against_Executive_Order_13769" title="Protests against Executive Order 13769">Protests against the ban</a> began at airports the next day.<sup id="cite_ref-frontline_297-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-frontline-297">&#91;296&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-airport_298-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-airport-298">&#91;297&#93;</a></sup> <a href="/wiki/Legal_challenges_to_the_Trump_travel_ban" title="Legal challenges to the Trump travel ban">Legal challenges</a> to the order resulted in <a href="/wiki/National_injunctions" class="mw-redirect" title="National injunctions">nationwide preliminary injunctions</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-299" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-299">&#91;298&#93;</a></sup> A March 6 <a href="/wiki/Executive_Order_13780" title="Executive Order 13780">revised order</a>, which excluded Iraq and gave other exemptions, again was blocked by federal judges in three states.<sup id="cite_ref-300" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-300">&#91;299&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-301" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-301">&#91;300&#93;</a></sup> In a <a href="/wiki/Int%27l_Refugee_Assistance_Project_v._Trump" title="Int&#39;l Refugee Assistance Project v. Trump">decision in June 2017</a>, the <a href="/wiki/Supreme_Court_of_the_United_States" title="Supreme Court of the United States">Supreme Court</a> ruled that the ban could be enforced on visitors who lack a "credible claim of a <i>bona fide</i> relationship with a person or entity in the United States".<sup id="cite_ref-302" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-302">&#91;301&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>The temporary order was replaced by <a href="/wiki/Presidential_Proclamation_9645" class="mw-redirect" title="Presidential Proclamation 9645">Presidential Proclamation 9645</a> on September 24, 2017, which restricted travel from the originally targeted countries except Iraq and Sudan, and further banned travelers from North Korea and Chad, along with certain Venezuelan officials.<sup id="cite_ref-303" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-303">&#91;302&#93;</a></sup> After lower courts partially blocked the new restrictions, the Supreme Court allowed the September version to go into full effect on December 4, 2017,<sup id="cite_ref-304" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-304">&#91;303&#93;</a></sup> and ultimately upheld the travel ban in a June 2019 ruling.<sup id="cite_ref-305" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-305">&#91;304&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h4><span class="mw-headline" id="Family_separation_at_border">Family separation at border</span></h4>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1033289096"><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Main article: <a href="/wiki/Trump_administration_family_separation_policy" title="Trump administration family separation policy">Trump administration family separation policy</a></div>
<style data-mw-deduplicate="TemplateStyles:r1096954695/mw-parser-output/.tmulti">.mw-parser-output .tmulti .multiimageinner{display:flex;flex-direction:column}.mw-parser-output .tmulti .trow{display:flex;flex-direction:row;clear:left;flex-wrap:wrap;width:100%;box-sizing:border-box}.mw-parser-output .tmulti .tsingle{margin:1px;float:left}.mw-parser-output .tmulti .thumbcaption{text-align:left}.mw-parser-output .tmulti .trow>.thumbcaption{text-align:center}}</style><div class="thumb tmulti tright"><div class="thumbinner multiimageinner" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/64/Ursula_%28detention_center%29_1.png/330px-Ursula_%28detention_center%29_1.png 1.5x, class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a5/Ursula_%28detention_center%29_2.jpg/330px-Ursula_%28detention_center%29_2.jpg 1.5x, title="Ursula (detention center)">Ursula detention facility</a> in <a href="/wiki/McAllen,_Texas" title="McAllen, Texas">McAllen, Texas</a>, June 2018</div></div></div></div>
<p>The Trump administration separated more than 5,400 children of migrant families from their parents at the U.S.–Mexico border, a sharp increase in the number of family separations at the border starting from the summer of 2017.<sup id="cite_ref-306" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-306">&#91;305&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-Spagat_307-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Spagat-307">&#91;306&#93;</a></sup> In April 2018, the Trump administration announced a "<a href="/wiki/Trump_administration_family_separation_policy" title="Trump administration family separation policy">zero tolerance</a>" policy whereby every adult suspected of <a href="/wiki/Illegal_entry" title="Illegal entry">illegal entry</a> would be criminally prosecuted.<sup id="cite_ref-308" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-308">&#91;307&#93;</a></sup> This resulted in family separations, as the migrant adults were put in criminal detention for prosecution, while their children were separated as unaccompanied alien minors.<sup id="cite_ref-309" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-309">&#91;308&#93;</a></sup> Administration officials described the policy as a way to deter illegal immigration.<sup id="cite_ref-Domonoske_310-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Domonoske-310">&#91;309&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>The policy of family separations was unprecedented in previous administrations and sparked public outrage.<sup id="cite_ref-Domonoske_310-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Domonoske-310">&#91;309&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-311" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-311">&#91;310&#93;</a></sup> Trump falsely asserted that his administration was merely following the law, blaming Democrats, despite the separations being his administration's policy.<sup id="cite_ref-312" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-312">&#91;311&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-313" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-313">&#91;312&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-314" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-314">&#91;313&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>Although Trump originally argued that the separations could not be stopped by an executive order, he acceded to intense public objection and signed an executive order on June 20, 2018, mandating that migrant families be detained together unless "there is a concern" doing so would pose a risk to the child.<sup id="cite_ref-315" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-315">&#91;314&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-316" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-316">&#91;315&#93;</a></sup> On June 26, 2018, Judge <a href="/wiki/Dana_Sabraw" title="Dana Sabraw">Dana Sabraw</a> concluded that the Trump administration had "no system in place to keep track of" the separated children, nor any effective measures for family communication and reunification;<sup id="cite_ref-317" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-317">&#91;316&#93;</a></sup> Sabraw ordered for the families to be reunited and family separations stopped except in limited circumstances.<sup id="cite_ref-318" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-318">&#91;317&#93;</a></sup> After the federal-court order, the Trump administration separated more than a thousand migrant children from their families; the ACLU contended that the Trump administration had abused its discretion and asked Sabraw to more narrowly define the circumstances warranting separation.<sup id="cite_ref-Spagat_307-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Spagat-307">&#91;306&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h4><span class="mw-headline" id="Trump_wall_and_government_shutdown">Trump wall and government shutdown</span></h4>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1033289096"><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Main articles: <a href="/wiki/Trump_wall" title="Trump wall">Trump wall</a> and <a href="/wiki/2018%E2%80%932019_United_States_federal_government_shutdown" title="2018–2019 United States federal government shutdown">2018–2019 United States federal government shutdown</a></div>
<figure class="mw-default-size mw-halign-left" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:Donald_Trump_visits_San_Diego_border_wall_prototypes.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img alt="Trump speaks with U.S. Border Patrol agents. Behind him are black SUVs, four short border wall prototype designs, and the current border wall in the background" src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/46/Donald_Trump_visits_San_Diego_border_wall_prototypes.jpg/220px-Donald_Trump_visits_San_Diego_border_wall_prototypes.jpg" decoding="async" width="220" height="164" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/46/Donald_Trump_visits_San_Diego_border_wall_prototypes.jpg/330px-Donald_Trump_visits_San_Diego_border_wall_prototypes.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/46/Donald_Trump_visits_San_Diego_border_wall_prototypes.jpg/440px-Donald_Trump_visits_San_Diego_border_wall_prototypes.jpg 2x" data-file-width="863" data-file-height="644" /></a><figcaption>Trump examines border wall prototypes in <a href="/wiki/Otay_Mesa,_California" class="mw-redirect" title="Otay Mesa, California">Otay Mesa, California</a>.</figcaption></figure>
<p>One of Trump's central campaign promises was to build a 1,000-mile (1,600&#160;km) border wall to Mexico and have Mexico pay for it.<sup id="cite_ref-timm_319-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-timm-319">&#91;318&#93;</a></sup> By the end of his term, the U.S. had built "40 miles [64&#160;km] of new primary wall and 33 miles [53&#160;km] of secondary wall" in locations where there had been no barriers and 365 miles (587&#160;km) of primary or secondary border fencing replacing dilapidated or outdated barriers.<sup id="cite_ref-320" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-320">&#91;319&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>In 2018, Trump refused to sign any <a href="/wiki/Appropriations_bill" class="mw-redirect" title="Appropriations bill">appropriations bill</a> from Congress unless it allocated $5.6&#160;billion in funds for the border wall,<sup id="cite_ref-321" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-321">&#91;320&#93;</a></sup> resulting in the federal government partially shutting down for 35 days from December 2018 to January 2019, the <a href="/wiki/List_of_United_States_federal_funding_gaps" title="List of United States federal funding gaps">longest U.S. government shutdown in history</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-Gambino_322-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Gambino-322">&#91;321&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-323" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-323">&#91;322&#93;</a></sup> Around 800,000 government employees were <a href="/wiki/Furlough" title="Furlough">furloughed</a> or worked without pay.<sup id="cite_ref-324" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-324">&#91;323&#93;</a></sup> Trump and Congress ended the shutdown by approving temporary funding that provided delayed payments to government workers but no funds for the wall.<sup id="cite_ref-Gambino_322-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Gambino-322">&#91;321&#93;</a></sup> The shutdown resulted in an estimated permanent loss of $3&#160;billion to the economy, according to the <a href="/wiki/Congressional_Budget_Office" title="Congressional Budget Office">Congressional Budget Office</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-325" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-325">&#91;324&#93;</a></sup> About half of those polled blamed Trump for the shutdown, and Trump's approval ratings dropped.<sup id="cite_ref-326" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-326">&#91;325&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>To prevent another imminent shutdown in February 2019, Congress passed and Trump signed a funding bill that included $1.375&#160;billion for 55 miles (89&#160;km) of bollard border fencing.<sup id="cite_ref-Wilkie_327-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Wilkie-327">&#91;326&#93;</a></sup> Trump also declared a <a href="/wiki/National_Emergency_Concerning_the_Southern_Border_of_the_United_States" title="National Emergency Concerning the Southern Border of the United States">National Emergency Concerning the Southern Border of the United States</a>, intending to divert $6.1&#160;billion of funds Congress had allocated to other purposes.<sup id="cite_ref-Wilkie_327-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Wilkie-327">&#91;326&#93;</a></sup> Trump <a href="/wiki/Veto_power_in_the_United_States#In_federal_government" title="Veto power in the United States">vetoed</a> a <a href="/wiki/Joint_resolution" title="Joint resolution">joint resolution</a> to overturn the declaration, and the Senate voted against a <a href="/wiki/Veto_override" class="mw-redirect" title="Veto override">veto override</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-328" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-328">&#91;327&#93;</a></sup> Legal challenges to the diversion of $2.5&#160;billion originally meant for the <a href="/wiki/United_States_Department_of_Defense" title="United States Department of Defense">Department of Defense</a>'s drug interdiction efforts<sup id="cite_ref-329" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-329">&#91;328&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-330" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-330">&#91;329&#93;</a></sup> and $3.6&#160;billion originally meant for military construction<sup id="cite_ref-331" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-331">&#91;330&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-332" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-332">&#91;331&#93;</a></sup> were unsuccessful.
</p>
<h3><span class="mw-headline" id="Foreign_policy">Foreign policy</span></h3>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1033289096"><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Main article: <a href="/wiki/Foreign_policy_of_the_Donald_Trump_administration" title="Foreign policy of the Donald Trump administration">Foreign policy of the Donald Trump administration</a></div>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1033289096"><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">See also: <a href="/wiki/List_of_international_presidential_trips_made_by_Donald_Trump" title="List of international presidential trips made by Donald Trump">List of international presidential trips made by Donald Trump</a></div>
<figure class="mw-default-size mw-halign-left" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:-G7Biarritz_(48616362963).jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img alt="Trump and other G7 leaders sit at a conference table" src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/33/-G7Biarritz_%2848616362963%29.jpg/220px--G7Biarritz_%2848616362963%29.jpg" decoding="async" width="220" height="147" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/33/-G7Biarritz_%2848616362963%29.jpg/330px--G7Biarritz_%2848616362963%29.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/33/-G7Biarritz_%2848616362963%29.jpg/440px--G7Biarritz_%2848616362963%29.jpg 2x" data-file-width="2800" data-file-height="1867" /></a><figcaption>Trump with the other <a href="/wiki/Group_of_Seven" class="mw-redirect" title="Group of Seven">G7</a> leaders at the <a href="/wiki/45th_G7_summit" title="45th G7 summit">45th summit</a> in France, 2019</figcaption></figure>
<p>Trump described himself as a "nationalist"<sup id="cite_ref-333" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-333">&#91;332&#93;</a></sup> and his foreign policy as "<a href="/wiki/America_First_(policy)" title="America First (policy)">America First</a>".<sup id="cite_ref-Bennhold_334-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Bennhold-334">&#91;333&#93;</a></sup> His foreign policy was marked by praise and support of <a href="/wiki/Populism" title="Populism">populist</a>, <a href="/wiki/Neo-nationalism" title="Neo-nationalism">neo-nationalist</a>, and authoritarian governments.<sup id="cite_ref-335" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-335">&#91;334&#93;</a></sup> Hallmarks of foreign relations during Trump's tenure included unpredictability and uncertainty,<sup id="cite_ref-Bennhold_334-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Bennhold-334">&#91;333&#93;</a></sup> a lack of a consistent foreign policy,<sup id="cite_ref-336" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-336">&#91;335&#93;</a></sup> and strained and sometimes antagonistic relationships with the U.S.'s European allies.<sup id="cite_ref-337" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-337">&#91;336&#93;</a></sup> He criticized <a href="/wiki/Member_states_of_NATO" title="Member states of NATO">NATO allies</a> and privately suggested on multiple occasions that the United States should <a href="/wiki/Withdrawal_from_NATO#United_States" title="Withdrawal from NATO">withdraw from the alliance</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-338" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-338">&#91;337&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-339" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-339">&#91;338&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h4><span class="mw-headline" id="Trade">Trade</span></h4>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1033289096"><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">See also: <a href="/wiki/Trump_tariffs" title="Trump tariffs">Trump tariffs</a></div>
<p>Trump withdrew the U.S. from the <a href="/wiki/Trans-Pacific_Partnership" title="Trans-Pacific Partnership">Trans-Pacific Partnership</a> (TPP) negotiations,<sup id="cite_ref-340" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-340">&#91;339&#93;</a></sup> imposed tariffs on steel and aluminum imports,<sup id="cite_ref-341" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-341">&#91;340&#93;</a></sup> and launched a <a href="/wiki/China%E2%80%93United_States_trade_war" title="China–United States trade war">trade war with China</a> by sharply increasing tariffs on 818 categories (worth $50&#160;billion) of Chinese goods imported into the U.S.<sup id="cite_ref-342" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-342">&#91;341&#93;</a></sup> While Trump said that import tariffs are paid by China into the <a href="/wiki/U.S._Treasury" class="mw-redirect" title="U.S. Treasury">U.S. Treasury</a>, they are paid by American companies that import goods from China.<sup id="cite_ref-343" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-343">&#91;342&#93;</a></sup> Although he pledged during the campaign to significantly reduce the U.S.'s large <a href="/wiki/Trade_deficits" class="mw-redirect" title="Trade deficits">trade deficits</a>, the trade deficit in July 2020, during the COVID-19 pandemic, "was the largest monthly deficit since July 2008".<sup id="cite_ref-344" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-344">&#91;343&#93;</a></sup> Following a 2017–2018 renegotiation, the <a href="/wiki/United_States-Mexico-Canada_Agreement" class="mw-redirect" title="United States-Mexico-Canada Agreement">United States-Mexico-Canada Agreement</a> (USMCA) became effective in July 2020 as the successor to NAFTA.<sup id="cite_ref-345" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-345">&#91;344&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h4><span class="mw-headline" id="Russia">Russia</span></h4>
<figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:President_Trump_at_the_G20_(48144047611).jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img alt="Trump and Putin, both seated, lean over and shake hands" src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a0/President_Trump_at_the_G20_%2848144047611%29.jpg/220px-President_Trump_at_the_G20_%2848144047611%29.jpg" decoding="async" width="220" height="147" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a0/President_Trump_at_the_G20_%2848144047611%29.jpg/330px-President_Trump_at_the_G20_%2848144047611%29.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a0/President_Trump_at_the_G20_%2848144047611%29.jpg/440px-President_Trump_at_the_G20_%2848144047611%29.jpg 2x" data-file-width="1200" data-file-height="800" /></a><figcaption>Putin and Trump shaking hands at the <a href="/wiki/2019_G20_Osaka_summit" title="2019 G20 Osaka summit">G20 Osaka summit</a>, June 2019</figcaption></figure>
<p>The Trump administration "water[ed] down the toughest penalties the U.S. had imposed on Russian entities" after its <a href="/wiki/2014_annexation_of_Crimea" class="mw-redirect" title="2014 annexation of Crimea">2014 annexation of Crimea</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-346" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-346">&#91;345&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-347" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-347">&#91;346&#93;</a></sup> Trump withdrew the U.S. from the <a href="/wiki/Intermediate-Range_Nuclear_Forces_Treaty" title="Intermediate-Range Nuclear Forces Treaty">Intermediate-Range Nuclear Forces Treaty</a>, citing alleged Russian non-compliance,<sup id="cite_ref-348" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-348">&#91;347&#93;</a></sup> and supported a potential return of Russia to the <a href="/wiki/G7" title="G7">G7</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-G8_349-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-G8-349">&#91;348&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>Trump repeatedly praised and rarely criticized Russian president <a href="/wiki/Vladimir_Putin" title="Vladimir Putin">Vladimir Putin</a><sup id="cite_ref-350" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-350">&#91;349&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-351" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-351">&#91;350&#93;</a></sup> but opposed some actions of the Russian government.<sup id="cite_ref-352" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-352">&#91;351&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-353" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-353">&#91;352&#93;</a></sup> After he met Putin at the <a href="/wiki/2018_Russia%E2%80%93United_States_summit" title="2018 Russia–United States summit">Helsinki Summit</a> in July 2018, Trump drew bipartisan criticism for accepting Putin's denial of <a href="/wiki/Russian_interference_in_the_2016_presidential_election" class="mw-redirect" title="Russian interference in the 2016 presidential election">Russian interference in the 2016 presidential election</a>, rather than accepting the findings of U.S. intelligence agencies.<sup id="cite_ref-354" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-354">&#91;353&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-355" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-355">&#91;354&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-356" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-356">&#91;355&#93;</a></sup> Trump did not discuss alleged <a href="/wiki/Russian_bounty_program" title="Russian bounty program">Russian bounties</a> offered to <a href="/wiki/Taliban" title="Taliban">Taliban</a> fighters for attacking American soldiers in <a href="/wiki/Afghanistan" title="Afghanistan">Afghanistan</a> with Putin, saying both that he doubted the intelligence and that he was not briefed on it.<sup id="cite_ref-357" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-357">&#91;356&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h4><span class="mw-headline" id="China">China</span></h4>
<p>Before and during his presidency, Trump repeatedly accused China of taking unfair advantage of the U.S.<sup id="cite_ref-358" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-358">&#91;357&#93;</a></sup> As president, Trump <a href="/wiki/China%E2%80%93United_States_trade_war" title="China–United States trade war">launched a trade war against China</a> that was widely characterized as a failure,<sup id="cite_ref-359" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-359">&#91;358&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-360" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-360">&#91;359&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-361" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-361">&#91;360&#93;</a></sup> sanctioned <a href="/wiki/Huawei" title="Huawei">Huawei</a> for its alleged ties to Iran,<sup id="cite_ref-362" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-362">&#91;361&#93;</a></sup> significantly increased visa restrictions on Chinese students and scholars,<sup id="cite_ref-363" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-363">&#91;362&#93;</a></sup> and classified China as a <a href="/wiki/Currency_manipulator" title="Currency manipulator">currency manipulator</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-364" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-364">&#91;363&#93;</a></sup> Trump also juxtaposed verbal attacks on China with praise of <a href="/wiki/Chinese_Communist_Party" title="Chinese Communist Party">Chinese Communist Party</a> <a href="/wiki/Leader_of_the_Chinese_Communist_Party" title="Leader of the Chinese Communist Party">leader</a> <a href="/wiki/Xi_Jinping" title="Xi Jinping">Xi Jinping</a>,<sup id="cite_ref-365" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-365">&#91;364&#93;</a></sup> which was attributed to trade war negotiations with the leader.<sup id="cite_ref-366" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-366">&#91;365&#93;</a></sup> After initially praising China for <a href="/wiki/Chinese_government_response_to_COVID-19" title="Chinese government response to COVID-19">its handling</a> of the <a href="/wiki/COVID-19_pandemic_in_China" title="COVID-19 pandemic in China">COVID-19 pandemic</a>,<sup id="cite_ref-367" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-367">&#91;366&#93;</a></sup> he began a campaign of criticism over its response starting in March 2020.<sup id="cite_ref-368" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-368">&#91;367&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>Trump said he resisted punishing China for <a href="/wiki/Human_rights_in_China" title="Human rights in China">its human rights abuses</a> against ethnic minorities in the northwestern <a href="/wiki/Xinjiang" title="Xinjiang">Xinjiang</a> region for fear of jeopardizing trade negotiations.<sup id="cite_ref-369" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-369">&#91;368&#93;</a></sup> In July 2020, <a href="/wiki/United_States_sanctions" title="United States sanctions">the Trump administration imposed sanctions</a> and visa restrictions against senior Chinese officials, in response to expanded mass <a href="/wiki/Xinjiang_re-education_camps" class="mw-redirect" title="Xinjiang re-education camps">detention camps</a> holding more than a million of the country's <a href="/wiki/Uyghurs" title="Uyghurs">Uyghur</a> <a href="/wiki/Islam_in_China" title="Islam in China">Muslim</a> ethnic minority.<sup id="cite_ref-370" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-370">&#91;369&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h4><span class="mw-headline" id="North_Korea">North Korea</span></h4>
