<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1033289096"><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">See also: <a href="/wiki/2018%E2%80%9319_Korean_peace_process" title="2018–19 Korean peace process">2018–19 Korean peace process</a></div>
<figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:Kim_and_Trump_shaking_hands_at_the_red_carpet_during_the_DPRK%E2%80%93USA_Singapore_Summit.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img alt="Trump and Kim shake hands on a stage with U.S. and North Korean flags in the background" src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/ab/Kim_and_Trump_shaking_hands_at_the_red_carpet_during_the_DPRK%E2%80%93USA_Singapore_Summit.jpg/220px-Kim_and_Trump_shaking_hands_at_the_red_carpet_during_the_DPRK%E2%80%93USA_Singapore_Summit.jpg" decoding="async" width="220" height="147" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/ab/Kim_and_Trump_shaking_hands_at_the_red_carpet_during_the_DPRK%E2%80%93USA_Singapore_Summit.jpg/330px-Kim_and_Trump_shaking_hands_at_the_red_carpet_during_the_DPRK%E2%80%93USA_Singapore_Summit.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/ab/Kim_and_Trump_shaking_hands_at_the_red_carpet_during_the_DPRK%E2%80%93USA_Singapore_Summit.jpg/440px-Kim_and_Trump_shaking_hands_at_the_red_carpet_during_the_DPRK%E2%80%93USA_Singapore_Summit.jpg 2x" data-file-width="1725" data-file-height="1150" /></a><figcaption>Trump meets <a href="/wiki/Kim_Jong_Un" title="Kim Jong Un">Kim Jong Un</a> at <a href="/wiki/2018_North_Korea%E2%80%93United_States_Singapore_Summit" title="2018 North Korea–United States Singapore Summit">the Singapore summit</a>, June 2018.</figcaption></figure>
<p>In 2017, when <a href="/wiki/North_Korea%27s_nuclear_weapons" class="mw-redirect" title="North Korea&#39;s nuclear weapons">North Korea's nuclear weapons</a> were increasingly seen as a serious threat,<sup id="cite_ref-371" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-371">&#91;370&#93;</a></sup> Trump escalated his rhetoric, warning that North Korean aggression would be met with "fire and fury like the world has never seen".<sup id="cite_ref-Windrem_372-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Windrem-372">&#91;371&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-373" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-373">&#91;372&#93;</a></sup> In 2017, Trump declared that he wanted North Korea's "complete denuclearization", and engaged in <a href="/wiki/Name-calling" class="mw-redirect" title="Name-calling">name-calling</a> with leader <a href="/wiki/Kim_Jong_Un" title="Kim Jong Un">Kim Jong Un</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-Windrem_372-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Windrem-372">&#91;371&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-374" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-374">&#91;373&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>After this period of tension, Trump and Kim exchanged at least 27 letters in which the two men described a warm personal friendship.<sup id="cite_ref-375" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-375">&#91;374&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-376" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-376">&#91;375&#93;</a></sup> Trump met Kim three times: <a href="/wiki/2018_North_Korea%E2%80%93United_States_Singapore_Summit" title="2018 North Korea–United States Singapore Summit">in Singapore</a> in 2018, <a href="/wiki/2019_North_Korea%E2%80%93United_States_Hanoi_Summit" title="2019 North Korea–United States Hanoi Summit">in Hanoi</a> in 2019, and <a href="/wiki/2019_Koreas%E2%80%93United_States_DMZ_Summit" title="2019 Koreas–United States DMZ Summit">in the Korean Demilitarized Zone</a> in 2019.<sup id="cite_ref-StepsInto_377-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-StepsInto-377">&#91;376&#93;</a></sup> Trump became the first sitting U.S. president to meet a North Korean leader or to set foot on North Korean soil.<sup id="cite_ref-StepsInto_377-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-StepsInto-377">&#91;376&#93;</a></sup> Trump also lifted some U.S. <a href="/wiki/Sanctions_against_North_Korea" class="mw-redirect" title="Sanctions against North Korea">sanctions against North Korea</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-378" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-378">&#91;377&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>However, no <a href="/wiki/Denuclearization" class="mw-redirect" title="Denuclearization">denuclearization</a> agreement was reached,<sup id="cite_ref-379" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-379">&#91;378&#93;</a></sup> and talks in October 2019 broke down after one day.<sup id="cite_ref-380" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-380">&#91;379&#93;</a></sup> While conducting no nuclear tests since 2017, North Korea continued to build up its arsenal of nuclear weapons and ballistic missiles.<sup id="cite_ref-381" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-381">&#91;380&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-382" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-382">&#91;381&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h4><span class="mw-headline" id="Afghanistan">Afghanistan</span></h4>
<figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:Secretary_Pompeo_Meets_With_the_Taliban_Delegation_(50333305012).jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img alt="U.S. and Taliban officials stand spaced apart in a formal room" src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/68/Secretary_Pompeo_Meets_With_the_Taliban_Delegation_%2850333305012%29.jpg/220px-Secretary_Pompeo_Meets_With_the_Taliban_Delegation_%2850333305012%29.jpg" decoding="async" width="220" height="147" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/68/Secretary_Pompeo_Meets_With_the_Taliban_Delegation_%2850333305012%29.jpg/330px-Secretary_Pompeo_Meets_With_the_Taliban_Delegation_%2850333305012%29.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/68/Secretary_Pompeo_Meets_With_the_Taliban_Delegation_%2850333305012%29.jpg/440px-Secretary_Pompeo_Meets_With_the_Taliban_Delegation_%2850333305012%29.jpg 2x" data-file-width="6758" data-file-height="4508" /></a><figcaption>U.S. Secretary of State <a href="/wiki/Mike_Pompeo" title="Mike Pompeo">Mike Pompeo</a> meeting with Taliban delegation in <a href="/wiki/Qatar" title="Qatar">Qatar</a> in September 2020</figcaption></figure>
<p>U.S. troop numbers in <a href="/wiki/Afghanistan" title="Afghanistan">Afghanistan</a> increased from 8,500 in January 2017 to 14,000 a year later,<sup id="cite_ref-383" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-383">&#91;382&#93;</a></sup> reversing Trump's pre-election position critical of further involvement in Afghanistan.<sup id="cite_ref-384" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-384">&#91;383&#93;</a></sup> In February 2020, the Trump administration signed a conditional <a href="/wiki/Afghan_peace_process" title="Afghan peace process">peace agreement with the Taliban</a>, which called for the <a href="/wiki/Withdrawal_of_United_States_troops_from_Afghanistan_(2021)" class="mw-redirect" title="Withdrawal of United States troops from Afghanistan (2021)">withdrawal of foreign troops</a> in 14 months "contingent on a guarantee from the Taliban that Afghan soil will not be used by terrorists with aims to attack the United States or its allies" and for the U.S. to seek the release of 5,000 <a href="/wiki/Taliban" title="Taliban">Taliban</a> imprisoned by the Afghan government.<sup id="cite_ref-385" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-385">&#91;384&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-386" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-386">&#91;385&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-5,000_387-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-5,000-387">&#91;386&#93;</a></sup> By the end of Trump's term, 5,000 Taliban had been released, and, despite the Taliban continuing attacks on Afghan forces and integrating <a href="/wiki/Al-Qaeda" title="Al-Qaeda">Al-Qaeda</a> members into its leadership, U.S. troops had been reduced to 2,500.<sup id="cite_ref-5,000_387-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-5,000-387">&#91;386&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h4><span class="mw-headline" id="Israel">Israel</span></h4>
<p>Trump supported many of the policies of Israeli Prime Minister <a href="/wiki/Benjamin_Netanyahu" title="Benjamin Netanyahu">Benjamin Netanyahu</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-388" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-388">&#91;387&#93;</a></sup> Under Trump, the U.S. <a href="/wiki/United_States_recognition_of_Jerusalem_as_capital_of_Israel" title="United States recognition of Jerusalem as capital of Israel">recognized Jerusalem as the capital of Israel</a><sup id="cite_ref-389" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-389">&#91;388&#93;</a></sup> and <a href="/wiki/United_States_recognition_of_the_Golan_Heights_as_part_of_Israel" title="United States recognition of the Golan Heights as part of Israel">Israeli sovereignty</a> over the <a href="/wiki/Golan_Heights" title="Golan Heights">Golan Heights</a>,<sup id="cite_ref-390" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-390">&#91;389&#93;</a></sup> leading to international condemnation including from the <a href="/wiki/United_Nations_General_Assembly" title="United Nations General Assembly">United Nations General Assembly</a>, the <a href="/wiki/European_Union" title="European Union">European Union</a>, and the <a href="/wiki/Arab_League" title="Arab League">Arab League</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-391" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-391">&#91;390&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-392" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-392">&#91;391&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h4><span class="mw-headline" id="Saudi_Arabia">Saudi Arabia</span></h4>
<figure class="mw-default-size mw-halign-left" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:Abdel_Fattah_el-Sisi,_King_Salman_of_Saudi_Arabia,_Melania_Trump,_and_Donald_Trump,_May_2017.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img alt="Trump, King Salman of Saudi Arabia, and Abdel Fattah el-Sisi place their hands on a glowing white orb light at waist level" src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/6d/Abdel_Fattah_el-Sisi%2C_King_Salman_of_Saudi_Arabia%2C_Melania_Trump%2C_and_Donald_Trump%2C_May_2017.jpg/220px-Abdel_Fattah_el-Sisi%2C_King_Salman_of_Saudi_Arabia%2C_Melania_Trump%2C_and_Donald_Trump%2C_May_2017.jpg" decoding="async" width="220" height="147" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/6d/Abdel_Fattah_el-Sisi%2C_King_Salman_of_Saudi_Arabia%2C_Melania_Trump%2C_and_Donald_Trump%2C_May_2017.jpg/330px-Abdel_Fattah_el-Sisi%2C_King_Salman_of_Saudi_Arabia%2C_Melania_Trump%2C_and_Donald_Trump%2C_May_2017.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/6d/Abdel_Fattah_el-Sisi%2C_King_Salman_of_Saudi_Arabia%2C_Melania_Trump%2C_and_Donald_Trump%2C_May_2017.jpg/440px-Abdel_Fattah_el-Sisi%2C_King_Salman_of_Saudi_Arabia%2C_Melania_Trump%2C_and_Donald_Trump%2C_May_2017.jpg 2x" data-file-width="1200" data-file-height="800" /></a><figcaption>Trump, King <a href="/wiki/Salman_of_Saudi_Arabia" title="Salman of Saudi Arabia">Salman of Saudi Arabia</a>, and Egyptian president <a href="/wiki/Abdel_Fattah_el-Sisi" title="Abdel Fattah el-Sisi">Abdel Fattah el-Sisi</a> at the <a href="/wiki/2017_Riyadh_summit" title="2017 Riyadh summit">2017 Riyadh summit</a> in Saudi Arabia</figcaption></figure>
<p>Trump actively supported the <a href="/wiki/Saudi_Arabian%E2%80%93led_intervention_in_Yemen" class="mw-redirect" title="Saudi Arabian–led intervention in Yemen">Saudi Arabian–led intervention in Yemen</a> against the <a href="/wiki/Houthis" class="mw-redirect" title="Houthis">Houthis</a> and in 2017 signed a $110&#160;billion agreement to sell arms to <a href="/wiki/Saudi_Arabia" title="Saudi Arabia">Saudi Arabia</a>,<sup id="cite_ref-393" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-393">&#91;392&#93;</a></sup> In 2018, the U.S. provided limited intelligence and logistical support for the intervention.<sup id="cite_ref-394" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-394">&#91;393&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-395" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-395">&#91;394&#93;</a></sup> Following the <a href="/wiki/Abqaiq%E2%80%93Khurais_attack" title="Abqaiq–Khurais attack">2019 attack on Saudi oil facilities</a>, which the U.S. and Saudi Arabia blamed on <a href="/wiki/Iran" title="Iran">Iran</a>, Trump approved the deployment of 3,000 additional U.S. troops, including fighter squadrons, two <a href="/wiki/MIM-104_Patriot" title="MIM-104 Patriot">Patriot batteries</a>, and a <a href="/wiki/Terminal_High_Altitude_Area_Defense" title="Terminal High Altitude Area Defense">Terminal High Altitude Area Defense</a> system (THAAD), to Saudi Arabia and the <a href="/wiki/United_Arab_Emirates" title="United Arab Emirates">United Arab Emirates</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-396" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-396">&#91;395&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h4><span class="mw-headline" id="Syria">Syria</span></h4>
<p>Trump ordered <a href="/wiki/2017_Shayrat_missile_strike" title="2017 Shayrat missile strike">missile strikes in April 2017</a> and <a href="/wiki/2018_missile_strikes_against_Syria" class="mw-redirect" title="2018 missile strikes against Syria">in April 2018</a> against the Assad regime in Syria, in retaliation for the <a href="/wiki/Khan_Shaykhun_chemical_attack" title="Khan Shaykhun chemical attack">Khan Shaykhun</a> and <a href="/wiki/Douma_chemical_attack" title="Douma chemical attack">Douma chemical attacks</a>, respectively.<sup id="cite_ref-397" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-397">&#91;396&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-398" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-398">&#91;397&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>In December 2018, Trump declared "we have won against ISIS", contradicting Department of Defense assessments, and ordered the withdrawal of all troops from Syria.<sup id="cite_ref-399" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-399">&#91;398&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-400" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-400">&#91;399&#93;</a></sup> The next day, Mattis resigned in protest, calling his decision an abandonment of the U.S.'s <a href="/wiki/Rojava" class="mw-redirect" title="Rojava">Kurdish allies</a> who played a key role in fighting ISIS.<sup id="cite_ref-401" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-401">&#91;400&#93;</a></sup> One week after his announcement, Trump said he would not approve any extension of the American deployment in Syria.<sup id="cite_ref-402" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-402">&#91;401&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:President_Trump_and_President_Erdo%C4%9Fan_joint_statement_in_the_Roosevelt_Room,_May_16,_2017.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/41/President_Trump_and_President_Erdo%C4%9Fan_joint_statement_in_the_Roosevelt_Room%2C_May_16%2C_2017.jpg/220px-President_Trump_and_President_Erdo%C4%9Fan_joint_statement_in_the_Roosevelt_Room%2C_May_16%2C_2017.jpg" decoding="async" width="220" height="147" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/41/President_Trump_and_President_Erdo%C4%9Fan_joint_statement_in_the_Roosevelt_Room%2C_May_16%2C_2017.jpg/330px-President_Trump_and_President_Erdo%C4%9Fan_joint_statement_in_the_Roosevelt_Room%2C_May_16%2C_2017.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/41/President_Trump_and_President_Erdo%C4%9Fan_joint_statement_in_the_Roosevelt_Room%2C_May_16%2C_2017.jpg/440px-President_Trump_and_President_Erdo%C4%9Fan_joint_statement_in_the_Roosevelt_Room%2C_May_16%2C_2017.jpg 2x" data-file-width="1200" data-file-height="800" /></a><figcaption>Trump and Turkish President <a href="/wiki/Recep_Tayyip_Erdo%C4%9Fan" title="Recep Tayyip Erdoğan">Recep Tayyip Erdoğan</a> at the White House in May 2017</figcaption></figure>
<p>In October 2019, after Trump spoke to Turkish president <a href="/wiki/Recep_Tayyip_Erdo%C4%9Fan" title="Recep Tayyip Erdoğan">Recep Tayyip Erdoğan</a>, <a href="/wiki/American-led_intervention_in_the_Syrian_Civil_War" class="mw-redirect" title="American-led intervention in the Syrian Civil War">U.S. troops in northern Syria</a> were withdrawn from the area and Turkey <a href="/wiki/2019_Turkish_offensive_into_north-eastern_Syria" title="2019 Turkish offensive into north-eastern Syria">invaded northern Syria</a>, attacking and <a href="/wiki/Forced_displacement" title="Forced displacement">displacing</a> American-allied <a href="/wiki/Kurds_in_Syria" title="Kurds in Syria">Kurds</a> in the area.<sup id="cite_ref-403" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-403">&#91;402&#93;</a></sup> Later that month, the U.S. House of Representatives, in a rare bipartisan vote of 354 to 60, condemned Trump's withdrawal of U.S. troops from Syria, for "abandoning U.S. allies, undermining the struggle against ISIS, and spurring a humanitarian catastrophe".<sup id="cite_ref-404" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-404">&#91;403&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-405" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-405">&#91;404&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h4><span class="mw-headline" id="Iran">Iran</span></h4>
<p>After an Iranian missile test on January 29, 2017, and Houthi attacks on Saudi warships, the Trump administration sanctioned 12 companies and 13 individuals suspected of being involved in Iran's missile program.<sup id="cite_ref-406" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-406">&#91;405&#93;</a></sup> In May 2018, Trump <a href="/wiki/United_States_withdrawal_from_the_Joint_Comprehensive_Plan_of_Action" title="United States withdrawal from the Joint Comprehensive Plan of Action">withdrew the United States</a> from the <a href="/wiki/Joint_Comprehensive_Plan_of_Action" title="Joint Comprehensive Plan of Action">Joint Comprehensive Plan of Action</a> (JCPOA), the 2015 agreement between Iran, the U.S., and five other countries that lifted most economic sanctions against Iran in return for Iran agreeing to restrictions on its nuclear program.<sup id="cite_ref-AP180508_407-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-AP180508-407">&#91;406&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-408" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-408">&#91;407&#93;</a></sup> Analysts determined that, after the United States's withdrawal, Iran moved closer to developing a nuclear weapon.<sup id="cite_ref-close_409-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-close-409">&#91;408&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>In January 2020, Trump ordered <a href="/wiki/Assassination_of_Qasem_Soleimani" title="Assassination of Qasem Soleimani">a U.S. airstrike</a> that killed Iranian general <a href="/wiki/Qasem_Soleimani" title="Qasem Soleimani">Qasem Soleimani</a>, who had planned nearly every significant operation by Iranian forces over the past two decades.<sup id="cite_ref-410" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-410">&#91;409&#93;</a></sup> Trump threatened to hit 52 Iranian sites, including some "important to Iran &amp; the Iranian culture", if Iran retaliated.<sup id="cite_ref-411" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-411">&#91;410&#93;</a></sup> The threat to hit cultural sites was seen as illegal and both Defense Secretary Mark Esper and Secretary of State Mike Pompeo said that the U.S. would not attack such sites, but would "follow the laws of armed conflict" and "behave inside the system".<sup id="cite_ref-Wamsley_1/6/2020_412-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Wamsley_1/6/2020-412">&#91;411&#93;</a></sup> Iran did retaliate with <a href="/wiki/Operation_Martyr_Soleimani" title="Operation Martyr Soleimani">ballistic missile strikes against two U.S. airbases</a> in Iraq.<sup id="cite_ref-close_409-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-close-409">&#91;408&#93;</a></sup> On the same day, amid the heightened tensions between the United States and Iran, Iran accidentally<sup id="cite_ref-Ward_1/9/2020_413-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Ward_1/9/2020-413">&#91;412&#93;</a></sup> shot down <a href="/wiki/Ukraine_International_Airlines_Flight_752" title="Ukraine International Airlines Flight 752">Ukraine International Airlines Flight 752</a> after takeoff from Tehran airport.<sup id="cite_ref-Baker_et_al_1/11/2020_414-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Baker_et_al_1/11/2020-414">&#91;413&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-Ward_1/9/2020_413-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Ward_1/9/2020-413">&#91;412&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-Motamedi_4/17/2021_415-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Motamedi_4/17/2021-415">&#91;414&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>In August 2020, the Trump administration unsuccessfully attempted to trigger a mechanism that was part of the agreement that would have led to the return of U.N. sanctions against Iran.<sup id="cite_ref-416" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-416">&#91;415&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h3><span class="mw-headline" id="Personnel">Personnel</span></h3>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1033289096"><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Main articles: <a href="/wiki/Political_appointments_by_Donald_Trump" title="Political appointments by Donald Trump">Political appointments by Donald Trump</a> and <a href="/wiki/Cabinet_of_Donald_Trump" title="Cabinet of Donald Trump">Cabinet of Donald Trump</a></div>
<p>The Trump administration had a high turnover of personnel, particularly among White House staff. By the end of Trump's first year in office, 34 percent of his original staff had resigned, been fired, or been reassigned.<sup id="cite_ref-417" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-417">&#91;416&#93;</a></sup> As of early&#32;July&#160;2018<sup class="plainlinks noexcerpt noprint asof-tag update" style="display:none;"><a class="external text" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Donald_Trump&amp;action=edit">&#91;update&#93;</a></sup>, 61 percent of Trump's senior aides had left<sup id="cite_ref-418" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-418">&#91;417&#93;</a></sup> and 141 staffers had left in the previous year.<sup id="cite_ref-419" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-419">&#91;418&#93;</a></sup> Both figures set a record for recent presidents—more change in the first 13 months than his four immediate predecessors saw in their first two years.<sup id="cite_ref-Keith_420-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Keith-420">&#91;419&#93;</a></sup> Notable early departures included National Security Advisor Flynn (after just 25 days in office), and Press Secretary <a href="/wiki/Sean_Spicer" title="Sean Spicer">Sean Spicer</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-Keith_420-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Keith-420">&#91;419&#93;</a></sup> Close personal aides to Trump including Bannon, <a href="/wiki/Hope_Hicks" title="Hope Hicks">Hope Hicks</a>, <a href="/wiki/John_McEntee_(political_aide)" title="John McEntee (political aide)">John McEntee</a>, and <a href="/wiki/Keith_Schiller" title="Keith Schiller">Keith Schiller</a> quit or were forced out.<sup id="cite_ref-Brookings_421-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Brookings-421">&#91;420&#93;</a></sup> Some, including Hicks and McEntee, later returned to the White House in different posts.<sup id="cite_ref-422" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-422">&#91;421&#93;</a></sup> Trump publicly disparaged several of his former top officials, calling them incompetent, stupid, or crazy.<sup id="cite_ref-423" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-423">&#91;422&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>Trump had four <a href="/wiki/White_House_chiefs_of_staff" class="mw-redirect" title="White House chiefs of staff">White House chiefs of staff</a>, marginalizing or pushing out several.<sup id="cite_ref-Keither_424-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Keither-424">&#91;423&#93;</a></sup> <a href="/wiki/Reince_Priebus" title="Reince Priebus">Reince Priebus</a> was replaced after seven months by retired Marine general <a href="/wiki/John_F._Kelly" title="John F. Kelly">John F. Kelly</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-425" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-425">&#91;424&#93;</a></sup> Kelly resigned in December 2018 after a tumultuous tenure in which his influence waned, and Trump subsequently disparaged him.<sup id="cite_ref-426" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-426">&#91;425&#93;</a></sup> Kelly was succeeded by <a href="/wiki/Mick_Mulvaney" title="Mick Mulvaney">Mick Mulvaney</a> as acting chief of staff; he was replaced in March 2020 by <a href="/wiki/Mark_Meadows" title="Mark Meadows">Mark Meadows</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-Keither_424-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Keither-424">&#91;423&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>On May 9, 2017, Trump <a href="/wiki/Dismissal_of_James_Comey" title="Dismissal of James Comey">dismissed FBI director James Comey</a>. While initially attributing this action to Comey's conduct in the investigation about <a href="/wiki/Hillary_Clinton_email_controversy#October_2016_–_Additional_investigation" title="Hillary Clinton email controversy">Hillary Clinton's emails</a>, Trump said a few days later that he was concerned with Comey's roles in the ongoing Trump-Russia investigations, and that he had intended to fire Comey earlier.<sup id="cite_ref-427" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-427">&#91;426&#93;</a></sup> At a private conversation in February, Trump said he hoped Comey would drop the investigation into Flynn.<sup id="cite_ref-cloud_428-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-cloud-428">&#91;427&#93;</a></sup> In March and April, Trump asked Comey to "lift the cloud impairing his ability to act" by saying publicly that the FBI was not investigating him.<sup id="cite_ref-cloud_428-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-cloud-428">&#91;427&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-429" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-429">&#91;428&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>Turnover was relatively high within the Trump Cabinet.<sup id="cite_ref-Brookings_421-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Brookings-421">&#91;420&#93;</a></sup> Trump lost three of his 15 original cabinet members within his first year.<sup id="cite_ref-538_Cabinet_430-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-538_Cabinet-430">&#91;429&#93;</a></sup> Health and Human Services secretary <a href="/wiki/Tom_Price_(American_politician)" title="Tom Price (American politician)">Tom Price</a> was forced to resign in September 2017 due to excessive use of private charter jets and military aircraft.<sup id="cite_ref-538_Cabinet_430-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-538_Cabinet-430">&#91;429&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-Brookings_421-2" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Brookings-421">&#91;420&#93;</a></sup> Environmental Protection Agency administrator <a href="/wiki/Scott_Pruitt" title="Scott Pruitt">Scott Pruitt</a> resigned in 2018 and Secretary of the Interior <a href="/wiki/Ryan_Zinke" title="Ryan Zinke">Ryan Zinke</a> in January 2019 amid multiple investigations into their conduct.<sup id="cite_ref-431" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-431">&#91;430&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-432" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-432">&#91;431&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>Trump was slow to appoint second-tier officials in the executive branch, saying many of the positions are unnecessary. In October 2017, there were still hundreds of sub-cabinet positions without a nominee.<sup id="cite_ref-433" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-433">&#91;432&#93;</a></sup> By January 8, 2019, of 706 key positions, 433 had been filled (61 percent) and Trump had no nominee for 264 (37 percent).<sup id="cite_ref-434" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-434">&#91;433&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h3><span class="mw-headline" id="Judiciary">Judiciary</span></h3>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1033289096"><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Further information: <a href="/wiki/List_of_federal_judges_appointed_by_Donald_Trump" title="List of federal judges appointed by Donald Trump">List of federal judges appointed by Donald Trump</a> and <a href="/wiki/Donald_Trump_judicial_appointment_controversies" title="Donald Trump judicial appointment controversies">Donald Trump judicial appointment controversies</a></div>
<figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:President_Trump_Nominates_Judge_Amy_Coney_Barrett_for_Associate_Justice_of_the_U.S._Supreme_Court_(50397882607).jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img alt="Donald Trump and Amy Coney Barrett walk side by side along the West Wing Colonnade; American flags hang between the columns to their right" src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/7f/President_Trump_Nominates_Judge_Amy_Coney_Barrett_for_Associate_Justice_of_the_U.S._Supreme_Court_%2850397882607%29.jpg/220px-President_Trump_Nominates_Judge_Amy_Coney_Barrett_for_Associate_Justice_of_the_U.S._Supreme_Court_%2850397882607%29.jpg" decoding="async" width="220" height="147" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/7f/President_Trump_Nominates_Judge_Amy_Coney_Barrett_for_Associate_Justice_of_the_U.S._Supreme_Court_%2850397882607%29.jpg/330px-President_Trump_Nominates_Judge_Amy_Coney_Barrett_for_Associate_Justice_of_the_U.S._Supreme_Court_%2850397882607%29.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/7f/President_Trump_Nominates_Judge_Amy_Coney_Barrett_for_Associate_Justice_of_the_U.S._Supreme_Court_%2850397882607%29.jpg/440px-President_Trump_Nominates_Judge_Amy_Coney_Barrett_for_Associate_Justice_of_the_U.S._Supreme_Court_%2850397882607%29.jpg 2x" data-file-width="3000" data-file-height="2000" /></a><figcaption>Trump and his third Supreme Court nominee, <a href="/wiki/Amy_Coney_Barrett" title="Amy Coney Barrett">Amy Coney Barrett</a></figcaption></figure>
<p>Trump appointed 226 <a href="/wiki/United_States_federal_judge" title="United States federal judge">Article III judges</a>, including 54 to the <a href="/wiki/United_States_courts_of_appeals" title="United States courts of appeals">courts of appeals</a> and <a href="/wiki/Donald_Trump_Supreme_Court_candidates" title="Donald Trump Supreme Court candidates">three</a> to the <a href="/wiki/Supreme_Court_of_the_United_States" title="Supreme Court of the United States">Supreme Court</a>: <a href="/wiki/Neil_Gorsuch" title="Neil Gorsuch">Neil Gorsuch</a>, <a href="/wiki/Brett_Kavanaugh" title="Brett Kavanaugh">Brett Kavanaugh</a>, and <a href="/wiki/Amy_Coney_Barrett" title="Amy Coney Barrett">Amy Coney Barrett</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-435" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-435">&#91;434&#93;</a></sup> Trump's Supreme Court nominees were noted as having politically shifted the Supreme Court to the right.<sup id="cite_ref-436" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-436">&#91;435&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-437" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-437">&#91;436&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-438" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-438">&#91;437&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-439" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-439">&#91;438&#93;</a></sup> In the 2016 campaign, Trump pledged that <i>Roe v. Wade</i> would be overturned "automatically" if he were elected and provided the opportunity to appoint two or three pro-life justices. Trump later took credit when <i>Roe</i> was overturned in <i><a href="/wiki/Dobbs_v._Jackson_Women%27s_Health_Organization" title="Dobbs v. Jackson Women&#39;s Health Organization">Dobbs v. Jackson Women's Health Organization</a></i>; all three of his Supreme Court nominees voted with the majority.<sup id="cite_ref-440" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-440">&#91;439&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-441" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-441">&#91;440&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-442" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-442">&#91;441&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>Trump disparaged courts and judges he disagreed with, often in personal terms, and questioned the judiciary's constitutional authority. Trump's attacks on the courts drew rebukes from observers, including sitting federal judges, concerned about the effect of Trump's statements on the <a href="/wiki/Judicial_independence" title="Judicial independence">judicial independence</a> and public confidence in the judiciary.<sup id="cite_ref-443" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-443">&#91;442&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-444" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-444">&#91;443&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-445" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-445">&#91;444&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h3><span class="mw-headline" id="COVID-19_pandemic">COVID-19 pandemic</span></h3>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1033289096"><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Main articles: <a href="/wiki/COVID-19_pandemic" title="COVID-19 pandemic">COVID-19 pandemic</a> and <a href="/wiki/COVID-19_pandemic_in_the_United_States" title="COVID-19 pandemic in the United States">COVID-19 pandemic in the United States</a></div>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1033289096"><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Further information: <a href="/wiki/U.S._federal_government_response_to_the_COVID-19_pandemic" title="U.S. federal government response to the COVID-19 pandemic">U.S. federal government response to the COVID-19 pandemic</a> and <a href="/wiki/Communication_of_the_Trump_administration_during_the_COVID-19_pandemic" title="Communication of the Trump administration during the COVID-19 pandemic">Communication of the Trump administration during the COVID-19 pandemic</a></div>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1033289096"><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">See also: <a href="/wiki/Economic_impact_of_the_COVID-19_pandemic_in_the_United_States" title="Economic impact of the COVID-19 pandemic in the United States">Economic impact of the COVID-19 pandemic in the United States</a></div>
<p>In December 2019, <a href="/wiki/Coronavirus_disease_2019" class="mw-redirect" title="Coronavirus disease 2019">COVID-19</a> erupted in <a href="/wiki/Wuhan" title="Wuhan">Wuhan</a>, China; the <a href="/wiki/SARS-CoV-2" title="SARS-CoV-2">SARS-CoV-2 virus</a> spread worldwide within weeks.<sup id="cite_ref-WHOpandemic2_446-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-WHOpandemic2-446">&#91;445&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-447" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-447">&#91;446&#93;</a></sup> The first confirmed case in the U.S. was reported on January 20, 2020.<sup id="cite_ref-448" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-448">&#91;447&#93;</a></sup> The outbreak was officially declared a public health emergency by <a href="/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_Health_and_Human_Services" title="United States Secretary of Health and Human Services">Health and Human Services (HHS) Secretary</a> <a href="/wiki/Alex_Azar" title="Alex Azar">Alex Azar</a> on January 31, 2020.<sup id="cite_ref-449" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-449">&#91;448&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>Trump's public statements on COVID-19 were at odds with his private statements. In February 2020 Trump publicly asserted that the outbreak in the U.S. was less deadly than influenza, was "very much under control", and would soon be over.<sup id="cite_ref-450" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-450">&#91;449&#93;</a></sup> At the same time he acknowledged the opposite in a private conversation with <a href="/wiki/Bob_Woodward" title="Bob Woodward">Bob Woodward</a>. In March 2020, Trump privately told Woodward that he was deliberately "playing it down" in public so as not to create panic.<sup id="cite_ref-451" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-451">&#91;450&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-452" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-452">&#91;451&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h4><span class="mw-headline" id="Initial_response">Initial response</span></h4>
<p>Trump was slow to address the spread of the disease, initially dismissing the threat and ignoring persistent public health warnings and calls for action from health officials within his administration and Secretary Azar.<sup id="cite_ref-453" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-453">&#91;452&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-NYT_4_11_20_454-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-NYT_4_11_20-454">&#91;453&#93;</a></sup> Throughout January and February he focused on economic and political considerations of the outbreak, and largely ignored the danger.<sup id="cite_ref-455" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-455">&#91;454&#93;</a></sup> By mid-March, most global financial markets had <a href="/wiki/2020_stock_market_crash" title="2020 stock market crash">severely contracted</a> in response to the emerging pandemic.<sup id="cite_ref-456" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-456">&#91;455&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>On March 6, Trump signed the <a href="/wiki/Coronavirus_Preparedness_and_Response_Supplemental_Appropriations_Act" class="mw-redirect" title="Coronavirus Preparedness and Response Supplemental Appropriations Act">Coronavirus Preparedness and Response Supplemental Appropriations Act</a> into law, which provided $8.3&#160;billion in emergency funding for federal agencies.<sup id="cite_ref-457" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-457">&#91;456&#93;</a></sup> On March 11, the <a href="/wiki/World_Health_Organization" title="World Health Organization">World Health Organization</a> (WHO) recognized the spread of COVID-19 as a <a href="/wiki/Pandemic" title="Pandemic">pandemic</a>,<sup id="cite_ref-WHOpandemic2_446-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-WHOpandemic2-446">&#91;445&#93;</a></sup> and Trump announced partial travel restrictions for most of Europe, effective March 13.<sup id="cite_ref-458" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-458">&#91;457&#93;</a></sup> That same day, he gave his first serious assessment of the virus in a nationwide Oval Office address, calling the outbreak "horrible" but "a temporary moment" and saying there was no financial crisis.<sup id="cite_ref-459" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-459">&#91;458&#93;</a></sup> On March 13, he declared a <a href="/wiki/State_of_emergency" title="State of emergency">national emergency</a>, freeing up federal resources.<sup id="cite_ref-460" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-460">&#91;459&#93;</a></sup> Trump falsely claimed that "anybody that wants a test can get a test", despite the availability of tests being severely limited.<sup id="cite_ref-461" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-461">&#91;460&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>In September 2019, the Trump administration terminated <a href="/wiki/United_States_Agency_for_International_Development" title="United States Agency for International Development">United States Agency for International Development</a>'s <a href="/wiki/PREDICT_(USAID)" class="mw-redirect" title="PREDICT (USAID)">PREDICT</a> program, a $200&#160;million <a href="/wiki/Epidemiological" class="mw-redirect" title="Epidemiological">epidemiological</a> research program initiated in 2009 to provide early warning of pandemics abroad.<sup id="cite_ref-462" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-462">&#91;461&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-463" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-463">&#91;462&#93;</a></sup> The program trained scientists in sixty foreign laboratories to detect and respond to viruses that have the potential to cause pandemics. One such laboratory was the Wuhan lab that first identified the virus that causes COVID-19. After revival in April 2020, the program was given two 6-month extensions to help fight COVID-19 in the U.S. and other countries.<sup id="cite_ref-LATimes_PREDICT_464-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-LATimes_PREDICT-464">&#91;463&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-465" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-465">&#91;464&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>On April 22, Trump signed an executive order restricting some forms of <a href="/wiki/Immigration_to_the_United_States" title="Immigration to the United States">immigration to the United States</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-466" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-466">&#91;465&#93;</a></sup> In late spring and early summer, with infections and death counts continuing to rise, he adopted a strategy of blaming the states for the growing pandemic, rather than accepting that his initial assessments of the course of the pandemic were overly optimistic or his failure to provide presidential leadership.<sup id="cite_ref-467" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-467">&#91;466&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h4><span class="mw-headline" id="White_House_Coronavirus_Task_Force">White House Coronavirus Task Force</span></h4>
<figure class="mw-default-size mw-halign-right" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:White_House_Press_Briefing_(49666120807).jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img alt="Trump speaks in the West Wing briefing room with various officials standing behind him, all in formal attire and without face masks" src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/d9/White_House_Press_Briefing_%2849666120807%29.jpg/220px-White_House_Press_Briefing_%2849666120807%29.jpg" decoding="async" width="220" height="147" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/d9/White_House_Press_Briefing_%2849666120807%29.jpg/330px-White_House_Press_Briefing_%2849666120807%29.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/d9/White_House_Press_Briefing_%2849666120807%29.jpg/440px-White_House_Press_Briefing_%2849666120807%29.jpg 2x" data-file-width="2500" data-file-height="1667" /></a><figcaption>Trump conducts a COVID-19 press briefing with members of the <a href="/wiki/White_House_Coronavirus_Task_Force" title="White House Coronavirus Task Force">White House Coronavirus Task Force</a> on March 15, 2020.</figcaption></figure>
<p>Trump established the <a href="/wiki/White_House_Coronavirus_Task_Force" title="White House Coronavirus Task Force">White House Coronavirus Task Force</a> on January 29, 2020.<sup id="cite_ref-468" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-468">&#91;467&#93;</a></sup> Beginning in mid-March, Trump held a daily task force press conference, joined by medical experts and other administration officials,<sup id="cite_ref-Karni_469-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Karni-469">&#91;468&#93;</a></sup> sometimes disagreeing with them by promoting unproven treatments.<sup id="cite_ref-470" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-470">&#91;469&#93;</a></sup> Trump was the main speaker at the briefings, where he praised his own response to the pandemic, frequently criticized rival presidential candidate Joe Biden, and denounced the press.<sup id="cite_ref-Karni_469-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Karni-469">&#91;468&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-471" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-471">&#91;470&#93;</a></sup> On March 16, he acknowledged for the first time that the pandemic was not under control and that months of disruption to daily lives and a recession might occur.<sup id="cite_ref-472" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-472">&#91;471&#93;</a></sup> His repeated use of the terms "Chinese virus" and "China virus" to describe COVID-19 drew criticism from health experts.<sup id="cite_ref-473" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-473">&#91;472&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-474" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-474">&#91;473&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-475" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-475">&#91;474&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>By early April, as the pandemic worsened and amid criticism of his administration's response, Trump refused to admit any mistakes in his handling of the outbreak, instead blaming the media, Democratic state governors, the previous administration, China, and the <a href="/wiki/World_Health_Organization" title="World Health Organization">World Health Organization</a> (WHO).<sup id="cite_ref-476" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-476">&#91;475&#93;</a></sup> The daily coronavirus task force briefings ended in late April, after a briefing at which Trump suggested the dangerous idea of injecting a disinfectant to treat COVID-19;<sup id="cite_ref-477" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-477">&#91;476&#93;</a></sup> the comment was widely condemned by medical professionals.<sup id="cite_ref-478" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-478">&#91;477&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-479" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-479">&#91;478&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:President_Trump_Visits_with_the_President_of_Poland_(50044008817).jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img alt="Donald Trump and Andrzej Duda sit in a packed Oval Office, surrounded by other officials and members of the press. Only the press are masked." src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/8a/President_Trump_Visits_with_the_President_of_Poland_%2850044008817%29.jpg/220px-President_Trump_Visits_with_the_President_of_Poland_%2850044008817%29.jpg" decoding="async" width="220" height="147" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/8a/President_Trump_Visits_with_the_President_of_Poland_%2850044008817%29.jpg/330px-President_Trump_Visits_with_the_President_of_Poland_%2850044008817%29.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/8a/President_Trump_Visits_with_the_President_of_Poland_%2850044008817%29.jpg/440px-President_Trump_Visits_with_the_President_of_Poland_%2850044008817%29.jpg 2x" data-file-width="5808" data-file-height="3872" /></a><figcaption><a href="/wiki/Poland" title="Poland">Poland</a>'s president <a href="/wiki/Andrzej_Duda" title="Andrzej Duda">Andrzej Duda</a> visited the <a href="/wiki/White_House" title="White House">White House</a> on June 24, 2020, the first foreign leader to do so since the start of the pandemic.</figcaption></figure>
<p>In early May, Trump proposed the phase-out of the coronavirus task force and its replacement with another group centered on reopening the economy. Amid a backlash, Trump said the task force would "indefinitely" continue.<sup id="cite_ref-480" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-480">&#91;479&#93;</a></sup> By the end of May, the coronavirus task force's meetings were sharply reduced.<sup id="cite_ref-481" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-481">&#91;480&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h4><span class="mw-headline" id="World_Health_Organization">World Health Organization</span></h4>
<p>Prior to the pandemic, Trump criticized the <a href="/wiki/World_Health_Organization" title="World Health Organization">World Health Organization</a> (WHO) and other international bodies, which he asserted were taking advantage of U.S. aid.<sup id="cite_ref-Politico_WHO_482-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Politico_WHO-482">&#91;481&#93;</a></sup> His administration's proposed 2021 federal budget, released in February, proposed reducing WHO funding by more than half.<sup id="cite_ref-Politico_WHO_482-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Politico_WHO-482">&#91;481&#93;</a></sup> In May and April, Trump accused the WHO of "severely mismanaging and covering up the spread of the coronavirus" and alleged without evidence that the organization was under Chinese control and had enabled the Chinese government's concealment of the origins of the pandemic.<sup id="cite_ref-Politico_WHO_482-2" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Politico_WHO-482">&#91;481&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-CNN_WHO_483-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-CNN_WHO-483">&#91;482&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-BBC_WHO_484-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-BBC_WHO-484">&#91;483&#93;</a></sup> He then announced that he was withdrawing funding for the organization.<sup id="cite_ref-Politico_WHO_482-3" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Politico_WHO-482">&#91;481&#93;</a></sup> Trump's criticisms and actions regarding the WHO were seen as attempts to distract attention from his own mishandling of the pandemic.<sup id="cite_ref-Politico_WHO_482-4" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Politico_WHO-482">&#91;481&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-485" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-485">&#91;484&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-486" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-486">&#91;485&#93;</a></sup> In July 2020, Trump announced the formal withdrawal of the United States from the WHO effective July 2021.<sup id="cite_ref-CNN_WHO_483-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-CNN_WHO-483">&#91;482&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-BBC_WHO_484-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-BBC_WHO-484">&#91;483&#93;</a></sup> The decision was widely condemned by health and government officials as "short-sighted", "senseless", and "dangerous".<sup id="cite_ref-CNN_WHO_483-2" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-CNN_WHO-483">&#91;482&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-BBC_WHO_484-2" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-BBC_WHO-484">&#91;483&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h4><span class="mw-headline" id="Testing">Testing</span></h4>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1033289096"><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Further information: <a href="/wiki/COVID-19_testing_in_the_United_States" title="COVID-19 testing in the United States">COVID-19 testing in the United States</a></div>
<p>In June and July, Trump said several times that the U.S. would have fewer cases of coronavirus if it did less testing, that having a large number of reported cases "makes us look bad".<sup id="cite_ref-487" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-487">&#91;486&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-488" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-488">&#91;487&#93;</a></sup> The CDC guideline at the time was that any person exposed to the virus should be "quickly identified and tested" even if they are not showing symptoms, because asymptomatic people can still spread the virus.<sup id="cite_ref-489" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-489">&#91;488&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-490" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-490">&#91;489&#93;</a></sup> In August 2020 the CDC quietly lowered its recommendation for testing, advising that people who have been exposed to the virus, but are not showing symptoms, "do not necessarily need a test". The change in guidelines was made by HHS political appointees under Trump administration pressure, against the wishes of CDC scientists.<sup id="cite_ref-CNN-testing-pressure_491-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-CNN-testing-pressure-491">&#91;490&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-Gumbrecht_492-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Gumbrecht-492">&#91;491&#93;</a></sup> The day after this <a href="/wiki/Trump_administration_political_interference_with_science_agencies" title="Trump administration political interference with science agencies">political interference</a> was reported, the testing guideline was changed back to its original recommendation, stressing that anyone who has been in contact with an infected person should be tested.<sup id="cite_ref-Gumbrecht_492-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Gumbrecht-492">&#91;491&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h4><span class="mw-headline" id="Pressure_to_abandon_pandemic_mitigation_measures">Pressure to abandon pandemic mitigation measures</span></h4>
<p>In April 2020, Republican-connected groups organized <a href="/wiki/Protests_in_the_United_States_over_responses_to_the_COVID-19_pandemic" class="mw-redirect" title="Protests in the United States over responses to the COVID-19 pandemic">anti-lockdown protests</a> against the measures state governments were taking to combat the pandemic;<sup id="cite_ref-493" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-493">&#91;492&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-494" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-494">&#91;493&#93;</a></sup> Trump encouraged the protests on <a href="/wiki/Twitter" title="Twitter">Twitter</a>,<sup id="cite_ref-495" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-495">&#91;494&#93;</a></sup> even though the targeted states did not meet the Trump administration's own guidelines for reopening.<sup id="cite_ref-496" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-496">&#91;495&#93;</a></sup> In April 2020, he first supported, then later criticized, <a href="/wiki/Georgia_(U.S._state)" title="Georgia (U.S. state)">Georgia</a> Governor <a href="/wiki/Brian_Kemp" title="Brian Kemp">Brian Kemp</a>'s plan to reopen some nonessential businesses.<sup id="cite_ref-497" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-497">&#91;496&#93;</a></sup> Throughout the spring he increasingly pushed for ending the restrictions as a way to reverse the damage to the country's economy.<sup id="cite_ref-498" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-498">&#91;497&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>Trump often refused to <a href="/wiki/Face_masks_during_the_COVID-19_pandemic" title="Face masks during the COVID-19 pandemic">wear a face mask</a> at public events, contrary to his own administration's April 2020 guidance that Americans should wear masks in public<sup id="cite_ref-99days_499-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-99days-499">&#91;498&#93;</a></sup> and despite nearly unanimous medical consensus that masks are important to preventing the spread of the virus.<sup id="cite_ref-WAPost_Mask_500-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-WAPost_Mask-500">&#91;499&#93;</a></sup> By June, Trump had said masks were a "double-edged sword"; ridiculed Biden for wearing masks; continually emphasized that mask-wearing was optional; and suggested that wearing a mask was a political statement against him personally.<sup id="cite_ref-WAPost_Mask_500-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-WAPost_Mask-500">&#91;499&#93;</a></sup> Trump's contradiction of medical recommendations weakened national efforts to mitigate the pandemic.<sup id="cite_ref-99days_499-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-99days-499">&#91;498&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-WAPost_Mask_500-2" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-WAPost_Mask-500">&#91;499&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>Despite record numbers of COVID-19 cases in the U.S. from mid-June onward and an increasing percentage of positive test results, Trump largely continued to downplay the pandemic, including his false claim in early July 2020 that 99 percent of COVID-19 cases are "totally harmless".<sup id="cite_ref-501" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-501">&#91;500&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-502" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-502">&#91;501&#93;</a></sup> He also began insisting that all states should open schools to in-person education in the fall despite a July spike in reported cases.<sup id="cite_ref-503" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-503">&#91;502&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h4><span class="mw-headline" id="Political_pressure_on_health_agencies">Political pressure on health agencies</span></h4>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1033289096"><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Main article: <a href="/wiki/Trump_administration_political_interference_with_science_agencies" title="Trump administration political interference with science agencies">Trump administration political interference with science agencies</a></div>
<p>Trump repeatedly pressured federal health agencies to take actions he favored,<sup id="cite_ref-CNN-testing-pressure_491-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-CNN-testing-pressure-491">&#91;490&#93;</a></sup> such as approving unproven treatments<sup id="cite_ref-504" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-504">&#91;503&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-pressed_505-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-pressed-505">&#91;504&#93;</a></sup> or speeding up the approval of vaccines.<sup id="cite_ref-pressed_505-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-pressed-505">&#91;504&#93;</a></sup> Trump administration political appointees at HHS sought to control CDC communications to the public that undermined Trump's claims that the pandemic was under control. CDC resisted many of the changes, but increasingly allowed HHS personnel to review articles and suggest changes before publication.<sup id="cite_ref-506" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-506">&#91;505&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-507" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-507">&#91;506&#93;</a></sup> Trump alleged without evidence that FDA scientists were part of a "<a href="/wiki/Deep_state" title="Deep state">deep state</a>" opposing him, and delaying approval of vaccines and treatments to hurt him politically.<sup id="cite_ref-508" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-508">&#91;507&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h4><span class="mw-headline" id="Outbreak_at_the_White_House">Outbreak at the White House</span></h4>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1033289096"><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Main article: <a href="/wiki/White_House_COVID-19_outbreak" title="White House COVID-19 outbreak">White House COVID-19 outbreak</a></div>
<figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:President_Trump_Boards_Marine_One_(50436803733).jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img alt="Donald Trump, wearing a black face mask, boards Marine One, a large green helicopter, from the White House lawn" src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/4c/President_Trump_Boards_Marine_One_%2850436803733%29.jpg/230px-President_Trump_Boards_Marine_One_%2850436803733%29.jpg" decoding="async" width="230" height="174" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/4c/President_Trump_Boards_Marine_One_%2850436803733%29.jpg/345px-President_Trump_Boards_Marine_One_%2850436803733%29.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/4c/President_Trump_Boards_Marine_One_%2850436803733%29.jpg/460px-President_Trump_Boards_Marine_One_%2850436803733%29.jpg 2x" data-file-width="2200" data-file-height="1669" /></a><figcaption>Trump boards <a href="/wiki/Marine_One" title="Marine One">Marine One</a> for COVID-19 treatment on October 2, 2020.</figcaption></figure>
<p>On October 2, 2020, Trump tweeted that he had tested positive for <a href="/wiki/Coronavirus_disease_2019" class="mw-redirect" title="Coronavirus disease 2019">COVID-19</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-509" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-509">&#91;508&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-510" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-510">&#91;509&#93;</a></sup> His wife, their son Barron, and numerous staff members and visitors also became infected.<sup id="cite_ref-downplay_511-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-downplay-511">&#91;510&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-drug_512-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-drug-512">&#91;511&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>Later that day <a href="/wiki/Donald_Trump%27s_COVID-19_infection" class="mw-redirect" title="Donald Trump&#39;s COVID-19 infection">Trump was hospitalized</a> at <a href="/wiki/Walter_Reed_National_Military_Medical_Center" title="Walter Reed National Military Medical Center">Walter Reed National Military Medical Center</a>, reportedly due to labored breathing and a fever. He was treated with antiviral and experimental antibody drugs and a steroid. He returned to the White House on October 5, still struggling with the disease.<sup id="cite_ref-sicker_513-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-sicker-513">&#91;512&#93;</a></sup> During and after his treatment he continued to downplay the virus.<sup id="cite_ref-downplay_511-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-downplay-511">&#91;510&#93;</a></sup> In 2021, it was revealed that his condition had been far more serious; he had dangerously low blood oxygen levels, a high fever, and lung infiltrates, indicating a severe case of the disease.<sup id="cite_ref-drug_512-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-drug-512">&#91;511&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h4><span class="mw-headline" id="Effects_on_the_2020_presidential_campaign">Effects on the 2020 presidential campaign</span></h4>
<p>By July 2020, Trump's handling of the COVID-19 pandemic had become a major issue for the 2020 presidential election.<sup id="cite_ref-Election_NBCNews_514-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Election_NBCNews-514">&#91;513&#93;</a></sup> Biden sought to make the pandemic the central issue of the election.<sup id="cite_ref-515" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-515">&#91;514&#93;</a></sup> Polls suggested voters blamed Trump for his pandemic response<sup id="cite_ref-Election_NBCNews_514-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Election_NBCNews-514">&#91;513&#93;</a></sup> and disbelieved his rhetoric concerning the virus, with an <a href="/wiki/Ipsos" title="Ipsos">Ipsos</a>/<a href="/wiki/ABC_News" title="ABC News">ABC News</a> poll indicating 65 percent of respondents disapproved of his pandemic response.<sup id="cite_ref-516" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-516">&#91;515&#93;</a></sup> In the final months of the campaign, Trump repeatedly claimed that the U.S. was "rounding the turn" in managing the pandemic, despite increasing numbers of reported cases and deaths.<sup id="cite_ref-517" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-517">&#91;516&#93;</a></sup> A few days before the November 3 election, the United States reported more than 100,000 cases in a single day for the first time.<sup id="cite_ref-518" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-518">&#91;517&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h3><span class="mw-headline" id="Investigations">Investigations</span></h3>
<p>After he assumed office, Trump was the subject of increasing Justice Department and congressional scrutiny, with investigations covering his election campaign, transition, and inauguration, actions taken during his presidency, along with his <a href="/wiki/The_Trump_Organization" title="The Trump Organization">private businesses</a>, personal taxes, and <a href="/wiki/Donald_J._Trump_Foundation" title="Donald J. Trump Foundation">charitable foundation</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-519" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-519">&#91;518&#93;</a></sup> There were 30 investigations of Trump, including ten federal criminal investigations, eight state and local investigations, and twelve congressional investigations.<sup id="cite_ref-520" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-520">&#91;519&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>In April 2019, the <a href="/wiki/House_Oversight_Committee" class="mw-redirect" title="House Oversight Committee">House Oversight Committee</a> issued <a href="/wiki/Subpoena" title="Subpoena">subpoenas</a> seeking financial details from Trump's banks, Deutsche Bank and <a href="/wiki/Capital_One" title="Capital One">Capital One</a>, and his accounting firm, <a href="/wiki/Mazars_USA" class="mw-redirect" title="Mazars USA">Mazars USA</a>. Trump then sued the banks, Mazars, and committee chair <a href="/wiki/Elijah_Cummings" title="Elijah Cummings">Elijah Cummings</a> to prevent the disclosures.<sup id="cite_ref-521" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-521">&#91;520&#93;</a></sup> In May, <a href="/wiki/United_States_District_Court_for_the_District_of_Columbia" title="United States District Court for the District of Columbia">DC District Court</a> judge <a href="/wiki/Amit_Mehta" title="Amit Mehta">Amit Mehta</a> ruled that Mazars must comply with the subpoena,<sup id="cite_ref-522" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-522">&#91;521&#93;</a></sup> and judge <a href="/wiki/Edgardo_Ramos" title="Edgardo Ramos">Edgardo Ramos</a> of the <a href="/wiki/United_States_District_Court_for_the_Southern_District_of_New_York" title="United States District Court for the Southern District of New York">Southern District Court of New York</a> ruled that the banks must also comply.<sup id="cite_ref-523" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-523">&#91;522&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-524" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-524">&#91;523&#93;</a></sup> Trump's attorneys appealed the rulings.<sup id="cite_ref-525" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-525">&#91;524&#93;</a></sup> In September 2022, the committee and Trump agreed to a settlement about Mazars, and the accounting firm began turning over documents.<sup id="cite_ref-526" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-526">&#91;525&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h4><span class="mw-headline" id="Hush_money_payments">Hush money payments</span></h4>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1033289096"><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Main article: <a href="/wiki/Stormy_Daniels%E2%80%93Donald_Trump_scandal" title="Stormy Daniels–Donald Trump scandal">Stormy Daniels–Donald Trump scandal</a></div>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1033289096"><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">See also: <a href="/wiki/Legal_affairs_of_Donald_Trump#Payments_related_to_alleged_affairs" class="mw-redirect" title="Legal affairs of Donald Trump">Legal affairs of Donald Trump §&#160;Payments related to alleged affairs</a>, <a href="/wiki/Karen_McDougal#Alleged_affair_with_Donald_Trump" title="Karen McDougal">Karen McDougal §&#160;Alleged affair with Donald Trump</a>, and <a href="/wiki/Prosecution_of_Donald_Trump_in_New_York#Hush_money_payments" title="Prosecution of Donald Trump in New York">Prosecution of Donald Trump in New York §&#160;Hush money payments</a></div>
<p>During the 2016 presidential election campaign, <a href="/wiki/American_Media,_Inc." class="mw-redirect" title="American Media, Inc.">American Media, Inc.</a> (AMI), the parent company of the <i><a href="/wiki/National_Enquirer" title="National Enquirer">National Enquirer</a></i>,<sup id="cite_ref-527" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-527">&#91;526&#93;</a></sup> and a company set up by Cohen paid <i><a href="/wiki/Playboy" title="Playboy">Playboy</a></i> model <a href="/wiki/Karen_McDougal" title="Karen McDougal">Karen McDougal</a> and <a href="/wiki/Pornographic_film_actor" title="Pornographic film actor">adult film actress</a> <a href="/wiki/Stormy_Daniels" title="Stormy Daniels">Stormy Daniels</a> for keeping silent about their alleged affairs with Trump between 2006 and 2007.<sup id="cite_ref-528" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-528">&#91;527&#93;</a></sup> Cohen pleaded guilty in 2018 to breaking campaign finance laws, saying he had arranged both payments at the direction of Trump to influence the presidential election.<sup id="cite_ref-529" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-529">&#91;528&#93;</a></sup> Trump denied the affairs and claimed he was not aware of Cohen's payment to Daniels, but he reimbursed him in 2017.<sup id="cite_ref-530" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-530">&#91;529&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-531" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-531">&#91;530&#93;</a></sup> Federal prosecutors asserted that Trump had been involved in discussions regarding non-disclosure payments as early as 2014.<sup id="cite_ref-532" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-532">&#91;531&#93;</a></sup> Court documents showed that the FBI believed Trump was directly involved in the payment to Daniels, based on calls he had with Cohen in October 2016.<sup id="cite_ref-533" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-533">&#91;532&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-534" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-534">&#91;533&#93;</a></sup> Federal prosecutors closed the investigation in 2019,<sup id="cite_ref-535" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-535">&#91;534&#93;</a></sup> but the <a href="/wiki/Manhattan_District_Attorney" class="mw-redirect" title="Manhattan District Attorney">Manhattan District Attorney</a> subpoenaed the Trump Organization and AMI for records related to the payments<sup id="cite_ref-536" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-536">&#91;535&#93;</a></sup> and Trump and the Trump Organization for eight years of tax returns.<sup id="cite_ref-537" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-537">&#91;536&#93;</a></sup> In November 2022, <i>The New York Times</i> reported that Manhattan prosecutors were "newly optimistic about building a case" against Trump.<sup id="cite_ref-538" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-538">&#91;537&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h4><span class="mw-headline" id="Russian_election_interference">Russian election interference</span></h4>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1033289096"><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Main articles: <a href="/wiki/Russian_interference_in_the_2016_United_States_elections" title="Russian interference in the 2016 United States elections">Russian interference in the 2016 United States elections</a> and <a href="/wiki/Timelines_related_to_Donald_Trump_and_Russian_interference_in_United_States_elections" title="Timelines related to Donald Trump and Russian interference in United States elections">Timelines related to Donald Trump and Russian interference in United States elections</a></div>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1033289096"><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">See also: <a href="/wiki/Senate_Intelligence_Committee_report_on_Russian_interference_in_the_2016_United_States_presidential_election" title="Senate Intelligence Committee report on Russian interference in the 2016 United States presidential election">Senate Intelligence Committee report on Russian interference in the 2016 United States presidential election</a> and <a href="/wiki/Steele_dossier" title="Steele dossier">Steele dossier</a></div>
<p>In January 2017, American intelligence agencies—the <a href="/wiki/CIA" class="mw-redirect" title="CIA">CIA</a>, the <a href="/wiki/FBI" class="mw-redirect" title="FBI">FBI</a>, and the <a href="/wiki/NSA" class="mw-redirect" title="NSA">NSA</a>, represented by the <a href="/wiki/Director_of_National_Intelligence" title="Director of National Intelligence">Director of National Intelligence</a>—jointly stated with "<a href="/wiki/Analytic_confidence#Levels_of_analytic_confidence_in_national_security_reports" title="Analytic confidence">high confidence</a>" that the Russian government interfered in the 2016 presidential election to favor the election of Trump.<sup id="cite_ref-539" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-539">&#91;538&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-540" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-540">&#91;539&#93;</a></sup> In March 2017, FBI Director <a href="/wiki/James_Comey" title="James Comey">James Comey</a> told Congress, "[T]he FBI, as part of our counterintelligence mission, is investigating the Russian government's efforts to interfere in the 2016 presidential election. That includes investigating the nature of any links between individuals associated with the Trump campaign and the Russian government, and whether there was any coordination between the campaign and Russia's efforts."<sup id="cite_ref-541" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-541">&#91;540&#93;</a></sup> Many suspicious<sup id="cite_ref-542" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-542">&#91;541&#93;</a></sup> <a href="/wiki/Links_between_Trump_associates_and_Russian_officials_and_spies" class="mw-redirect" title="Links between Trump associates and Russian officials and spies">links between Trump associates and Russian officials and spies</a> were discovered and the relationships between Russians and "team Trump" were widely reported by the press.<sup id="cite_ref-543" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-543">&#91;542&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-544" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-544">&#91;543&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>Manafort, one of Trump's campaign managers, worked from December 2004 to February 2010 to help pro-Russian politician <a href="/wiki/Viktor_Yanukovych" title="Viktor Yanukovych">Viktor Yanukovych</a> win the Ukrainian presidency.<sup id="cite_ref-545" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-545">&#91;544&#93;</a></sup> Other Trump associates, including Flynn and Stone, were connected to Russian officials.<sup id="cite_ref-546" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-546">&#91;545&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-547" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-547">&#91;546&#93;</a></sup> Russian agents were overheard during the campaign saying they could use Manafort and Flynn to influence Trump.<sup id="cite_ref-548" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-548">&#91;547&#93;</a></sup> Members of Trump's campaign and later his White House staff, particularly Flynn, were in contact with Russian officials both before and after the November election.<sup id="cite_ref-549" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-549">&#91;548&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-550" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-550">&#91;549&#93;</a></sup> On December 29, 2016, Flynn talked with Russian Ambassador <a href="/wiki/Sergey_Kislyak" title="Sergey Kislyak">Sergey Kislyak</a> about sanctions that were imposed that same day; Flynn later resigned in the midst of controversy over whether he misled Pence.<sup id="cite_ref-551" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-551">&#91;550&#93;</a></sup> Trump told Kislyak and <a href="/wiki/Sergei_Lavrov" class="mw-redirect" title="Sergei Lavrov">Sergei Lavrov</a> in May 2017 he was unconcerned about Russian interference in U.S. elections.<sup id="cite_ref-552" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-552">&#91;551&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>Trump and his allies promoted <a href="/wiki/Conspiracy_theories_related_to_the_Trump%E2%80%93Ukraine_scandal" title="Conspiracy theories related to the Trump–Ukraine scandal">a conspiracy theory</a> that Ukraine, rather than Russia, interfered in the 2016 election—which was also promoted by Russia to <a href="/wiki/Frameup" title="Frameup">frame</a> Ukraine.<sup id="cite_ref-553" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-553">&#91;552&#93;</a></sup> After the <a href="/wiki/Democratic_National_Committee" title="Democratic National Committee">Democratic National Committee</a> was hacked, Trump first claimed it withheld "its server" from the FBI (in actuality there were more than 140 servers, of which digital copies were given to the FBI); second, that <a href="/wiki/CrowdStrike" title="CrowdStrike">CrowdStrike</a>, the company that investigated the servers, was Ukraine-based and Ukrainian-owned (in actuality, CrowdStrike is U.S.-based, with the largest owners being American companies); and third that "the server" was hidden in Ukraine. Members of the Trump administration spoke out against the conspiracy theories.<sup id="cite_ref-554" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-554">&#91;553&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h4><span class="mw-headline" id="FBI_Crossfire_Hurricane_and_2017_counterintelligence_investigations">FBI Crossfire Hurricane and 2017 counterintelligence investigations</span></h4>
<p>In July 2016, the FBI launched an investigation, codenamed <a href="/wiki/Crossfire_Hurricane_(FBI_investigation)" title="Crossfire Hurricane (FBI investigation)">Crossfire Hurricane</a>, into possible links between Russia and the Trump campaign.<sup id="cite_ref-555" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-555">&#91;554&#93;</a></sup> After Trump fired FBI director James Comey in May 2017, the FBI opened a counterintelligence investigation into Trump's personal and <a href="/wiki/Business_projects_of_Donald_Trump_in_Russia" title="Business projects of Donald Trump in Russia">business dealings with Russia</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-556" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-556">&#91;555&#93;</a></sup> Crossfire Hurricane was transferred to the Mueller investigation,<sup id="cite_ref-557" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-557">&#91;556&#93;</a></sup> but deputy attorney general <a href="/wiki/Rod_Rosenstein" title="Rod Rosenstein">Rod Rosenstein</a> ended the investigation into Trump's direct ties to Russia while giving the bureau the false impression that Mueller would pursue the matter.<sup id="cite_ref-never_558-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-never-558">&#91;557&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-559" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-559">&#91;558&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h4><span class="mw-headline" id="Mueller_investigation">Mueller investigation</span></h4>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1033289096"><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Main articles: <a href="/wiki/Mueller_special_counsel_investigation" title="Mueller special counsel investigation">Mueller special counsel investigation</a>, <a href="/wiki/Mueller_report" title="Mueller report">Mueller report</a>, and <a href="/wiki/Criminal_charges_brought_in_the_Mueller_special_counsel_investigation" title="Criminal charges brought in the Mueller special counsel investigation">Criminal charges brought in the Mueller special counsel investigation</a></div>
<p>In May 2017, <a href="/wiki/United_States_Deputy_Attorney_General" title="United States Deputy Attorney General">Deputy Attorney General</a> Rod Rosenstein appointed <a href="/wiki/Robert_Mueller" title="Robert Mueller">Robert Mueller</a>, a former <a href="/wiki/Director_of_the_FBI" class="mw-redirect" title="Director of the FBI">director of the FBI</a>, <a href="/wiki/Special_counsel" title="Special counsel">special counsel</a> for the <a href="/wiki/United_States_Department_of_Justice" title="United States Department of Justice">Department of Justice</a> (DOJ), ordering him to "examine 'any links and/or coordination between the Russian government' and the Trump campaign". He privately told Mueller to restrict the investigation to criminal matters "in connection with Russia's 2016 election interference".<sup id="cite_ref-never_558-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-never-558">&#91;557&#93;</a></sup> The special counsel also investigated whether Trump's <a href="/wiki/Dismissal_of_James_Comey" title="Dismissal of James Comey">dismissal of James Comey</a> as FBI director constituted obstruction of justice<sup id="cite_ref-560" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-560">&#91;559&#93;</a></sup> and the Trump campaign's possible ties to Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates, <a href="/wiki/Turkey" title="Turkey">Turkey</a>, <a href="/wiki/Qatar" title="Qatar">Qatar</a>, Israel, and China.<sup id="cite_ref-561" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-561">&#91;560&#93;</a></sup> Trump sought to fire Mueller and shut down the investigation multiple times but backed down after his staff objected or after changing his mind.<sup id="cite_ref-562" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-562">&#91;561&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>In March 2019, Mueller concluded his investigation and gave <a href="/wiki/Mueller_report" title="Mueller report">his report</a> to Attorney General William Barr.<sup id="cite_ref-563" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-563">&#91;562&#93;</a></sup> Two days later, <a href="/wiki/Barr_letter" title="Barr letter">Barr sent a letter to Congress</a> purporting to summarize the report's main conclusions. A federal court, as well as Mueller himself, said Barr mischaracterized the investigation's conclusions and, in so doing, confused the public.<sup id="cite_ref-564" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-564">&#91;563&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-565" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-565">&#91;564&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-566" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-566">&#91;565&#93;</a></sup> Trump repeatedly and falsely claimed that the investigation exonerated him; the Mueller report expressly stated that it did not exonerate him.<sup id="cite_ref-567" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-567">&#91;566&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>A redacted version of the report was publicly released in April 2019.
