It found that Russia interfered in 2016 to favor Trump's candidacy and hinder Clinton's.<sup id="cite_ref-568" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-568">&#91;567&#93;</a></sup> Despite "numerous links between the Russian government and the Trump campaign", the report found that the prevailing evidence "did not establish" that Trump campaign members conspired or coordinated with Russian interference.<sup id="cite_ref-569" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-569">&#91;568&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-takeaways_570-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-takeaways-570">&#91;569&#93;</a></sup> The report revealed sweeping Russian interference<sup id="cite_ref-takeaways_570-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-takeaways-570">&#91;569&#93;</a></sup> and detailed how Trump and his campaign welcomed and encouraged it, believing "[they] would benefit electorally from information stolen and released through Russian efforts".<sup id="cite_ref-571" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-571">&#91;570&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-572" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-572">&#91;571&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-573" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-573">&#91;572&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-574" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-574">&#91;573&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>The report also detailed multiple acts of potential obstruction of justice by Trump but did not make a "traditional prosecutorial judgment" on whether Trump broke the law, suggesting that Congress should make such a determination.<sup id="cite_ref-575" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-575">&#91;574&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-576" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-576">&#91;575&#93;</a></sup> Investigators decided they could not "apply an approach that could potentially result in a judgment that the President committed crimes" as an <a href="/wiki/Office_of_Legal_Counsel" title="Office of Legal Counsel">Office of Legal Counsel</a> opinion stated that a sitting president could not be indicted,<sup id="cite_ref-LM_577-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-LM-577">&#91;576&#93;</a></sup> and investigators would not accuse him of a crime when he cannot clear his name in court.<sup id="cite_ref-578" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-578">&#91;577&#93;</a></sup> The report concluded that Congress, having the authority to take action against a president for wrongdoing, "may apply the obstruction laws".<sup id="cite_ref-LM_577-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-LM-577">&#91;576&#93;</a></sup> The House of Representatives subsequently launched an <a href="/wiki/Impeachment_inquiry_against_Donald_Trump" title="Impeachment inquiry against Donald Trump">impeachment inquiry</a> following the <a href="/wiki/Trump%E2%80%93Ukraine_scandal" title="Trump–Ukraine scandal">Trump–Ukraine scandal</a>, but did not pursue an article of impeachment related to the Mueller investigation.<sup id="cite_ref-579" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-579">&#91;578&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-580" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-580">&#91;579&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>Several Trump associates pleaded guilty or were convicted in connection with Mueller's investigation and related cases, including Manafort, <a href="/wiki/Trials_of_Paul_Manafort" title="Trials of Paul Manafort">convicted on eight felony counts</a>,<sup id="cite_ref-581" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-581">&#91;580&#93;</a></sup> deputy campaign manager <a href="/wiki/Rick_Gates_(political_consultant)" title="Rick Gates (political consultant)">Rick Gates</a>,<sup id="cite_ref-582" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-582">&#91;581&#93;</a></sup> foreign policy advisor Papadopoulos,<sup id="cite_ref-583" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-583">&#91;582&#93;</a></sup> and Flynn.<sup id="cite_ref-584" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-584">&#91;583&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-585" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-585">&#91;584&#93;</a></sup> Cohen pleaded guilty to lying to Congress about Trump's 2016 attempts to reach a deal with Russia to build <a href="/wiki/Trump_Tower_Moscow" title="Trump Tower Moscow">a Trump Tower in Moscow</a>. Cohen said he had made the false statements on behalf of Trump, who was identified as "Individual-1" in the court documents.<sup id="cite_ref-586" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-586">&#91;585&#93;</a></sup> In February 2020, Stone was sentenced to 40 months in prison for lying to Congress and witness tampering regarding his attempts to learn more about hacked Democratic emails during the 2016 election. The sentencing judge said Stone "was prosecuted for covering up for the president".<sup id="cite_ref-587" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-587">&#91;586&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h3><span class="mw-headline" id="First_impeachment">First impeachment</span></h3>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1033289096"><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Main articles: <a href="/wiki/First_impeachment_of_Donald_Trump" title="First impeachment of Donald Trump">First impeachment of Donald Trump</a> and <a href="/wiki/Trump%E2%80%93Ukraine_scandal" title="Trump–Ukraine scandal">Trump–Ukraine scandal</a></div>
<figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:House_of_Representatives_Votes_to_Adopt_the_Articles_of_Impeachment_Against_Donald_Trump.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img alt="Nancy Pelosi presides over a crowded House of Representatives chamber floor during the impeachment vote" src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/b8/House_of_Representatives_Votes_to_Adopt_the_Articles_of_Impeachment_Against_Donald_Trump.jpg/260px-House_of_Representatives_Votes_to_Adopt_the_Articles_of_Impeachment_Against_Donald_Trump.jpg" decoding="async" width="260" height="146" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/b8/House_of_Representatives_Votes_to_Adopt_the_Articles_of_Impeachment_Against_Donald_Trump.jpg/390px-House_of_Representatives_Votes_to_Adopt_the_Articles_of_Impeachment_Against_Donald_Trump.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/b8/House_of_Representatives_Votes_to_Adopt_the_Articles_of_Impeachment_Against_Donald_Trump.jpg/520px-House_of_Representatives_Votes_to_Adopt_the_Articles_of_Impeachment_Against_Donald_Trump.jpg 2x" data-file-width="3197" data-file-height="1796" /></a><figcaption>Members of House of Representatives vote on two <a href="/wiki/Articles_of_impeachment" class="mw-redirect" title="Articles of impeachment">articles of impeachment</a> <span class="nowrap">(<a rel="nofollow" class="external text" href="https://www.congress.gov/bill/116th-congress/house-resolution/755">H.Res.&#160;755</a>)</span>, December 18, 2019.</figcaption></figure>
<p>In August 2019, a <a href="/wiki/Whistleblower_protection_in_the_United_States" title="Whistleblower protection in the United States">whistleblower</a> filed a complaint with the <a href="/wiki/Inspector_General_of_the_Intelligence_Community" title="Inspector General of the Intelligence Community">Inspector General of the Intelligence Community</a> about a July 25 phone call between Trump and President of Ukraine <a href="/wiki/Volodymyr_Zelenskyy" title="Volodymyr Zelenskyy">Volodymyr Zelenskyy</a>, during which Trump had pressured Zelenskyy to investigate CrowdStrike and Democratic presidential candidate Biden and his son <a href="/wiki/Hunter_Biden" title="Hunter Biden">Hunter</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-undermine_588-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-undermine-588">&#91;587&#93;</a></sup> The whistleblower said that the White House had attempted to cover-up the incident and that the call was part of a wider campaign by the Trump administration and Giuliani that may have included withholding financial aid from Ukraine in July 2019 and canceling Pence's May 2019 Ukraine trip.<sup id="cite_ref-abuse_589-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-abuse-589">&#91;588&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>House Speaker <a href="/wiki/Nancy_Pelosi" title="Nancy Pelosi">Nancy Pelosi</a> initiated <a href="/wiki/Impeachment_inquiry_against_Donald_Trump" title="Impeachment inquiry against Donald Trump">a formal impeachment inquiry</a> on September 24.<sup id="cite_ref-590" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-590">&#91;589&#93;</a></sup> Trump then confirmed that he withheld military aid from Ukraine, offering contradictory reasons for the decision.<sup id="cite_ref-591" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-591">&#91;590&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-592" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-592">&#91;591&#93;</a></sup> On September 25, the Trump administration released a memorandum of the phone call which confirmed that, after Zelenskyy mentioned purchasing American anti-tank missiles, Trump asked him to discuss investigating Biden and his son with Giuliani and Barr.<sup id="cite_ref-undermine_588-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-undermine-588">&#91;587&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-593" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-593">&#91;592&#93;</a></sup> The testimony of multiple administration officials and former officials confirmed that this was part of a broader effort to further Trump's personal interests by giving him an advantage in the upcoming presidential election.<sup id="cite_ref-594" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-594">&#91;593&#93;</a></sup> In October, <a href="/wiki/William_B._Taylor_Jr." title="William B. Taylor Jr.">William B. Taylor Jr.</a>, the <a href="/wiki/List_of_ambassadors_of_the_United_States_to_Ukraine" title="List of ambassadors of the United States to Ukraine">chargé d'affaires for Ukraine</a>, testified before congressional committees that soon after arriving in Ukraine in June 2019, he found that Zelenskyy was being subjected to pressure directed by Trump and led by Giuliani. According to Taylor and others, the goal was to coerce Zelenskyy into making a public commitment investigating the company that employed Hunter Biden, as well as rumors about Ukrainian involvement in the 2016 U.S. presidential election.<sup id="cite_ref-595" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-595">&#91;594&#93;</a></sup> He said it was made clear that until Zelenskyy made such an announcement, the administration would not release scheduled military aid for Ukraine and not invite Zelenskyy to the White House.<sup id="cite_ref-596" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-596">&#91;595&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>On December 13, the <a href="/wiki/House_Judiciary_Committee" class="mw-redirect" title="House Judiciary Committee">House Judiciary Committee</a> voted along party lines to pass two articles of impeachment: one for <a href="/wiki/Abuse_of_power" title="Abuse of power">abuse of power</a> and one for <a href="/wiki/Obstruction_of_Congress" class="mw-redirect" title="Obstruction of Congress">obstruction of Congress</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-597" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-597">&#91;596&#93;</a></sup> After debate, the House of Representatives <a href="/wiki/Impeachment_in_the_United_States" title="Impeachment in the United States">impeached</a> Trump on both articles on December 18.<sup id="cite_ref-598" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-598">&#91;597&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h4><span class="mw-headline" id="Impeachment_trial_in_the_Senate">Impeachment trial in the Senate</span></h4>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1033289096"><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Main article: <a href="/wiki/First_impeachment_trial_of_Donald_Trump" title="First impeachment trial of Donald Trump">First impeachment trial of Donald Trump</a></div>
<p>During the trial in January 2020, the House impeachment managers presented their case for three days. They cited evidence to support charges of abuse of power and obstruction of Congress, and asserted that Trump's actions were exactly what the founding fathers had in mind when they created the Constitution's impeachment process.<sup id="cite_ref-599" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-599">&#91;598&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:President_Trump_Delivers_Remarks_(49498772251).jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img alt="Trump displaying the front page of The Washington Post reporting his acquittal by the Senate" src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/ff/President_Trump_Delivers_Remarks_%2849498772251%29.jpg/220px-President_Trump_Delivers_Remarks_%2849498772251%29.jpg" decoding="async" width="220" height="147" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/ff/President_Trump_Delivers_Remarks_%2849498772251%29.jpg/330px-President_Trump_Delivers_Remarks_%2849498772251%29.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/ff/President_Trump_Delivers_Remarks_%2849498772251%29.jpg/440px-President_Trump_Delivers_Remarks_%2849498772251%29.jpg 2x" data-file-width="3000" data-file-height="2000" /></a><figcaption>Trump displaying the headline "Trump acquitted"</figcaption></figure>
<p>Responding over the next three days, Trump's lawyers did not deny the facts as presented in the charges but said Trump had not broken any laws or obstructed Congress.<sup id="cite_ref-brazen_600-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-brazen-600">&#91;599&#93;</a></sup> They argued that the impeachment was "constitutionally and legally invalid" because Trump was not charged with a crime and that abuse of power is not an impeachable offense.<sup id="cite_ref-brazen_600-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-brazen-600">&#91;599&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>On January 31, the Senate voted against allowing subpoenas for witnesses or documents; 51 Republicans formed the majority for this vote.<sup id="cite_ref-601" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-601">&#91;600&#93;</a></sup> The impeachment trial was the first in U.S. history without witness testimony.<sup id="cite_ref-602" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-602">&#91;601&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>Trump was acquitted of both charges by the Republican majority, 52–48 on abuse of power and 53–47 on obstruction of Congress. Senator <a href="/wiki/Mitt_Romney" title="Mitt Romney">Mitt Romney</a> was the only Republican who voted to convict Trump on one charge, the abuse of power.<sup id="cite_ref-603" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-603">&#91;602&#93;</a></sup> Following his acquittal, Trump fired impeachment witnesses and other political appointees and career officials he deemed insufficiently loyal.<sup id="cite_ref-604" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-604">&#91;603&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h3><span class="mw-headline" id="2020_presidential_campaign">2020 presidential campaign</span></h3>
<figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:Donald_Trump_(50548265318).jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img alt="Trump points his finger at a campaign rally, with crowds behind him" src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/9f/Donald_Trump_%2850548265318%29.jpg/220px-Donald_Trump_%2850548265318%29.jpg" decoding="async" width="220" height="147" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/9f/Donald_Trump_%2850548265318%29.jpg/330px-Donald_Trump_%2850548265318%29.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/9f/Donald_Trump_%2850548265318%29.jpg/440px-Donald_Trump_%2850548265318%29.jpg 2x" data-file-width="4134" data-file-height="2756" /></a><figcaption>Trump at a 2020 campaign rally in <a href="/wiki/Arizona" title="Arizona">Arizona</a></figcaption></figure>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1033289096"><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Main article: <a href="/wiki/Donald_Trump_2020_presidential_campaign" title="Donald Trump 2020 presidential campaign">Donald Trump 2020 presidential campaign</a></div>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1033289096"><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">See also: <a href="/wiki/2020_United_States_presidential_debates" title="2020 United States presidential debates">2020 United States presidential debates</a></div>
<p>Breaking with precedent, Trump filed to run for a second term with the FEC within a few hours of assuming the presidency.<sup id="cite_ref-605" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-605">&#91;604&#93;</a></sup> He held his first re-election rally less than a month after taking office<sup id="cite_ref-606" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-606">&#91;605&#93;</a></sup> and officially became the <a href="/wiki/2020_Republican_Party_presidential_primaries" title="2020 Republican Party presidential primaries">Republican nominee</a> in August 2020.<sup id="cite_ref-607" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-607">&#91;606&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>In his first two years in office, Trump's reelection committee reported raising $67.5&#160;million and began 2019 with $19.3&#160;million in cash.<sup id="cite_ref-608" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-608">&#91;607&#93;</a></sup> By July 2020, the Trump campaign and the Republican Party had raised $1.1&#160;billion and spent $800&#160;million, losing their cash advantage over Biden.<sup id="cite_ref-609" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-609">&#91;608&#93;</a></sup> The cash shortage forced the campaign to scale back advertising spending.<sup id="cite_ref-610" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-610">&#91;609&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>Trump campaign advertisements focused on crime, claiming that cities would descend into lawlessness if Biden won the presidency.<sup id="cite_ref-611" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-611">&#91;610&#93;</a></sup> Trump repeatedly misrepresented Biden's positions<sup id="cite_ref-612" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-612">&#91;611&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-613" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-613">&#91;612&#93;</a></sup> and shifted to appeals to racism.<sup id="cite_ref-614" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-614">&#91;613&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h3><span class="mw-headline" id="2020_presidential_election">2020 presidential election</span></h3>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1033289096"><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Main article: <a href="/wiki/2020_United_States_presidential_election" title="2020 United States presidential election">2020 United States presidential election</a></div>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1033289096"><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">See also: <a href="/wiki/2020_United_States_Postal_Service_crisis" title="2020 United States Postal Service crisis">2020 United States Postal Service crisis</a></div>
<p>Starting in spring 2020, Trump began to sow doubts about the election, claiming without evidence that the election would be rigged and that the expected widespread use of mail balloting would produce massive election fraud.<sup id="cite_ref-615" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-615">&#91;614&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-616" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-616">&#91;615&#93;</a></sup> In July, Trump raised the idea of delaying the election.<sup id="cite_ref-617" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-617">&#91;616&#93;</a></sup> When, in August, the House of Representatives voted for a $25&#160;billion grant to the U.S. Postal Service for the expected surge in mail voting, Trump blocked funding, saying he wanted to prevent any increase in voting by mail.<sup id="cite_ref-618" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-618">&#91;617&#93;</a></sup> He repeatedly refused to say whether he would accept the results of the election and commit to a <a href="/wiki/Peaceful_transition_of_power" title="Peaceful transition of power">peaceful transition of power</a> if he lost.<sup id="cite_ref-619" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-619">&#91;618&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-620" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-620">&#91;619&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>Biden won the election on November 3, receiving 81.3&#160;million votes (51.3 percent) to Trump's 74.2&#160;million (46.8 percent)<sup id="cite_ref-vote1_621-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-vote1-621">&#91;620&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-vote2_622-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-vote2-622">&#91;621&#93;</a></sup> and 306 <a href="/wiki/United_States_Electoral_College" title="United States Electoral College">Electoral College</a> votes to Trump's 232.<sup id="cite_ref-formalize_623-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-formalize-623">&#91;622&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h4><span id="False_claims_of_voting_fraud.2C_attempt_to_prevent_presidential_transition"></span><span class="mw-headline" id="False_claims_of_voting_fraud,_attempt_to_prevent_presidential_transition">False claims of voting fraud, attempt to prevent presidential transition</span></h4>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1033289096"><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Further information: <a href="/wiki/Big_lie#Donald_Trump&#39;s_false_claims_of_a_stolen_election" title="Big lie">Big lie §&#160;Donald Trump's false claims of a stolen election</a>, <a href="/wiki/Attempts_to_overturn_the_2020_United_States_presidential_election" title="Attempts to overturn the 2020 United States presidential election">Attempts to overturn the 2020 United States presidential election</a>, and <a href="/wiki/2020%E2%80%9321_United_States_election_protests" title="2020–21 United States election protests">2020–21 United States election protests</a></div>
<figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:ElectoralCollege2020.svg" class="mw-file-description"><img alt="Electoral college map, depicting Trump winning many states in the South and Rocky Mountains and Biden winning many states in the Northeast, Midwest, and Pacific West" src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/49/ElectoralCollege2020.svg/290px-ElectoralCollege2020.svg.png" decoding="async" width="290" height="169" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/49/ElectoralCollege2020.svg/435px-ElectoralCollege2020.svg.png 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/49/ElectoralCollege2020.svg/580px-ElectoralCollege2020.svg.png 2x" data-file-width="1020" data-file-height="593" /></a><figcaption>2020 Electoral College results; Trump lost 232–306.</figcaption></figure>
<p>At 2 a.m. the morning after the election, with the results still unclear, Trump declared victory.<sup id="cite_ref-624" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-624">&#91;623&#93;</a></sup> After Biden was projected the winner days later, Trump stated that "this election is far from over" and baselessly alleged election fraud.<sup id="cite_ref-625" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-625">&#91;624&#93;</a></sup> Trump and his allies filed many <a href="/wiki/Post-election_lawsuits_related_to_the_2020_United_States_presidential_election" class="mw-redirect" title="Post-election lawsuits related to the 2020 United States presidential election">legal challenges to the results</a>, which were rejected by at least 86 judges in both the <a href="/wiki/State_court_(United_States)" title="State court (United States)">state</a> and <a href="/wiki/United_States_federal_courts" class="mw-redirect" title="United States federal courts">federal courts</a>, including by federal judges appointed by Trump himself, finding no factual or legal basis.<sup id="cite_ref-626" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-626">&#91;625&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-627" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-627">&#91;626&#93;</a></sup> Trump's unsubstantiated allegations of widespread voting fraud were also refuted by state election officials.<sup id="cite_ref-628" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-628">&#91;627&#93;</a></sup> After <a href="/wiki/Cybersecurity_and_Infrastructure_Security_Agency" title="Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency">Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency</a> (CISA) director <a href="/wiki/Chris_Krebs" title="Chris Krebs">Chris Krebs</a> contradicted Trump's fraud allegations, Trump dismissed him on November 17.<sup id="cite_ref-BBC_election_629-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-BBC_election-629">&#91;628&#93;</a></sup> On December 11, the U.S. Supreme Court declined to hear <a href="/wiki/Texas_v._Pennsylvania" title="Texas v. Pennsylvania">a case from the Texas attorney general</a> that asked the court to overturn the election results in four states won by Biden.<sup id="cite_ref-630" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-630">&#91;629&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>Trump withdrew from public activities in the weeks following the election.<sup id="cite_ref-631" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-631">&#91;630&#93;</a></sup> He initially blocked government officials from cooperating in <a href="/wiki/Presidential_transition_of_Joe_Biden" title="Presidential transition of Joe Biden">Biden's presidential transition</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-632" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-632">&#91;631&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-633" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-633">&#91;632&#93;</a></sup> After three weeks, the administrator of the <a href="/wiki/General_Services_Administration" title="General Services Administration">General Services Administration</a> declared Biden the "apparent winner" of the election, allowing the disbursement of transition resources to his team.<sup id="cite_ref-634" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-634">&#91;633&#93;</a></sup> Trump still did not formally concede while claiming he recommended the GSA begin transition protocols.<sup id="cite_ref-635" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-635">&#91;634&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-636" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-636">&#91;635&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>The Electoral College formalized Biden's victory on December 14.<sup id="cite_ref-formalize_623-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-formalize-623">&#91;622&#93;</a></sup> From November to January, Trump repeatedly sought help to <a href="/wiki/Attempts_to_overturn_the_2020_United_States_presidential_election" title="Attempts to overturn the 2020 United States presidential election">overturn the results of the election</a>, personally pressuring various Republican local and state office-holders,<sup id="cite_ref-637" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-637">&#91;636&#93;</a></sup> Republican state and federal legislators,<sup id="cite_ref-pressure_638-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-pressure-638">&#91;637&#93;</a></sup> the Justice Department,<sup id="cite_ref-639" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-639">&#91;638&#93;</a></sup> and Vice President Pence,<sup id="cite_ref-640" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-640">&#91;639&#93;</a></sup> urging various actions such as <a href="/wiki/Trump_fake_electors_plot" title="Trump fake electors plot">replacing presidential electors</a>, or a request for Georgia officials to "find" votes and announce a "recalculated" result.<sup id="cite_ref-pressure_638-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-pressure-638">&#91;637&#93;</a></sup> On February 10, 2021, Georgia prosecutors opened a criminal investigation into Trump's efforts to subvert the election in Georgia.<sup id="cite_ref-641" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-641">&#91;640&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>Trump did not attend Biden's inauguration, leaving Washington for Florida hours before.<sup id="cite_ref-642" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-642">&#91;641&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h4><span class="mw-headline" id="Concern_about_a_possible_coup_attempt_or_military_action">Concern about a possible coup attempt or military action</span></h4>
<p>In December 2020, <i><a href="/wiki/Newsweek" title="Newsweek">Newsweek</a></i> reported <a href="/wiki/The_Pentagon" title="The Pentagon">the Pentagon</a> was on red alert, and ranking officers had discussed what they would do if Trump decided to declare <a href="/wiki/Martial_law" title="Martial law">martial law</a>. The Pentagon responded with quotes from defense leaders that the military has no role to play in the outcome of elections.<sup id="cite_ref-643" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-643">&#91;642&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>When Trump moved supporters into positions of power at the Pentagon after the November 2020 election, Chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff <a href="/wiki/Mark_Milley" title="Mark Milley">Mark Milley</a> and CIA director <a href="/wiki/Gina_Haspel" title="Gina Haspel">Gina Haspel</a> became concerned about the threat of a possible <a href="/wiki/Self-coup" title="Self-coup">coup</a> attempt or military action against China or Iran.<sup id="cite_ref-644" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-644">&#91;643&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-645" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-645">&#91;644&#93;</a></sup> Milley insisted that he should be consulted about any military orders from Trump, including the use of nuclear weapons, and he instructed Haspel and NSA director <a href="/wiki/Paul_Nakasone" title="Paul Nakasone">Paul Nakasone</a> to monitor developments closely.<sup id="cite_ref-646" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-646">&#91;645&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-647" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-647">&#91;646&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h4><span class="mw-headline" id="January_6_Capitol_attack">January 6 Capitol attack</span></h4>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1033289096"><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Main article: <a href="/wiki/January_6_United_States_Capitol_attack" title="January 6 United States Capitol attack">January 6 United States Capitol attack</a></div>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1033289096"><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">See also: <a href="/wiki/Timeline_of_the_January_6_United_States_Capitol_attack" title="Timeline of the January 6 United States Capitol attack">Timeline of the January 6 United States Capitol attack</a></div>
<p>On January 6, 2021, while <a href="/wiki/2021_United_States_Electoral_College_vote_count" title="2021 United States Electoral College vote count">congressional certification of the presidential election results</a> was taking place in the United States Capitol, Trump held a noon rally at <a href="/wiki/The_Ellipse" title="The Ellipse">the Ellipse</a>, <a href="/wiki/Washington,_D.C." title="Washington, D.C.">Washington, D.C.</a>. He called for the election result to be overturned and urged his supporters to "take back our country" by marching to the Capitol to "show strength" and "fight like hell".<sup id="cite_ref-648" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-648">&#91;647&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-649" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-649">&#91;648&#93;</a></sup> Many supporters did, joining a crowd already there. Around 2:15<span class="nowrap">&#160;</span>p.m. the mob broke into the building, disrupting certification and causing the evacuation of Congress.<sup id="cite_ref-650" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-650">&#91;649&#93;</a></sup> During the violence, Trump watched TV and posted messages on Twitter without asking the rioters to disperse. At 6<span class="nowrap">&#160;</span>p.m., Trump tweeted that the rioters should "go home with love &amp; in peace", calling them "great patriots" and "very special" and repeating that the election was stolen from him.<sup id="cite_ref-651" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-651">&#91;650&#93;</a></sup> After the mob was removed from the Capitol, Congress reconvened and confirmed the Biden election win in the early hours of the following morning.<sup id="cite_ref-652" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-652">&#91;651&#93;</a></sup> According to the Department of Justice, more than 140 police officers were injured, and five people died.<sup id="cite_ref-653" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-653">&#91;652&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-654" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-654">&#91;653&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>In March 2023, Trump collaborated with incarcerated rioters on a <a href="/wiki/Justice_for_All_(song)" title="Justice for All (song)">song to benefit the prisoners</a>, and, in June, he said that, if elected, he would pardon a large number of them.<sup id="cite_ref-655" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-655">&#91;654&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h4><span class="mw-headline" id="Second_impeachment">Second impeachment</span></h4>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1033289096"><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Main articles: <a href="/wiki/Second_impeachment_of_Donald_Trump" title="Second impeachment of Donald Trump">Second impeachment of Donald Trump</a> and <a href="/wiki/Second_impeachment_trial_of_Donald_Trump" title="Second impeachment trial of Donald Trump">Second impeachment trial of Donald Trump</a></div>
<figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:Pelosi_Signing_Second_Trump_Impeachment.png" class="mw-file-description"><img alt="Speaker of the House Nancy Pelosi seated at a table and surrounded by public officials. She is signing the second impeachment of Trump." src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/55/Pelosi_Signing_Second_Trump_Impeachment.png/300px-Pelosi_Signing_Second_Trump_Impeachment.png" decoding="async" width="300" height="146" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/55/Pelosi_Signing_Second_Trump_Impeachment.png/450px-Pelosi_Signing_Second_Trump_Impeachment.png 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/55/Pelosi_Signing_Second_Trump_Impeachment.png/600px-Pelosi_Signing_Second_Trump_Impeachment.png 2x" data-file-width="2152" data-file-height="1046" /></a><figcaption>Speaker of the House <a href="/wiki/Nancy_Pelosi" title="Nancy Pelosi">Nancy Pelosi</a> signing the second impeachment of Trump</figcaption></figure>
<p>On January 11, 2021, an article of impeachment charging Trump with <a href="/wiki/Incitement_of_insurrection" class="mw-redirect" title="Incitement of insurrection">incitement of insurrection</a> against the U.S. government was introduced to the House.<sup id="cite_ref-656" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-656">&#91;655&#93;</a></sup> The House voted 232–197 to impeach Trump on January 13, making him the first U.S. president to be impeached twice.<sup id="cite_ref-SecondImpeachment_657-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-SecondImpeachment-657">&#91;656&#93;</a></sup> Ten Republicans voted for the impeachment—the most members of a party ever to vote to impeach a president of their own party.<sup id="cite_ref-658" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-658">&#91;657&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>On February 13, following a <a href="/wiki/Second_impeachment_trial_of_Donald_Trump" title="Second impeachment trial of Donald Trump">five-day Senate trial</a>, Trump was acquitted when the Senate voted 57–43 for conviction, falling ten votes short of the two-thirds majority required to convict; seven Republicans joined every Democrat in voting to convict, the most bipartisan support in any Senate impeachment trial of a president or former president.<sup id="cite_ref-659" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-659">&#91;658&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-660" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-660">&#91;659&#93;</a></sup> Most Republicans voted to acquit Trump, although some held him responsible but felt the Senate did not have jurisdiction over former presidents (Trump had left office on January 20; the Senate voted 56–44 the trial was constitutional);<sup id="cite_ref-661" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-661">&#91;660&#93;</a></sup> included in the latter group was <a href="/wiki/Mitch_McConnell" title="Mitch McConnell">Mitch McConnell</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-662" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-662">&#91;661&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h2><span id="Post-presidency_.282021.E2.80.93present.29"></span><span class="mw-headline" id="Post-presidency_(2021–present)">Post-presidency (2021–present)</span></h2>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1033289096"><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">See also: <a href="/wiki/Legal_affairs_of_Donald_Trump" class="mw-redirect" title="Legal affairs of Donald Trump">Legal affairs of Donald Trump</a></div>
<p>At the end of his term, Trump went to live at his Mar-a-Lago club.<sup id="cite_ref-663" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-663">&#91;662&#93;</a></sup> As provided for by the <a href="/wiki/Former_Presidents_Act#Staff_and_office" title="Former Presidents Act">Former Presidents Act</a>,<sup id="cite_ref-safe_664-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-safe-664">&#91;663&#93;</a></sup> he established an office there to handle his post-presidential activities.<sup id="cite_ref-safe_664-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-safe-664">&#91;663&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-665" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-665">&#91;664&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p><a href="/wiki/Big_lie#Donald_Trump&#39;s_false_claims_of_a_stolen_election" title="Big lie">Trump's false claims</a> concerning the 2020 election were commonly referred to as the "<a href="/wiki/Big_lie" title="Big lie">big lie</a>" in the press and by his critics. In May 2021, Trump and his supporters attempted to co-opt the term, using it to refer to the election itself.<sup id="cite_ref-666" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-666">&#91;665&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-key_667-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-key-667">&#91;666&#93;</a></sup> The Republican Party used Trump's false election narrative to justify the <a href="/wiki/Republican_efforts_to_restrict_voting_following_the_2020_presidential_election" title="Republican efforts to restrict voting following the 2020 presidential election">imposition of new voting restrictions</a> in its favor.<sup id="cite_ref-key_667-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-key-667">&#91;666&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-668" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-668">&#91;667&#93;</a></sup> As late as July 2022, Trump was still pressuring state legislators to overturn the 2020 election by rescinding the state's electoral votes for Biden.<sup id="cite_ref-669" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-669">&#91;668&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>Trump resumed his campaign-style rallies with an 85-minute speech at the annual <a href="/wiki/North_Carolina_Republican_Party" title="North Carolina Republican Party">North Carolina Republican Party</a> convention on June 6, 2021.<sup id="cite_ref-akmh_670-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-akmh-670">&#91;669&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-671" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-671">&#91;670&#93;</a></sup> On June 26, he held his first public rally since the January 6 rally that preceded the <a href="/wiki/January_6_United_States_Capitol_attack" title="January 6 United States Capitol attack">riot at the Capitol</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-672" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-672">&#91;671&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>Unlike other former presidents, Trump continued to dominate his party; he has been compared to a modern-day <a href="/wiki/Party_boss" class="mw-redirect" title="Party boss">party boss</a>. He continued fundraising, raising more than twice as much as the Republican Party itself, hinted at a third candidacy, and profited from fundraisers many Republican candidates held at Mar-a-Lago. Much of his focus was on the people in charge of elections and how elections are run. In the <a href="/wiki/2022_United_States_elections" title="2022 United States elections">2022 midterm elections</a> he endorsed over 200 candidates for various offices, most of whom supported his false claim that the 2020 presidential election was stolen from him.<sup id="cite_ref-nyt1_673-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-nyt1-673">&#91;672&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-nyt2_674-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-nyt2-674">&#91;673&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-lat_675-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-lat-675">&#91;674&#93;</a></sup> A majority of candidates endorsed by him won in Republican primary elections.<sup id="cite_ref-nyt2_674-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-nyt2-674">&#91;673&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>Trump registered a new company in February 2021. <a href="/wiki/Trump_Media_%26_Technology_Group" title="Trump Media &amp; Technology Group">Trump Media &amp; Technology Group</a> (TMTG) was formed for providing "social networking services" to "customers in the United States".<sup id="cite_ref-soc_us_676-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-soc_us-676">&#91;675&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-677" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-677">&#91;676&#93;</a></sup> In October 2021, Trump announced the planned merger of TMTG with Digital World Acquisition,<sup id="cite_ref-spac_678-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-spac-678">&#91;677&#93;</a></sup> a <a href="/wiki/Special-purpose_acquisition_company" title="Special-purpose acquisition company">special-purpose acquisition company</a> (SPAC). A main backer of the SPAC is China-based financier ARC Group, who was reportedly involved in setting up the proposed merger. The transaction is under investigation by the <a href="/wiki/U.S._Securities_and_Exchange_Commission" title="U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission">U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-679" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-679">&#91;678&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-680" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-680">&#91;679&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>In February 2022, TMTG launched <a href="/wiki/Truth_Social" title="Truth Social">Truth Social</a>, a <a href="/wiki/Twitter" title="Twitter">Twitter</a>-like social-media platform.<sup id="cite_ref-681" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-681">&#91;680&#93;</a></sup> As of March 2023, Trump Media, which had taken $8&#160;million from Russia-connected entities, was being investigated by federal prosecutors for possible money laundering.<sup id="cite_ref-682" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-682">&#91;681&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-:11_683-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-:11-683">&#91;682&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h3><span id="Investigations.2C_criminal_charges.2C_civil_lawsuits"></span><span class="mw-headline" id="Investigations,_criminal_charges,_civil_lawsuits">Investigations, criminal charges, civil lawsuits</span></h3>
<p>Trump is the subject of numerous probes into his actions and business dealings before, during and after his presidency.<sup id="cite_ref-684" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-684">&#91;683&#93;</a></sup> In February 2021, the district attorney for <a href="/wiki/Fulton_County,_Georgia" title="Fulton County, Georgia">Fulton County, Georgia</a>, <a href="/wiki/Fani_Willis" title="Fani Willis">Fani Willis</a>, announced a criminal probe into <a href="/wiki/Trump%E2%80%93Raffensperger_phone_call" title="Trump–Raffensperger phone call">Trump's phone calls</a> to Georgia Secretary of State <a href="/wiki/Brad_Raffensperger" title="Brad Raffensperger">Brad Raffensperger</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-685" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-685">&#91;684&#93;</a></sup> The <a href="/wiki/Attorney_General_of_New_York" title="Attorney General of New York">New York State Attorney General's Office</a> is conducting criminal investigations into Trump's business activities in conjunction with the <a href="/wiki/New_York_County_District_Attorney" title="New York County District Attorney">Manhattan District Attorney's Office</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-686" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-686">&#91;685&#93;</a></sup> By May 2021, a special <a href="/wiki/Grand_jury#United_States" title="Grand jury">grand jury</a> was considering indictments.<sup id="cite_ref-687" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-687">&#91;686&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-688" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-688">&#91;687&#93;</a></sup> In July 2021, New York prosecutors charged the Trump Organization with a "15 year 'scheme to defraud' the government".<sup id="cite_ref-689" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-689">&#91;688&#93;</a></sup> In January 2023, the organization's chief financial officer, <a href="/wiki/Allen_Weisselberg" title="Allen Weisselberg">Allen Weisselberg</a>, was sentenced to five months in jail and five years probation for tax fraud after a plea deal.<sup id="cite_ref-690" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-690">&#91;689&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h4><span class="mw-headline" id="FBI_investigations">FBI investigations</span></h4>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1033289096"><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Main articles: <a href="/wiki/FBI_investigation_into_Donald_Trump%27s_handling_of_government_documents" title="FBI investigation into Donald Trump&#39;s handling of government documents">FBI investigation into Donald Trump's handling of government documents</a>, <a href="/wiki/FBI_search_of_Mar-a-Lago" title="FBI search of Mar-a-Lago">FBI search of Mar-a-Lago</a>, and <a href="/wiki/Smith_special_counsel_investigation" title="Smith special counsel investigation">Smith special counsel investigation</a></div>
<figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:Classified_intelligence_material_found_during_search_of_Mar-a-Lago.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/df/Classified_intelligence_material_found_during_search_of_Mar-a-Lago.jpg/220px-Classified_intelligence_material_found_during_search_of_Mar-a-Lago.jpg" decoding="async" width="220" height="146" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/df/Classified_intelligence_material_found_during_search_of_Mar-a-Lago.jpg/330px-Classified_intelligence_material_found_during_search_of_Mar-a-Lago.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/df/Classified_intelligence_material_found_during_search_of_Mar-a-Lago.jpg/440px-Classified_intelligence_material_found_during_search_of_Mar-a-Lago.jpg 2x" data-file-width="3717" data-file-height="2473" /></a><figcaption>Classified intelligence material found during search of Mar-a-Lago</figcaption></figure>
<p>When Trump left the White House in January 2021, he took government documents and material with him to Mar-a-Lago. By May 2021, the <a href="/wiki/National_Archives_and_Records_Administration" title="National Archives and Records Administration">National Archives and Records Administration</a> (NARA), the federal agency that preserves government records, realized that important documents had not been turned over to them at the end of Trump's term and asked his office to locate them. In January 2022, they retrieved 15 boxes of White House records from Mar-a-Lago. NARA later informed the Department of Justice that some of the retrieved documents were classified material.<sup id="cite_ref-cnn-tl_691-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-cnn-tl-691">&#91;690&#93;</a></sup> The Justice Department began an investigation in April 2022 and convened a grand jury.<sup id="cite_ref-692" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-692">&#91;691&#93;</a></sup> The Justice Department sent Trump a subpoena for additional material on May 11.<sup id="cite_ref-cnn-tl_691-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-cnn-tl-691">&#91;690&#93;</a></sup> On June 3, Justice Department officials visited Mar-a-Lago and received some classified documents from Trump's lawyers.<sup id="cite_ref-cnn-tl_691-2" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-cnn-tl-691">&#91;690&#93;</a></sup> One of the lawyers signed a statement affirming that all material marked as classified had been returned to the government.<sup id="cite_ref-693" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-693">&#91;692&#93;</a></sup> Later that month an additional subpoena was sent requesting surveillance footage from Mar-a-Lago, which was provided.<sup id="cite_ref-cnn-tl_691-3" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-cnn-tl-691">&#91;690&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-694" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-694">&#91;693&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-nuclear_695-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-nuclear-695">&#91;694&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>On August 8, 2022, FBI agents searched Trump's residence, office, and storage areas at Mar-a-Lago to recover government documents and material Trump had taken with him when he left office in violation of the <a href="/wiki/Presidential_Records_Act" title="Presidential Records Act">Presidential Records Act</a>,<sup id="cite_ref-bddj0812_696-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-bddj0812-696">&#91;695&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-NYT-20220812_697-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-NYT-20220812-697">&#91;696&#93;</a></sup> reportedly including some related to nuclear weapons.<sup id="cite_ref-nuclear_695-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-nuclear-695">&#91;694&#93;</a></sup> The search warrant, authorized by U.S. Attorney General <a href="/wiki/Merrick_Garland" title="Merrick Garland">Merrick Garland</a> and approved by a federal magistrate judge, and the written inventory of the seized items were made public on August 12. The text of the search warrant indicates an investigation of potential violations of the Espionage Act and obstruction of justice laws.<sup id="cite_ref-698" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-698">&#91;697&#93;</a></sup> The items taken in the search included 11 sets of classified documents, four of them tagged as "top secret" and one as "top secret/SCI", the highest level of classification.<sup id="cite_ref-bddj0812_696-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-bddj0812-696">&#91;695&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-NYT-20220812_697-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-NYT-20220812-697">&#91;696&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>On November 18, 2022, Garland appointed a special counsel, federal prosecutor <a href="/wiki/Jack_Smith_(lawyer)" title="Jack Smith (lawyer)">Jack Smith</a>, to oversee the federal criminal investigations into Trump retaining government property at Mar-a-Lago and <a href="/wiki/United_States_Justice_Department_investigation_into_attempts_to_overturn_the_2020_presidential_election" title="United States Justice Department investigation into attempts to overturn the 2020 presidential election">examining Trump's role in the events leading up to the January 6, 2021, Capitol attack</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-699" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-699">&#91;698&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-700" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-700">&#91;699&#93;</a></sup> 
</p>
<h4><span class="mw-headline" id="Criminal_referral_by_the_House_January_6_Committee">Criminal referral by the House January 6 Committee</span></h4>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1033289096"><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Main article: <a href="/wiki/United_States_House_Select_Committee_on_the_January_6_Attack" title="United States House Select Committee on the January 6 Attack">United States House Select Committee on the January 6 Attack</a></div>
<p>On December 19, 2022, the <a href="/wiki/United_States_House_Select_Committee_on_the_January_6_Attack" title="United States House Select Committee on the January 6 Attack">United States House Select Committee on the January 6 Attack</a> recommended criminal charges against Trump for obstructing an official proceeding, conspiracy to defraud the United States, and inciting or assisting an insurrection.<sup id="cite_ref-701" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-701">&#91;700&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h4><span class="mw-headline" id="Federal_and_state_criminal_cases_against_Trump">Federal and state criminal cases against Trump</span></h4>
<h5><span class="mw-headline" id="New_York_prosecution_for_falsifying_business_records">New York prosecution for falsifying business records</span></h5>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1033289096"><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Main article: <a href="/wiki/Prosecution_of_Donald_Trump_in_New_York" title="Prosecution of Donald Trump in New York">Prosecution of Donald Trump in New York</a></div>
<p>On March 30, 2023, a New York grand jury indicted Trump on 34 felony counts of falsifying business records.<sup id="cite_ref-702" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-702">&#91;701&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-703" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-703">&#91;702&#93;</a></sup> On April 4, he surrendered and was arrested and arraigned; he pleaded not guilty on all counts and was released.<sup id="cite_ref-704" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-704">&#91;703&#93;</a></sup> The trial is scheduled to begin on March 25, 2024.<sup id="cite_ref-slate_705-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-slate-705">&#91;704&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h5><span class="mw-headline" id="Government_and_classified_documents_case">Government and classified documents case</span></h5>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1033289096"><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Main article: <a href="/wiki/Federal_prosecution_of_Donald_Trump_(classified_documents_case)" title="Federal prosecution of Donald Trump (classified documents case)">Federal prosecution of Donald Trump (classified documents case)</a></div>
<p>On June 8, the Justice Department indicted Trump in Miami federal court for 31 counts of "willfully retaining national defense information under the Espionage Act", one count of making false statements, and, jointly with a personal aide, single counts of conspiracy to obstruct justice, withholding government documents, corruptly concealing records, concealing a document in a federal investigation and scheming to conceal their efforts.<sup id="cite_ref-706" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-706">&#91;705&#93;</a></sup> Trump pleaded not guilty to all charges.<sup id="cite_ref-707" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-707">&#91;706&#93;</a></sup> In July a superseding indictment added three additional criminal charges, bringing the number of charges in the case to 40.<sup id="cite_ref-708" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-708">&#91;707&#93;</a></sup> The trial is scheduled to begin on May 20, 2024.<sup id="cite_ref-slate_705-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-slate-705">&#91;704&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h5><span class="mw-headline" id="Election_obstruction_case">Election obstruction case</span></h5>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1033289096"><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Main article: <a href="/wiki/Federal_prosecution_of_Donald_Trump_(election_obstruction_case)" title="Federal prosecution of Donald Trump (election obstruction case)">Federal prosecution of Donald Trump (election obstruction case)</a></div>
<p>On August 1, a Washington, D.C., federal grand jury indicted Trump on four counts for his efforts to overturn the 2020 election results. He was charged with conspiring with unnamed co-conspirators to <a href="/wiki/Conspiracy_against_the_United_States" title="Conspiracy against the United States">defraud the United States</a>, obstruct the certification of the Electoral College vote, and <a href="/wiki/Conspiracy_against_rights" title="Conspiracy against rights">deprive people of the civil right</a> to have their votes counted, as well as obstructing an official proceeding.<sup id="cite_ref-709" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-709">&#91;708&#93;</a></sup> Trump pleaded not guilty to all charges.<sup id="cite_ref-710" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-710">&#91;709&#93;</a></sup> The case is slated to go to trial on March 4, 2024.<sup id="cite_ref-slate_705-2" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-slate-705">&#91;704&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h5><span class="mw-headline" id="Georgia_election_interference_case">Georgia election interference case</span></h5>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1033289096"><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Main article: <a href="/wiki/Georgia_election_racketeering_prosecution" title="Georgia election racketeering prosecution">Georgia election racketeering prosecution</a></div>
<p>On August 14, a <a href="/wiki/Fulton_County,_Georgia" title="Fulton County, Georgia">Fulton County, Georgia</a>, grand jury indicted Trump and 18 allies for racketeering &#8211; among other felonies &#8211; after Trump campaign officials accessed voting machines with election officials.<sup id="cite_ref-711" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-711">&#91;710&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-712" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-712">&#91;711&#93;</a></sup> On August 24, Trump surrendered, was placed under arrest and processed at Fulton County Jail, and released on bail. He posted <a href="/wiki/Mug_shot_of_Donald_Trump" title="Mug shot of Donald Trump">the booking photo</a> on Twitter and on his campaign website with a fundraising pitch.<sup id="cite_ref-713" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-713">&#91;712&#93;</a></sup> On August 31, he pleaded not guilty.<sup id="cite_ref-714" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-714">&#91;713&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h4><span class="mw-headline" id="Civil_lawsuits_against_Trump">Civil lawsuits against Trump</span></h4>
<h5><span class="mw-headline" id="Class_action_lawsuit_for_fraud">Class action lawsuit for fraud</span></h5>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1033289096"><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Main article: <a href="/wiki/Doe_et_al._v._Trump_Corp._et_al." title="Doe et al. v. Trump Corp. et al.">Doe et al. v. Trump Corp. et al.</a></div>
<p>In 2018, four investors filed a federal <a href="/wiki/Class_action#United_States_2" title="Class action">class action lawsuit</a> against Trump, the Trump Organization, and his three eldest children for not disclosing that they were paid by <a href="/wiki/ACN,_Inc." class="mw-redirect" title="ACN, Inc.">ACN, Inc.</a>, when they recommended the company as a sound investment on <i>The Apprentice</i>.<sup id="cite_ref-715" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-715">&#91;714&#93;</a></sup> In July 2019, a  district judge permitted the lawsuit to proceed with state-level claims of fraud, false advertising, and unfair competition.<sup id="cite_ref-716" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-716">&#91;715&#93;</a></sup> The case is slated to go to trial on January 29, 2024.<sup id="cite_ref-717" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-717">&#91;716&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h5><span id="New_York_State.27s_civil_fraud_case"></span><span class="mw-headline" id="New_York_State's_civil_fraud_case">New York State's civil fraud case</span></h5>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1033289096"><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Main article: <a href="/wiki/New_York_civil_investigation_of_The_Trump_Organization" title="New York civil investigation of The Trump Organization">New York civil investigation of The Trump Organization</a></div>
<p>In September 2022, the New York State Attorney General filed a civil fraud case against Trump, his three oldest children, and the Trump Organization.<sup id="cite_ref-718" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-718">&#91;717&#93;</a></sup> In December 2021, the Attorney General's office had subpoenaed Trump to produce documents related to his business.<sup id="cite_ref-719" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-719">&#91;718&#93;</a></sup> In April 2022, a New York state judge held Trump in contempt of court for failing to comply with the subpoena and imposed a fine of $10,000 per day until he does.<sup id="cite_ref-720" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-720">&#91;719&#93;</a></sup> Trump was deposed in August and invoked his <a href="/wiki/Self-incrimination_clause" class="mw-redirect" title="Self-incrimination clause">Fifth Amendment right against self-incrimination</a> more than 400 times.<sup id="cite_ref-721" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-721">&#91;720&#93;</a></sup> The trial is slated to begin on October 2, 2023.<sup id="cite_ref-722" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-722">&#91;721&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h5><span id="E._Jean_Carroll.27s_lawsuits"></span><span class="mw-headline" id="E._Jean_Carroll's_lawsuits">E. Jean Carroll's lawsuits</span></h5>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1033289096"><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Main article: <a href="/wiki/E._Jean_Carroll_v._Donald_J._Trump" title="E. Jean Carroll v. Donald J. Trump">E. Jean Carroll v. Donald J. Trump</a></div>
<p>In May 2023, a New York jury in a federal lawsuit brought by journalist <a href="/wiki/E._Jean_Carroll" title="E. Jean Carroll">E. Jean Carroll</a> found Trump liable for sexual abuse and defamation and ordered him to pay her $5&#160;million.<sup id="cite_ref-723" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-723">&#91;722&#93;</a></sup> Trump asked the district court for a new trial or a reduction of the damage award, arguing that the jury had not found him liable for rape, and also, in a separate lawsuit, countersued Carroll for defamation. The judge for the two lawsuits ruled against Trump in July and August.<sup id="cite_ref-bid_724-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-bid-724">&#91;723&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-725" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-725">&#91;724&#93;</a></sup> Trump appealed both decisions to an appeals court.<sup id="cite_ref-bid_724-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-bid-724">&#91;723&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-726" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-726">&#91;725&#93;</a></sup> The trial in the defamation case is scheduled to begin on January 15, 2024.<sup id="cite_ref-slate_705-3" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-slate-705">&#91;704&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h3><span class="mw-headline" id="2024_presidential_campaign">2024 presidential campaign</span></h3>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1033289096"><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Main article: <a href="/wiki/Donald_Trump_2024_presidential_campaign" title="Donald Trump 2024 presidential campaign">Donald Trump 2024 presidential campaign</a></div>
<p>On November 15, 2022, Trump announced his candidacy for the <a href="/wiki/2024_United_States_presidential_election" title="2024 United States presidential election">2024 United States presidential election</a> and set up a fundraising account.<sup id="cite_ref-727" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-727">&#91;726&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-728" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-728">&#91;727&#93;</a></sup> In March 2023, the campaign began diverting 10 percent of the donations to Trump's <a href="/wiki/Political_action_committee#Leadership_PACs" title="Political action committee">leadership PAC</a> which had paid $16&#160;million for his legal bills by June 2023.<sup id="cite_ref-729" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-729">&#91;728&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h2><span class="mw-headline" id="Public_image">Public image</span></h2>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1033289096"><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Main article: <a href="/wiki/Public_image_of_Donald_Trump" title="Public image of Donald Trump">Public image of Donald Trump</a></div>
<h3><span class="mw-headline" id="Approval_ratings_and_scholar_surveys">Approval ratings and scholar surveys</span></h3>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1033289096"><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Further information: <a href="/wiki/Opinion_polling_on_the_Donald_Trump_administration" title="Opinion polling on the Donald Trump administration">Opinion polling on the Donald Trump administration</a> and <a href="/wiki/Historical_rankings_of_presidents_of_the_United_States" title="Historical rankings of presidents of the United States">Historical rankings of presidents of the United States</a></div>
<p>Trump was the only president to never reach a 50 percent approval rating in the Gallup poll dating to 1938. His approval ratings showed a record-high partisan gap: 88 percent among Republicans and 7 percent among Democrats.<sup id="cite_ref-Jones_730-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Jones-730">&#91;729&#93;</a></sup> Until September 2020, the ratings were unusually stable, reaching a high of 49 percent and a low of 35 percent.<sup id="cite_ref-731" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-731">&#91;730&#93;</a></sup> Trump finished his term with an approval rating between 29 percent and 34 percent—the lowest of any president since modern <a href="/wiki/Opinion_poll" title="Opinion poll">polling</a> began—and a record-low average of 41 percent throughout his presidency.<sup id="cite_ref-Jones_730-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Jones-730">&#91;729&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-732" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-732">&#91;731&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>In <a href="/wiki/Gallup%27s_most_admired_man_and_woman_poll" title="Gallup&#39;s most admired man and woman poll">Gallup's annual poll</a> asking Americans to name the man they admire the most, Trump placed second to Obama in 2017 and 2018, tied with Obama for most admired man in 2019, and was named most admired in 2020.<sup id="cite_ref-733" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-733">&#91;732&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-734" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-734">&#91;733&#93;</a></sup> Since <a href="/wiki/Gallup_(company)" class="mw-redirect" title="Gallup (company)">Gallup</a> started conducting the poll in 1948, Trump is the first elected president not to be named most admired in his first year in office.<sup id="cite_ref-735" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-735">&#91;734&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>A Gallup poll in 134 countries comparing the approval ratings of U.S. leadership between the years 2016 and 2017 found that Trump led Obama in job approval in only 29 countries, most of them non-democracies;<sup id="cite_ref-736" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-736">&#91;735&#93;</a></sup> approval of U.S. leadership plummeted among allies and G7 countries. Overall ratings were similar to those in the last two years of the <a href="/wiki/Presidency_of_George_W._Bush" title="Presidency of George W. Bush">George W. Bush presidency</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-737" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-737">&#91;736&#93;</a></sup> By mid-2020, only 16 percent of international respondents to a 13-nation <a href="/wiki/Pew_Research" class="mw-redirect" title="Pew Research">Pew Research</a> poll expressed confidence in Trump, a lower score than those historically accorded to Russia's Vladimir Putin and China's Xi Jinping.<sup id="cite_ref-738" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-738">&#91;737&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p><a href="/wiki/C-SPAN" title="C-SPAN">C-SPAN</a>, which has surveyed presidential historians on presidential leadership each time the administration changed since 2000,<sup id="cite_ref-739" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-739">&#91;738&#93;</a></sup> ranked Trump fourth–lowest overall in their <a href="/wiki/Historical_rankings_of_presidents_of_the_United_States#2021_C-SPAN_Presidential_Historians_Survey" title="Historical rankings of presidents of the United States">Presidential Historians Survey 2021</a>, with Trump rated lowest in the leadership characteristics categories for moral authority and administrative skills.<sup id="cite_ref-:1_2-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-:1-2">&#91;1&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-740" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-740">&#91;739&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-741" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-741">&#91;740&#93;</a></sup> The <a href="/wiki/Siena_College_Research_Institute" title="Siena College Research Institute">Siena College Research Institute</a> (SCRI) has surveyed presidential scholars during the second year of the first term of each president since 1982. In their 2022 survey, <a href="/wiki/Historical_rankings_of_presidents_of_the_United_States#Siena_College_Research_Institute,_Presidential_Expert_Poll_of_2022" title="Historical rankings of presidents of the United States">SCRI ranked Trump</a> 43rd out of 45 presidents. He was ranked last on background, integrity, intelligence, foreign policy accomplishments, and executive appointments, and second to last on ability to compromise, executive ability, and present overall view. He was ranked near the bottom in all categories except for luck, willingness to take risks, and party leadership.<sup id="cite_ref-scri_22_3-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-scri_22-3">&#91;2&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h3><span class="mw-headline" id="Social_media">Social media</span></h3>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1033289096"><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Main article: <a href="/wiki/Social_media_use_by_Donald_Trump" title="Social media use by Donald Trump">Social media use by Donald Trump</a></div>
<p>Trump's social media presence attracted worldwide attention after he joined <a href="/wiki/Twitter" title="Twitter">Twitter</a> in 2009. He tweeted frequently during the 2016 election campaign and as president until Twitter banned him in the final days of his term.<sup id="cite_ref-742" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-742">&#91;741&#93;</a></sup> Trump often used Twitter as a direct means of communication with the public and sidelining of the press.<sup id="cite_ref-gone_743-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-gone-743">&#91;742&#93;</a></sup> In June 2017, a White House press secretary said that Trump's tweets were official presidential statements.<sup id="cite_ref-744" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-744">&#91;743&#93;</a></sup> Trump often announced terminations of administration officials over Twitter.<sup id="cite_ref-745" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-745">&#91;744&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>After years of criticism for allowing Trump to post misinformation and falsehoods, Twitter began to tag some of his tweets with fact-checking warnings in May 2020.<sup id="cite_ref-746" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-746">&#91;745&#93;</a></sup> In response, Trump tweeted that "Social Media Platforms totally silence conservative[] voices" and that he would "strongly regulate[] or close them down".<sup id="cite_ref-747" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-747">&#91;746&#93;</a></sup> In the days after the storming of the United States Capitol, Trump was banned from <a href="/wiki/Facebook" title="Facebook">Facebook</a>, <a href="/wiki/Instagram" title="Instagram">Instagram</a>, Twitter and other platforms.<sup id="cite_ref-748" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-748">&#91;747&#93;</a></sup> The loss of Trump's social media presence diminished his ability to shape events<sup id="cite_ref-749" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-749">&#91;748&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-750" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-750">&#91;749&#93;</a></sup> and prompted a dramatic decrease in the volume of misinformation shared on Twitter.<sup id="cite_ref-751" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-751">&#91;750&#93;</a></sup> Trump's early attempts to re-establish a social media presence were unsuccessful.<sup id="cite_ref-752" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-752">&#91;751&#93;</a></sup> In February 2022, he launched social media platform <a href="/wiki/Truth_Social" title="Truth Social">Truth Social</a> where he only attracted a fraction of his Twitter following.<sup id="cite_ref-753" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-753">&#91;752&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p><a href="/wiki/Elon_Musk" title="Elon Musk">Elon Musk</a>, the new owner of Twitter, reinstated Trump's Twitter account in November 2022.<sup id="cite_ref-754" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-754">&#91;753&#93;</a></sup> Trump did not use the reinstated account until August 25, 2023, when he posted his mug shot.<sup id="cite_ref-755" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-755">&#91;754&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h3><span class="mw-headline" id="Relationship_with_the_press">Relationship with the press</span></h3>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1033289096"><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Further information: <a href="/wiki/Presidency_of_Donald_Trump#Relationship_with_the_news_media" title="Presidency of Donald Trump">Presidency of Donald Trump §&#160;Relationship with the news media</a></div>
<figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:President_Trump%27s_First_100_Days-_45_(33573172373).jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img alt="Trump, seated at the Resolute Desk in the White House, speaking to a crowd of reporters with boom microphones in front of him and public officials behind him" src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/04/President_Trump%27s_First_100_Days-_45_%2833573172373%29.jpg/220px-President_Trump%27s_First_100_Days-_45_%2833573172373%29.jpg" decoding="async" width="220" height="147" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/04/President_Trump%27s_First_100_Days-_45_%2833573172373%29.jpg/330px-President_Trump%27s_First_100_Days-_45_%2833573172373%29.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/04/President_Trump%27s_First_100_Days-_45_%2833573172373%29.jpg/440px-President_Trump%27s_First_100_Days-_45_%2833573172373%29.jpg 2x" data-file-width="1200" data-file-height="800" /></a><figcaption>Trump talking to the press, March 2017</figcaption></figure>
<p>Trump sought media attention throughout his career, sustaining a "love–hate" relationship with the press.<sup id="cite_ref-756" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-756">&#91;755&#93;</a></sup> In the 2016 campaign, Trump benefited from a record amount of free media coverage, elevating his standing in the Republican primaries.<sup id="cite_ref-Cillizza-160614_155-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Cillizza-160614-155">&#91;154&#93;</a></sup> <i>The New York Times</i> writer <a href="/wiki/Amy_Chozick" title="Amy Chozick">Amy Chozick</a> wrote in 2018 that Trump's media dominance enthralled the public and created "must-see TV."<sup id="cite_ref-757" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-757">&#91;756&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>As a candidate and as president, Trump frequently accused the press of bias, calling it the "fake news media" and "the <a href="/wiki/Enemy_of_the_people" title="Enemy of the people">enemy of the people</a>".<sup id="cite_ref-758" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-758">&#91;757&#93;</a></sup> In 2018, journalist <a href="/wiki/Lesley_Stahl" title="Lesley Stahl">Lesley Stahl</a> recounted Trump's saying he intentionally demeaned and discredited the media "so when you write negative stories about me no one will believe you".<sup id="cite_ref-759" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-759">&#91;758&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>As president, Trump privately and publicly mused about revoking the press credentials of journalists he viewed as critical.<sup id="cite_ref-760" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-760">&#91;759&#93;</a></sup> His administration moved to revoke the press passes of two White House reporters, which were restored by the courts.<sup id="cite_ref-auto2_761-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-auto2-761">&#91;760&#93;</a></sup> In 2019, a member of the foreign press reported many of the same concerns as those of media in the U.S., expressing concern that a normalization process by reporters and media results in an inaccurate characterization of Trump.<sup id="cite_ref-762" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-762">&#91;761&#93;</a></sup> The Trump White House held about a hundred formal press briefings in 2017, declining by half during 2018 and to two in 2019.<sup id="cite_ref-auto2_761-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-auto2-761">&#91;760&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>Trump also deployed the legal system to intimidate the press.<sup id="cite_ref-Atlantic_Press_763-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Atlantic_Press-763">&#91;762&#93;</a></sup> In early 2020, the Trump campaign sued <i>The New York Times</i>, <i>The Washington Post</i>, and CNN for defamation in opinion pieces about Russian election interference.<sup id="cite_ref-764" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-764">&#91;763&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-765" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-765">&#91;764&#93;</a></sup> Legal experts said that the lawsuits lacked merit and were not likely to succeed.<sup id="cite_ref-Atlantic_Press_763-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Atlantic_Press-763">&#91;762&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-766" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-766">&#91;765&#93;</a></sup> By March 2021, the lawsuits against <i>The New York Times</i> and CNN had been dismissed.<sup id="cite_ref-767" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-767">&#91;766&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-768" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-768">&#91;767&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h3><span class="mw-headline" id="False_or_misleading_statements">False or misleading statements</span></h3>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1033289096"><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">See also: <a href="/wiki/False_or_misleading_statements_by_Donald_Trump" title="False or misleading statements by Donald Trump">False or misleading statements by Donald Trump</a> and <a href="/wiki/Big_lie#Donald_Trump&#39;s_false_claims_of_a_stolen_election" title="Big lie">Big lie §&#160;Donald Trump's false claims of a stolen election</a></div>
<figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:2017-_Donald_Trump_veracity_-_composite_graph.png" class="mw-file-description"><img alt="Chart depicting false or misleading claims made by Trump" src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/04/2017-_Donald_Trump_veracity_-_composite_graph.png/330px-2017-_Donald_Trump_veracity_-_composite_graph.png" decoding="async" width="330" height="208" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/04/2017-_Donald_Trump_veracity_-_composite_graph.png/495px-2017-_Donald_Trump_veracity_-_composite_graph.png 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/04/2017-_Donald_Trump_veracity_-_composite_graph.png/660px-2017-_Donald_Trump_veracity_-_composite_graph.png 2x" data-file-width="2775" data-file-height="1750" /></a><figcaption><a href="/wiki/Fact-checkers" class="mw-redirect" title="Fact-checkers">Fact-checkers</a> from <i>The Washington Post</i>,<sup id="cite_ref-database_769-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-database-769">&#91;768&#93;</a></sup> the <i>Toronto Star</i>,<sup id="cite_ref-770" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-770">&#91;769&#93;</a></sup> and CNN<sup id="cite_ref-771" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-771">&#91;770&#93;</a></sup> compiled data on "false or misleading claims" (orange background), and "false claims" (violet foreground), respectively.</figcaption></figure>
