<p>As a candidate and as president, Trump frequently made false statements in public speeches and remarks<sup id="cite_ref-finnegan_162-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-finnegan-162">&#91;161&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-whoppers_158-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-whoppers-158">&#91;157&#93;</a></sup> to an extent unprecedented in <a href="/wiki/American_politics" class="mw-redirect" title="American politics">American politics</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-Glasser-180803_772-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Glasser-180803-772">&#91;771&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-Konnikova_773-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Konnikova-773">&#91;772&#93;</a></sup> His falsehoods became a distinctive part of his political identity.<sup id="cite_ref-Glasser-180803_772-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Glasser-180803-772">&#91;771&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>Trump's false and misleading statements were documented by <a href="/wiki/Fact-checker" class="mw-redirect" title="Fact-checker">fact-checkers</a>, including at <i>The Washington Post</i>, which tallied a total of 30,573 false or misleading statements made by Trump over his four-year term.<sup id="cite_ref-database_769-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-database-769">&#91;768&#93;</a></sup> Trump's falsehoods increased in frequency over time, rising from about six false or misleading claims per day in his first year as president to 16 per day in his second year, 22 per day in his third year, and 39 per day in his final year.<sup id="cite_ref-TermUntruth_774-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-TermUntruth-774">&#91;773&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>Some of Trump's falsehoods were inconsequential, such as his claim of the "biggest inaugural crowd ever".<sup id="cite_ref-775" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-775">&#91;774&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-776" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-776">&#91;775&#93;</a></sup> Others had more far-reaching effects, such as his promotion of unproven antimalarial drugs as a treatment for COVID-19 in a press conference and on Twitter.<sup id="cite_ref-777" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-777">&#91;776&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-778" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-778">&#91;777&#93;</a></sup> The claims had consequences worldwide, such as a shortage of these drugs in the United States and <a href="/wiki/Panic-buying" class="mw-redirect" title="Panic-buying">panic-buying</a> in Africa and South Asia.<sup id="cite_ref-779" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-779">&#91;778&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-780" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-780">&#91;779&#93;</a></sup> Other misinformation, such as misattributing a rise in crime in <a href="/wiki/England_and_Wales" title="England and Wales">England and Wales</a> to the "spread of radical Islamic terror", served Trump's domestic political purposes.<sup id="cite_ref-781" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-781">&#91;780&#93;</a></sup> As a matter of principle, Trump does not apologize for his falsehoods.<sup id="cite_ref-782" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-782">&#91;781&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>Despite the frequency of Trump's falsehoods, the media rarely referred to them as lies.<sup id="cite_ref-783" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-783">&#91;782&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-DBauder_784-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-DBauder-784">&#91;783&#93;</a></sup> The first time <i>The Washington Post</i> did so was in August 2018, when it declared that some of Trump's misstatements, in particular those concerning hush money paid to Stormy Daniels and <i>Playboy</i> model Karen McDougal, were lies.<sup id="cite_ref-785" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-785">&#91;784&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-DBauder_784-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-DBauder-784">&#91;783&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>In 2020, Trump was a significant source of disinformation on mail-in voting and misinformation on the COVID-19 pandemic.<sup id="cite_ref-USAT-Disinfo_786-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-USAT-Disinfo-786">&#91;785&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-787" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-787">&#91;786&#93;</a></sup> His attacks on mail-in ballots and other election practices served to weaken public faith in the integrity of the 2020 presidential election,<sup id="cite_ref-788" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-788">&#91;787&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-789" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-789">&#91;788&#93;</a></sup> while his disinformation about the pandemic delayed and weakened the national response to it.<sup id="cite_ref-NYT_4_11_20_454-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-NYT_4_11_20-454">&#91;453&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-USAT-Disinfo_786-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-USAT-Disinfo-786">&#91;785&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>James Pfiffner, professor of policy and government at George Mason University, wrote in 2019 that Trump lies differently from previous presidents, because he offers "egregious false statements that are demonstrably contrary to well-known facts"; these lies are the "most important" of all Trump lies. By calling facts into question, people will be unable to properly evaluate their government, with beliefs or policy irrationally settled by "political power"; this erodes <a href="/wiki/Liberal_democracy" title="Liberal democracy">liberal democracy</a>, wrote Pfiffner.<sup id="cite_ref-790" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-790">&#91;789&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h3><span class="mw-headline" id="Promotion_of_conspiracy_theories">Promotion of conspiracy theories</span></h3>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1033289096"><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Main article: <a href="/wiki/List_of_conspiracy_theories_promoted_by_Donald_Trump" title="List of conspiracy theories promoted by Donald Trump">List of conspiracy theories promoted by Donald Trump</a></div>
<p>Before and throughout his presidency, Trump has promoted numerous conspiracy theories, including <a href="/wiki/Barack_Obama_citizenship_conspiracy_theories" title="Barack Obama citizenship conspiracy theories">Obama birtherism</a>, the <a href="/wiki/Clinton_body_count_conspiracy_theory" title="Clinton body count conspiracy theory">Clinton body count conspiracy theory</a>, <a href="/wiki/QAnon" title="QAnon">QAnon</a>, the <a href="/wiki/Global_warming_conspiracy_theory" class="mw-redirect" title="Global warming conspiracy theory">Global warming hoax</a> theory, <a href="/wiki/Trump_Tower_wiretapping_allegations" title="Trump Tower wiretapping allegations">Trump Tower wiretapping allegations</a>, a <a href="/wiki/John_F._Kennedy_assassination_conspiracy_theories" title="John F. Kennedy assassination conspiracy theories">John F. Kennedy assassination conspiracy theory</a> involving <a href="/wiki/Rafael_Cruz" title="Rafael Cruz">Rafael Cruz</a>, linking talk show host <a href="/wiki/Joe_Scarborough" title="Joe Scarborough">Joe Scarborough</a> to the death of a staffer,<sup id="cite_ref-791" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-791">&#91;790&#93;</a></sup> alleged foul-play in the death of Justice <a href="/wiki/Antonin_Scalia" title="Antonin Scalia">Antonin Scalia</a>, <a href="/wiki/Conspiracy_theories_related_to_the_Trump%E2%80%93Ukraine_scandal" title="Conspiracy theories related to the Trump–Ukraine scandal">alleged Ukrainian interference in U.S. elections</a>, and that <a href="/wiki/Osama_bin_Laden_death_conspiracy_theories" title="Osama bin Laden death conspiracy theories">Osama bin Laden was alive</a> and Obama and Biden had members of <a href="/wiki/Navy_SEAL_Team_6" class="mw-redirect" title="Navy SEAL Team 6">Navy SEAL Team 6</a> killed.<sup id="cite_ref-792" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-792">&#91;791&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-793" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-793">&#91;792&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-:0_794-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-:0-794">&#91;793&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-795" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-795">&#91;794&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-796" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-796">&#91;795&#93;</a></sup> In at least two instances, Trump clarified to press that he also believed the conspiracy theory in question.<sup id="cite_ref-:0_794-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-:0-794">&#91;793&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>During and since the 2020 presidential election, Trump has promoted various conspiracy theories for his defeat including dead people voting,<sup id="cite_ref-797" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-797">&#91;796&#93;</a></sup> voting machines changing or deleting Trump votes, fraudulent mail-in voting, throwing out Trump votes, and "finding" suitcases full of Biden votes.<sup id="cite_ref-798" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-798">&#91;797&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-799" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-799">&#91;798&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h3><span class="mw-headline" id="Racial_views">Racial views</span></h3>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1033289096"><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Main article: <a href="/wiki/Racial_views_of_Donald_Trump" title="Racial views of Donald Trump">Racial views of Donald Trump</a></div>
<p>Many of Trump's comments and actions have been considered racist.<sup id="cite_ref-800" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-800">&#91;799&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-801" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-801">&#91;800&#93;</a></sup> In national polling, about half of respondents said that Trump is racist; a greater proportion believed that he emboldened racists.<sup id="cite_ref-802" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-802">&#91;801&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-803" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-803">&#91;802&#93;</a></sup> Several studies and surveys found that racist attitudes fueled Trump's political ascent and were more important than economic factors in determining the allegiance of Trump voters.<sup id="cite_ref-804" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-804">&#91;803&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-805" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-805">&#91;804&#93;</a></sup> Racist and <a href="/wiki/Islamophobic" class="mw-redirect" title="Islamophobic">Islamophobic</a> attitudes are a powerful indicator of support for Trump.<sup id="cite_ref-806" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-806">&#91;805&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>In 1975, he settled a 1973 Department of Justice lawsuit that alleged <a href="/wiki/Housing_discrimination" title="Housing discrimination">housing discrimination</a> against black renters.<sup id="cite_ref-Mahler_50-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Mahler-50">&#91;49&#93;</a></sup> He has also been accused of racism for insisting a group of black and Latino teenagers were guilty of raping a white woman in the 1989 <a href="/wiki/Central_Park_jogger_case" title="Central Park jogger case">Central Park jogger case</a>, even after they were exonerated by DNA evidence in 2002. As of 2019, he maintained this position.<sup id="cite_ref-807" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-807">&#91;806&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>In 2011, when he was reportedly considering a presidential run, he became the leading proponent of the racist <a href="/wiki/Barack_Obama_citizenship_conspiracy_theories" title="Barack Obama citizenship conspiracy theories">"birther" conspiracy theory</a>, alleging that Barack Obama, the first black U.S. president, was not born in the United States.<sup id="cite_ref-808" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-808">&#91;807&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-809" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-809">&#91;808&#93;</a></sup> In April, he claimed credit for pressuring the White House to publish the "long-form" birth certificate, which he considered fraudulent, and later said this made him "very popular".<sup id="cite_ref-810" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-810">&#91;809&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-811" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-811">&#91;810&#93;</a></sup> In September 2016, amid pressure, he acknowledged that Obama was born in the U.S.<sup id="cite_ref-812" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-812">&#91;811&#93;</a></sup> In 2017, he reportedly expressed birther views in private.<sup id="cite_ref-813" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-813">&#91;812&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>According to an analysis in <i><a href="/wiki/Political_Science_Quarterly" title="Political Science Quarterly">Political Science Quarterly</a></i>, Trump made "explicitly racist appeals to whites" during his 2016 presidential campaign.<sup id="cite_ref-814" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-814">&#91;813&#93;</a></sup> In particular, his campaign launch speech drew widespread criticism for claiming Mexican immigrants were "bringing drugs, they're bringing crime, they're rapists".<sup id="cite_ref-815" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-815">&#91;814&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-816" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-816">&#91;815&#93;</a></sup> His later comments about a Mexican-American judge presiding over a civil suit regarding <a href="/wiki/Trump_University" title="Trump University">Trump University</a> were also criticized as racist.<sup id="cite_ref-817" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-817">&#91;816&#93;</a></sup>
</p>

<p>Trump's comments on the <a href="/wiki/Unite_the_Right_rally" title="Unite the Right rally">2017 far-right rally in Charlottesville, Virginia</a>, condemning "this egregious display of hatred, bigotry and violence on many sides" and stating that there were "very fine people on both sides", were widely criticized as implying a <a href="/wiki/Moral_equivalence" title="Moral equivalence">moral equivalence</a> between the white supremacist demonstrators and the counter-protesters.<sup id="cite_ref-818" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-818">&#91;817&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-819" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-819">&#91;818&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-820" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-820">&#91;819&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-KruzelCharlottesville_821-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-KruzelCharlottesville-821">&#91;820&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>In a January 2018 <a href="/wiki/Oval_Office" title="Oval Office">Oval Office</a> meeting to discuss immigration legislation, Trump reportedly referred to El Salvador, Haiti, Honduras, and African nations as "shithole countries".<sup id="cite_ref-822" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-822">&#91;821&#93;</a></sup> His remarks were condemned as racist.<sup id="cite_ref-Weaver-2018_823-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Weaver-2018-823">&#91;822&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-824" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-824">&#91;823&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>In July 2019, Trump tweeted that four Democratic congresswomen—all from minorities, three of whom are native-born Americans—should "<a href="/wiki/Go_back_where_you_came_from" class="mw-redirect" title="Go back where you came from">go back</a>" to the countries they "came from".<sup id="cite_ref-825" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-825">&#91;824&#93;</a></sup> Two days later the House of Representatives voted 240–187, mostly along party lines, to condemn his "racist comments".<sup id="cite_ref-826" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-826">&#91;825&#93;</a></sup> <a href="/wiki/White_nationalist" class="mw-redirect" title="White nationalist">White nationalist</a> publications and social media sites praised his remarks, which continued over the following days.<sup id="cite_ref-827" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-827">&#91;826&#93;</a></sup> Trump continued to make similar remarks during his 2020 campaign.<sup id="cite_ref-828" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-828">&#91;827&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h3><span class="mw-headline" id="Misogyny_and_allegations_of_sexual_misconduct">Misogyny and allegations of sexual misconduct</span></h3>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1033289096"><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Main article: <a href="/wiki/Donald_Trump_sexual_misconduct_allegations" title="Donald Trump sexual misconduct allegations">Donald Trump sexual misconduct allegations</a></div>
<p>Trump has a history of insulting and belittling women when speaking to media and on social media.<sup id="cite_ref-829" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-829">&#91;828&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-demeans_830-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-demeans-830">&#91;829&#93;</a></sup> He made lewd comments, demeaned women's looks, and called them names, such as "dog", "crazed", "crying lowlife", "face of a pig", or "horseface".<sup id="cite_ref-demeans_830-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-demeans-830">&#91;829&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-831" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-831">&#91;830&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-832" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-832">&#91;831&#93;</a></sup> 
</p><p>At least 26 women publicly accused Trump of rape, kissing, and groping without consent; looking under women's skirts; and walking in on naked teenage pageant contestants.<sup id="cite_ref-833" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-833">&#91;832&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-834" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-834">&#91;833&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-no26_835-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-no26-835">&#91;834&#93;</a></sup> Trump has denied all of the allegations.<sup id="cite_ref-no26_835-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-no26-835">&#91;834&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>In October 2016, two days before the <a href="/wiki/2016_United_States_presidential_debates#Second_presidential_debate_(Washington_University_in_St._Louis)" title="2016 United States presidential debates">second presidential debate</a>, a 2005 "<a href="/wiki/Hot_mic" title="Hot mic">hot mic</a>" recording surfaced in which <a href="/wiki/Donald_Trump_Access_Hollywood_tape" title="Donald Trump Access Hollywood tape">Trump was heard bragging</a> about kissing and groping women without their consent, saying that "when you're a star, they let you do it. You can do anything. ... Grab 'em by the <a href="/wiki/Pussy#Female_genitalia" title="Pussy">pussy</a>."<sup id="cite_ref-836" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-836">&#91;835&#93;</a></sup> The incident's widespread media exposure led to Trump's first public apology during the campaign<sup id="cite_ref-837" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-837">&#91;836&#93;</a></sup> and caused outrage across the political spectrum.<sup id="cite_ref-838" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-838">&#91;837&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h3><span class="mw-headline" id="Incitement_of_violence">Incitement of violence</span></h3>
<p>Research suggests Trump's rhetoric caused an increased incidence of hate crimes.<sup id="cite_ref-839" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-839">&#91;838&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-840" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-840">&#91;839&#93;</a></sup> During his 2016 campaign, he urged or praised physical attacks against protesters or reporters.<sup id="cite_ref-841" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-841">&#91;840&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-842" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-842">&#91;841&#93;</a></sup> Numerous defendants investigated or prosecuted for violent acts and hate crimes, including participants of the January 6, 2021, storming of the U.S. Capitol, cited Trump's rhetoric in arguing that they were not culpable or should receive a lighter sentence.<sup id="cite_ref-843" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-843">&#91;842&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-844" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-844">&#91;843&#93;</a></sup> A nationwide review by ABC News in May 2020 identified at least 54 criminal cases from August 2015 to April 2020 in which Trump was invoked in direct connection with violence or threats of violence mostly by white men and primarily against members of minority groups.<sup id="cite_ref-845" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-845">&#91;844&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h3><span class="mw-headline" id="Popular_culture">Popular culture</span></h3>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1033289096"><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Main articles: <a href="/wiki/Donald_Trump_in_popular_culture" title="Donald Trump in popular culture">Donald Trump in popular culture</a> and <a href="/wiki/Donald_Trump_in_music" title="Donald Trump in music">Donald Trump in music</a></div>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1033289096"><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">See also: <a href="/wiki/Musicians_who_oppose_Donald_Trump%27s_use_of_their_music" title="Musicians who oppose Donald Trump&#39;s use of their music">Musicians who oppose Donald Trump's use of their music</a></div>
<p>Trump has been the subject of parody, comedy, and caricature on television, in films, and in comics. He has been named in hundreds of <a href="/wiki/Hip_hop_music" title="Hip hop music">hip hop</a> songs since the 1980s—until 2015, most of these references cast Trump in a positive light, but they turned largely negative after he began running for office.<sup id="cite_ref-846" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-846">&#91;845&#93;</a></sup>
</p>

Each state names a number of electors equal to its representation in <a href="/wiki/United_States_Congress" title="United States Congress">Congress</a> and (in most states) all electors vote for the winner of their state's popular vote.</span>
